question.html:
Question 15
?

Evaluate the integral of the function f(x,y)=xy3 along the polar curve r=2 for 0≤θ≤π6.

a
45
b
1625
c
34
d
74
e
423
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

∫Cf(x,y)ds=∫θ1θ2f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

x=rcos⁡θ=2cos⁡θ,y=rsin⁡θ=2sin⁡θ.

So, along our curve, we have x=3cos⁡θ and y=3sin⁡θ, where 0≤θ≤π6.

Now, since f(x,y)=xy3, we obtain

f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)=2cos⁡θ⋅(2sin⁡θ)3=42sin3/2⁡θcos⁡θ.

Next, we have

drdθ=ddθ(2)=0,

and therefore

r2+(drdθ)2dθ=22+02=2.

We can now write the integral as

∫Cxy3ds=∫0π/6f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r2+(drdθ)2dθ=∫0π/642sin3/2⁡θcos⁡θ⋅2⋅dθ=82∫0π/6sin3/2⁡θcos⁡θdθ.

We can solve this using the substitution u=sin⁡θ, du=cos⁡θdθ as follows:

82∫0π/6sin3/2⁡θcos⁡θdθ=82∫01/2u3/2du=82⋅25u5/2|01/2=1625((12)5/2−05/2)=1625⋅125=1625⋅142=45
question.knowledge_point: Finding the Line Integral of a Scalar Function Along a Curve Using Substitution

solution.reasoning: Along r=2, x=2\cos\theta, y=2\sin\theta, and ds=2\,d\theta. Since dy=2\cos\theta\,d\theta, x\,ds=2\,dy. Also y increases from 0 to 1, so the integral is 2\int_0^1 y^{3/2}\,dy=2[(2/5)y^{5/2}]_0^1=4/5, option a. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes the current key.

feedback.name: Question 15
feedback.problem: Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y)=x\sqrt{{y}^{3}}$ along the polar curve $r=2$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{6}.$
feedback.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{6}.$

Now, since $f(x,y)=x\sqrt{{y}^{3}}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot \sqrt{(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{3}} \\  & =4\sqrt{2}{sin}^{3/2}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(2)=0,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x\sqrt{{y}^{3}}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}4\sqrt{2}{sin}^{3/2}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot 2\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & =8\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}{sin}^{3/2}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ $\text{d}u=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta $ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}8\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}{sin}^{3/2}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  & =8\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{1/2}{u}^{3/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =8\sqrt{2}\cdot \frac{2}{5}{u}^{5/2}{|}_{0}^{1/2} \\  & =\frac{16\sqrt{2}}{5}({(\frac{1}{2})}^{5/2}-{0}^{5/2}) \\  & =\frac{16\sqrt{2}}{5}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{{2}^{5}}} \\  & =\frac{16\sqrt{2}}{5}\cdot \frac{1}{4\sqrt{2}} \\  & =\frac{4}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
Consider the matrix $E=[\begin{aligned}-32 & 40 \\ -30 & 38\end{aligned}].$ You're given that ${\lambda }_{1}=-2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=8$ are the eigenvalues of $E$, and
${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}]$, ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$ are the respective eigenvectors. Find the matrices $P$ and $D$ such that $PD{P}^{-1}=E,$ where $D$ is a diagonal matrix.
questions.worked_solution:
Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=-2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=8,$ we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & 8\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, to construct the matrix $P,$ we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns: 

- the $1$st column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=-2,$ and

- the $2$nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=8.$

Therefore, we get

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem:
Consider the matrix $A$ for which ${\lambda }_{1}=-2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-1$ are eigenvalues, and

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -4\end{aligned}]
$$

are the respective eigenvectors. What are the values of $a,b,c$ given that

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & b \\ c & -4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}a & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}1 & b \\ c & -4\end{aligned}]}^{-1}?
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=-2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-1,$ we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, to construct the matrix $P,$ we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns: 

- the $1$st column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=-2,$ and

- the $2$nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=-1.$

Therefore, we get

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ -2 & -4\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ -2 & -4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ -2 & -4\end{aligned}]}^{-1}.
$$

 

In conclusion, we get $a=-2,$ $b=3,$ and $c=-2.$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem:
Consider the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}6 & 8 \\ -4 & -6\end{aligned}].$ You're given that ${\lambda }_{1}=2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2$ are the eigenvalues of $A$, and
${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$, ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ are the respective eigenvectors. Find the matrices $P$ and $D$ such that $PD{P}^{-1}=A,$ where $D$ is a diagonal matrix.
questions.worked_solution:
Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, to construct the matrix $P,$ we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns: 

- the $1$st column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=2,$ and

- the $2$nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=-2.$

Therefore, we get

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the matrix $B=[\begin{aligned}5 & 3 \\ -4 & -3\end{aligned}].$ You're given that ${\lambda }_{1}=-1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=3$ are the eigenvalues of $B$, and
${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 10\end{aligned}]$, ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -2\end{aligned}]$ are the respective eigenvectors. Find the matrices $P$ and $D$ such that $PD{P}^{-1}=B,$ where $D$ is a diagonal  matrix.
questions.worked_solution:
Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=-1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=3,$ we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, to construct the matrix $P,$ we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns: 

- the $1$st column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=-1,$ and

- the $2$nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=3.$

Therefore, we get

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}-5 & 3 \\ 10 & -2\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem:
Consider the matrix $B$ for which ${\lambda }_{1}=4$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-6$ are eigenvalues, and

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]
$$

are the respective eigenvectors. What are the values of $a,b,c$ given that

$$
B=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ b & c\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & a\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ b & c\end{aligned}]}^{-1}?
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=4$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-6,$ we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & -6\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, to construct the matrix $P,$ we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns: 

- the $1$st column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=4,$ and

- the $2$nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=-6.$

Therefore, we get

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
B=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & -6\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}.
$$

 

In conclusion, we get  $a=-6,$ $b=3,$ and $c=-1.$

questions.name: Question 6
questions.problem:
Determine if the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}10 & -4 \\ 24 & -10\end{aligned}]$ 
is diagonalizable or not, and if it is diagonalizable, find a corresponding diagonal matrix $D.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ by solving $det(A-\lambda I)=0$:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}10-\lambda  & -4 \\ 24 & -10-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (10-\lambda )(-10-\lambda )-24\cdot (-4) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-4 & =0 \\ (\lambda +2)(\lambda -2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}=2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2.$ Since we get two distinct eigenvalues, the matrix $A$ is diagonalizable.

Now, we construct the diagonal matrix $D,$ as follows:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]
$$

questions.name: Question 7
questions.problem:
Determine if the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 \\ -3 & 4\end{aligned}]$
is diagonalizable or not, and if it is diagonalizable, find a corresponding diagonal matrix $D.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ by solving $det(A-\lambda I)=0$:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}-2-\lambda  & 3 \\ -3 & 4-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-2-\lambda )(4-\lambda )-(3)(-3) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda +1 & =0 \\ (\lambda -1)(\lambda -1) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=1.$ Since we get one repeated eigenvalue, the matrix might not be diagonalizable. To check this, we row-reduce the matrix $(A-1I)\text{x}=0:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}A-1I & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 \\ -3 & 4\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 \\ -3 & 3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has only $1$ pivot column. This implies that we will have only $2-1=1$ linearly independent eigenvector corresponding to the current eigenvalue. Therefore, $A$ is not diagonalizable.

questions.name: Question 8
questions.problem:
Determine if the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}3 & -4 \\ 2 & -3\end{aligned}]$ 
is diagonalizable or not, and if it is diagonalizable, find a corresponding diagonal matrix $D.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ by solving $det(A-\lambda I)=0$:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}3-\lambda  & -4 \\ 2 & -3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )(-3-\lambda )-2\cdot (-4) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-1 & =0 \\ (\lambda +1)(\lambda -1) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-1.$ Since we get two distinct eigenvalues, the matrix $A$ is diagonalizable.

Now, we construct the diagonal matrix $D,$ as follows:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]
$$

questions.name: Question 9
questions.problem:
Determine if the matrix
$A=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 5 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]$
is diagonalizable or not, and if it is diagonalizable, find a corresponding diagonal matrix $D.$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $A$ is triangular, the eigenvalues are the entries on the main diagonal. 

So, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=-2.$ Since we get one repeated eigenvalue, the matrix might not be diagonalizable. To check this, we row-reduce the matrix $(A-(-2)I)\text{x}=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-2)I & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 5 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]+2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 5 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has only $1$ pivot column. This implies that we will have only $2-1=1$ linearly independent eigenvector corresponding to the current eigenvalue. Therefore, $A$ is not diagonalizable.

questions.name: Question 10
questions.problem:
Determine if the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -3 & 5\end{aligned}]$ 
is diagonalizable or not, and if it is diagonalizable, find a corresponding diagonal matrix $D.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ by solving $det(A-\lambda I)=0$:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 1 \\ -3 & 5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )(5-\lambda )-(1)(-3) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-6\lambda +5+3 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-6\lambda +8 & =0 \\ (\lambda -2)(\lambda -4) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}=2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=4.$ Since we get two distinct eigenvalues, the matrix $A$ is diagonalizable.

Now, we construct the diagonal matrix $D,$ as follows:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

questions.name: Question 11
questions.problem:
Consider the following matrices:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ -6 & 6\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}2 & a \\ 3 & b\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $D={P}^{-1}AP,$ find the value of $\frac{b}{a}.$
questions.worked_solution:
From the diagonal matrix $D=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]$, we deduce that the eigenvalues of $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=3.$

So, the second column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=3.$ 

Now, we simply need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{2}=3.$ Computing $A-3I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ -6 & 6\end{aligned}]-(3)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & 2 \\ -6 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & 2 & 0 \\ -6 & 3 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-\frac{3}{2}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-4 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=2,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $\frac{b}{a}=\frac{2}{1}=2.$

questions.name: Question 12
questions.problem:
Consider the following matrices:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-5 & -2 \\ 12 & 5\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}1 & ∗ \\ -3 & ∗\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $A=PD{P}^{-1},$ find the second column of the matrix $P.$
questions.worked_solution:
From the diagonal matrix $D=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]$, we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-1.$

So, the second column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=-1.$ 

Now, we simply need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{2}=-1.$ Computing $A-(-1)I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-1)I & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & -2 \\ 12 & 5\end{aligned}]-(-1)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & -2 \\ 12 & 6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & -2 & 0 \\ 12 & 6 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-4 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=2,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $P=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}].$

questions.name: Question 13
questions.problem:
Consider the following matrices:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-5 & 2 \\ -12 & 5\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}-1 & a \\ -2 & b\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $D={P}^{-1}AP,$ find the value of $\frac{b}{a}.$
questions.worked_solution:
From the diagonal matrix $D=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]$, we deduce that the eigenvalues of $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=1.$

So, the second column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=1.$ 

Now, we simply need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{2}=1.$ Computing $A-I,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}A-I & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & 2 \\ -12 & 5\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & 2 \\ -12 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & 2 & 0 \\ -12 & 4 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-6 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=\frac{1}{3}{x}_{2}.$  Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=3,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $\frac{b}{a}=\frac{3}{1}=3.$

questions.name: Question 14
questions.problem:
Consider the following matrices:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-8 & 6 \\ -9 & 7\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}1 & a \\ 1 & b\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $D={P}^{-1}AP,$ find the value of $\frac{a}{b}.$
questions.worked_solution:
From the diagonal matrix $D=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]$, we deduce that the eigenvalues of $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=1.$

So, the second column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=1.$ 

Now, we simply need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{2}=1.$ Computing $A-I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-I & =[\begin{aligned}-8 & 6 \\ -9 & 7\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-9 & 6 \\ -9 & 6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-9 & 6 & 0 \\ -9 & 6 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-9 & 6 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=\frac{2}{3}{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=3,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $\frac{a}{b}=\frac{2}{3}.$

questions.name: Question 15
questions.problem:
Consider the following matrices:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-3 & -1 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}∗ & 1 \\ ∗ & -1\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $D={P}^{-1}AP,$   find the first column of the matrix $P.$
questions.worked_solution:
From the diagonal matrix $D=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]$, we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2.$  

So, the first column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=-1.$ 

Now, we simply need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{1}=-1.$ Computing $A-(-1)I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-1)I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & -1 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}]-(-1)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=2,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $P=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}].$

questions.name: Question 16
questions.problem: Find matrices $P$ and $D$ such that $PD{P}^{-1}=B,$ where $D$ is a diagonal matrix and $B=[\begin{aligned}-5 & 3 \\ -6 & 4\end{aligned}].$
questions.worked_solution:
We apply the diagonalization algorithm.

**Step 1.** We need to find the eigenvalues of the matrix $B$ using its characteristic equation $det(B-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}-5-\lambda  & 3 \\ -6 & 4-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-5-\lambda )(4-\lambda )-3\cdot (-6) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+\lambda -2 & =0 \\ (\lambda -1)(\lambda +2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the eigenvalues of $B$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2.$ 

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $B.$

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}B-I & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & 3 \\ -6 & 4\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 \\ -6 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 & 0 \\ -6 & 3 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2}.$  Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=2,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}B-(-2)I & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & 3 \\ -6 & 4\end{aligned}]-(-2)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 \\ -6 & 6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 & 0 \\ -6 & 6 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & ={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ as follows:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

questions.name: Question 17
questions.problem: Find matrices $P$ and $D$ such that $PD{P}^{-1}=B,$ where $D$ is a diagonal matrix and $B=[\begin{aligned}7 & -6 \\ 8 & -7\end{aligned}].$
questions.worked_solution:
We apply the diagonalization algorithm.

**Step 1.** We need to find the eigenvalues of the matrix $B$ using its characteristic equation $det(B-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}7-\lambda  & -6 \\ 8 & -7-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (7-\lambda )(-7-\lambda )-(-6)\cdot 8 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-49+48 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-1 & =0 \\ (\lambda +1)(\lambda -1) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the eigenvalues of $B$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=1.$

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $B.$

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=-1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}B-(-1)I & =[\begin{aligned}7 & -6 \\ 8 & -7\end{aligned}]-(-1)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 & -6 \\ 8 & -6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}8 & -6 & 0 \\ 8 & -6 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}8 & -6 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=\frac{3}{4}{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{4}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=4,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 4\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}B-1I & =[\begin{aligned}7 & -6 \\ 8 & -7\end{aligned}]-1[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6 & -6 \\ 8 & -8\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}6 & -6 & 0 \\ 8 & -8 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & ={R}_{2}+(-\frac{4}{3}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}6 & -6 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ as follows:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 4 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

questions.name: Question 18
questions.problem:
Given the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -6 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]$, 
find a diagonal matrix $D$ and an invertible matrix $P$ such that $D={P}^{-1}AP.$
questions.worked_solution:
We apply the diagonalization algorithm.

**Step 1.**  We need to find the eigenvalues of the matrix. Since matrix $A$ is triangular, its eigenvalues are the entries on the main diagonal: 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=-1\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{2}=3$

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=-1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-1)I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -6 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]-(-1)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -6 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -6 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+\frac{2}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}0 & -6 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $2$nd one). Thus, ${x}_{1}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}=0.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -6 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & -6 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a homogeneous system of linear equations with the matrix as above. Note, the matrix is already in row echelon form. There is one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-\frac{3}{2}{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{2}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=2,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ as follows:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

questions.name: Question 19
questions.problem: Find matrices $P$ and $D$ such that $PD{P}^{-1}=B,$ where $D$ is a diagonal matrix and $B=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}].$
questions.worked_solution:
We apply the diagonalization algorithm.

**Step 1.** We need to find the eigenvalues of the matrix $B$ using its characteristic equation $det(B-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 2 \\ -1 & -2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )(-2-\lambda )-2\cdot (-1) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+\lambda  & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda +1) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the eigenvalues of $B$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=0$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-1.$ 

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $B.$

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}B-0I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}]-0[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 0 \\ -1 & -2 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-2{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=-1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}B-(-1)I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}]-(-1)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & 0 \\ -1 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & ={R}_{2}+(\frac{1}{2}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=-1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ as follows:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}]
$$

questions.name: Question 20
questions.problem:
Given the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}-3 & -2 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]$, 
find a diagonal matrix $D$ and an invertible matrix $P$ such that $D={P}^{-1}AP.$
questions.worked_solution:
We apply the diagonalization algorithm.

**Step 1.**  We need to find the eigenvalues of the matrix. Since matrix $A$ is triangular, its eigenvalues are the entries on the main diagonal: 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=-3\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{2}=-2$

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=-3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-3)I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & -2 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]+3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $2$nd one). Thus, ${x}_{1}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}=0.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-2)I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & -2 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]+2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a homogeneous system of linear equations with the matrix as above. Note, the matrix is already in row echelon form. There is one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-2{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ as follows:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are $\lambda_1={\color{blue}4}$ and $\lambda_2={\color{red}3},$ we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14152180/assets/427a788b1c9f78e8ce25f06b54cef549d7be04757f6275cc66f12bd48652e40b.svg)

Now, to construct the matrix $P,$ we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns: 

- the $1$st column is the eigenvector corresponding to $\lambda_1={\color{blue}4},$ and

- the $2$nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to $\lambda_2={\color{red}3}.$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Diagonalizing a 2x2 Matrix Given Its Eigenvalues

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Identifying Whether a Given 2x2 Matrix Is Diagonalizable
canonical_examples.problem:
Determine if the matrix
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14152180/assets/af05cedf7b2015f4f61df71e833390aa845d50126c3203369320ac6feb8b2cc3.svg)
is diagonalizable or not, and if it is diagonalizable, find a corresponding diagonal matrix $D.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Since $A$ is triangular, the eigenvalues are the entries on the main diagonal. 

So, the eigenvalues are $\lambda_1=\lambda_2=3.$ Since we get one repeated eigenvalue, the matrix might not be diagonalizable. To check this, we row-reduce the matrix $A-3I\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -5 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -5 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has only $1$ pivot column. This implies that we will have only $2-1=1$ linearly independent eigenvector corresponding to the current eigenvalue. Therefore, $A$ is not diagonalizable.

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Diagonalizing a 2x2 Matrix Given Part of the Diagonalization
canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the following matrices:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14152180/assets/6e51c22c33c32d52c51657552a3c174d706a316ec10c78a4a953d2fcebc304ff.svg)
Given that $D=P^{-1}AP,$ find the value of $\dfrac{a}{b}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
From the diagonal matrix ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14152180/assets/0e25fe1b46b828e6fac168d1755af7aed9a7c3f657d1a6d6677fd71746b7ce31.svg) we deduce that the eigenvalues of $A$ are $\lambda_1=5$ and $\lambda_2=-1.$

So, the second column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda_2=-1.$ 

Now, we simply need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to $\lambda_2=-1.$ Computing $A-(-1)I,$ we get  

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-1)I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 4 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ 2 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

To solve the corresponding system of linear equations, we construct the augmented matrix $M$ and reduce it to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & 0 \\ 2 & 4 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2}={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). So, $x_2$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain $x_1= -{2}x_2.$ Therefore, the general solution is

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14152180/assets/54dad1c9d747fead6f27dd0e9af7cca434c40a83d56c02c854bb610a1cdc6087.svg)

By setting $x_2=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14152180/assets/d28cf572126716928bc9ded7c2646871540e20b1d93d1efc929599b4c379d38b.svg)

Finally, $\dfrac{a}{b}=\dfrac{-2}{1} = -2.$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Diagonalizing a 2x2 Matrix
canonical_examples.problem:
Given the matrix 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14152180/assets/3da867d461c2b42c21badd67ce59c9ec5f6448597b4d2dcbb7e8b28ffe397768.svg) 
find a diagonal matrix $D$ and an invertible matrix $P$ such that $D=P^{-1}AP.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We apply the diagonalization algorithm. 

**Step 1.**  We need to find the eigenvalues of the matrix. Since matrix $A$ is triangular, its eigenvalues are the entries on the main diagonal: 

$$
\lambda_1=3, \quad\quad\lambda_2=-2.
$$

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$

- For $\lambda_1=3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -8 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -8 \\ 0 & -5\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

To solve the corresponding system of linear equations, we construct the augmented matrix $M$ and reduce it to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -8 & 0 \\ 0 & -5 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2}={R}_{2}+(-\frac{5}{8}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}0 & -8 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $2$nd one). So, $x_1$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain $x_2=0.$ Therefore, the general solution is
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14152180/assets/04f6efaa2bb141940040a04905e52aacd7aa739e1bd58dd71666a10543ff0f74.svg)
Setting $x_1=1,$ we get the eigenvector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14152180/assets/dd78cbf2025fdf012dc27429596c84be09825b436c32a5410f50f78cd4943a66.svg)

- For $\lambda_2=-2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-2)I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -8 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]+2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & -8 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The above matrix corresponds to a homogeneous system of linear equations. Note, the matrix is already in row echelon form. There is one pivot column (the $1$st one). So, $x_2$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain $x_1=\dfrac{8}{5}x_2.$ Therefore, the general solution is
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14152180/assets/5b5b06d4cd243ca0370807b58bc9d0da68f34aa008956016bab3da29377df219.svg)
Setting  $x_2=5,$ we get the eigenvector  ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14152180/assets/3ea698aa474cb6d28b3fb511215fbe5da7d01b6653e884719d99483eac5635a0.svg)

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ as follows:

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Diagonalizing a 2x2 Matrix

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
A square matrix $A$ is called **diagonalizable** if there exists a diagonal matrix $D$ and an invertible matrix $P$ such that

$$
A = PDP^{-1}.
$$

So, to **diagonalize** a matrix $A,$ we need to find a diagonal matrix $D$ and an invertible matrix $P$ that satisfy the equation above.

For example, let's diagonalize the matrix $A,$ given by

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14152180/assets/9dee6d9184932a79f36305b9fca2bbb5a2a18bc79b49ad97038f780a2f125e49.svg)

To diagonalize a $2\times 2$ matrix, we follow a three-step **diagonalization algorithm.**

**Step 1:** Find the eigenvalues of the matrix.

We solve the characteristic equation $\vert A - \lambda I \vert = 0.$ For the given matrix, the eigenvalues are $\color{red}\lambda_1 =2$ and $\color{blue}\lambda_2 =3.$

**Step 2:** Find a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$ consisting of eigenvectors of the matrix.

Following the usual method for computing eigenvectors, we get 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14152180/assets/caa7716ce45eef38d92092d27827d30fd539fca27067c1e12f485a719b4f37ae.svg)

corresponding to the eigenvalues $\color{red}\lambda_1 =2$ and $\color{blue}\lambda_2 =3,$ respectively.

Note that $\left\{ {\color{red}\mathbf{v_1}}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{v_2}}\right\}$ is a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$ since eigenvectors corresponding to distinct eigenvalues are linearly independent. This becomes important later.

**Step 3: ** Construct the matrices $D$ and $P.$

Now that we have our eigenvalues and corresponding eigenvectors, we can construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and invertible matrix $P.$

The matrix $D$ has the eigenvalues of the matrix as its entries on the diagonal. For now, we can write them in any order. So, we let

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14152180/assets/3e0df792d822773528cb07cceb39fcb98b7397ae70ab4f114e1450f1d91256d1.svg)

Then, the columns of $P$ are the corresponding eigenvectors. We need to write each eigenvector in the *same* column as its respective eigenvalue in the matrix $D.$ So, we get

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14152180/assets/869a05b6273dbbb1b53d9f842d8b2c612017517a0b007c1c5f494f55439a11b4.svg)

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A=PD{P}^{-1} & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can check our solution by computing the product on the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1} & =[\begin{aligned}6 & -6 \\ -2 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -6 \\ 1 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =A\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.content:
A square matrix $A$ is called **diagonalizable** if there exists a diagonal matrix $D$ and an invertible matrix $P$ such that

$$
A = PDP^{-1}.
$$

So, to **diagonalize** a matrix $A,$ we need to find a diagonal matrix $D$ and an invertible matrix $P$ that satisfy the equation above.

For example, let's diagonalize the matrix $A,$ given by

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14152180/assets/9dee6d9184932a79f36305b9fca2bbb5a2a18bc79b49ad97038f780a2f125e49.svg)

To diagonalize a $2\times 2$ matrix, we follow a three-step **diagonalization algorithm.**

**Step 1:** Find the eigenvalues of the matrix.

We solve the characteristic equation $\vert A - \lambda I \vert = 0.$ For the given matrix, the eigenvalues are $\color{red}\lambda_1 =2$ and $\color{blue}\lambda_2 =3.$

**Step 2:** Find a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$ consisting of eigenvectors of the matrix.

Following the usual method for computing eigenvectors, we get 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14152180/assets/caa7716ce45eef38d92092d27827d30fd539fca27067c1e12f485a719b4f37ae.svg)

corresponding to the eigenvalues $\color{red}\lambda_1 =2$ and $\color{blue}\lambda_2 =3,$ respectively.

Note that $\left\{ {\color{red}\mathbf{v_1}}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{v_2}}\right\}$ is a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$ since eigenvectors corresponding to distinct eigenvalues are linearly independent. This becomes important later.

**Step 3: ** Construct the matrices $D$ and $P.$

Now that we have our eigenvalues and corresponding eigenvectors, we can construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and invertible matrix $P.$

The matrix $D$ has the eigenvalues of the matrix as its entries on the diagonal. For now, we can write them in any order. So, we let

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14152180/assets/3e0df792d822773528cb07cceb39fcb98b7397ae70ab4f114e1450f1d91256d1.svg)

Then, the columns of $P$ are the corresponding eigenvectors. We need to write each eigenvector in the *same* column as its respective eigenvalue in the matrix $D.$ So, we get

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14152180/assets/869a05b6273dbbb1b53d9f842d8b2c612017517a0b007c1c5f494f55439a11b4.svg)

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A=PD{P}^{-1} & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can check our solution by computing the product on the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1} & =[\begin{aligned}6 & -6 \\ -2 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -6 \\ 1 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =A\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.problem:
There is a theorem that states the following:

*If $A$ is a $2 \times 2$ matrix, then it is diagonalizable if and only if there exists a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$ that consists of eigenvectors of $A.$*

We can break this down into two possible cases:

- If $A$ has two distinct eigenvalues, then it is indeed diagonalizable. This is because two distinct eigenvalues will give rise to two linearly independent eigenvectors (one for each eigenvalue). 

So, for a matrix $A$ with eigenvalues $\color{red}\lambda_1$ and $\color{blue}\lambda_2$ and corresponding eigenvectors $\color{red}\mathbf{v_1}$ and $\color{blue}\mathbf{v_2},$ we have
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14152180/assets/e1468bc5ccdff43e33587c7b4b500bc527ab0ac7e74410ea53df1f803a19b520.svg)

- If we get a double root $\lambda$ of the characteristic equation, the matrix will be diagonalizable *only if* we can find exactly two linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to $\lambda,$ which may or may not be possible. Another way of saying this is that the corresponding eigenspace $V_\lambda$ must be of dimension $2.$

tutorials.content:
There is a theorem that states the following:

*If $A$ is a $2 \times 2$ matrix, then it is diagonalizable if and only if there exists a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$ that consists of eigenvectors of $A.$*

We can break this down into two possible cases:

- If $A$ has two distinct eigenvalues, then it is indeed diagonalizable. This is because two distinct eigenvalues will give rise to two linearly independent eigenvectors (one for each eigenvalue). 

So, for a matrix $A$ with eigenvalues $\color{red}\lambda_1$ and $\color{blue}\lambda_2$ and corresponding eigenvectors $\color{red}\mathbf{v_1}$ and $\color{blue}\mathbf{v_2},$ we have
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14152180/assets/e1468bc5ccdff43e33587c7b4b500bc527ab0ac7e74410ea53df1f803a19b520.svg)

- If we get a double root $\lambda$ of the characteristic equation, the matrix will be diagonalizable *only if* we can find exactly two linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to $\lambda,$ which may or may not be possible. Another way of saying this is that the corresponding eigenspace $V_\lambda$ must be of dimension $2.$
tutorials.title: Diagonalizable vs. Non-Diagonalizable Matrices

tutorials.name: The Connection Between a Matrix and Its Diagonal Form
tutorials.problem:
If $A$ is a diagonalizable matrix, then we can write

$$
A=PDP^{-1}.
$$

 

We can write this equation in an equivalent form, making $D$ the subject.

First, we left-multiply both sides of the equation by $P^{-1}\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =PD{P}^{-1} \\ {P}^{-1}\cdot A & ={P}^{-1}\cdot PD{P}^{-1} \\ {P}^{-1}A & ={I}_{2}D{P}^{-1} \\ {P}^{-1}A & =D{P}^{-1}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we right-multiply both sides of the equation by $P{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{-1}A\cdot P & =D{P}^{-1}\cdot P \\ {P}^{-1}AP & =D{I}_{2} \\ {P}^{-1}AP & =D\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
A=PDP^{-1}
\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad
D = P^{-1}A P.
$$

tutorials.name: Uniqueness of the Diagonalization
tutorials.problem:
Given a matrix $A,$ the diagonalization 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14152180/assets/76843143729d2bc62fc74dc6f03c24eb6a12dfc16a2609a8f2b36499cf39ce90.svg)

is almost unique, but not quite.

When we construct the diagonal matrix $D,$ we can put the eigenvalues in any order. So this matrix is unique up to permutations of the order of the eigenvalues. Note that by swapping the eigenvalues in $D,$ we then have to swap the corresponding eigenvectors (columns) in $P{:}$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14152180/assets/dec5fece3d89eaa022b4e951e63259b0f87213997397b1f8a91fb8fdabed0f74.svg)

Also, since any non-zero multiple of an eigenvector is an eigenvector as well, the eigenvector basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$ can consist of these multiples instead. So the invertible matrix $P$ is unique up to multiples of its columns.

tutorials.content:
Given a matrix $A,$ the diagonalization 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14152180/assets/76843143729d2bc62fc74dc6f03c24eb6a12dfc16a2609a8f2b36499cf39ce90.svg)

is almost unique, but not quite.

When we construct the diagonal matrix $D,$ we can put the eigenvalues in any order. So this matrix is unique up to permutations of the order of the eigenvalues. Note that by swapping the eigenvalues in $D,$ we then have to swap the corresponding eigenvectors (columns) in $P{:}$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14152180/assets/dec5fece3d89eaa022b4e951e63259b0f87213997397b1f8a91fb8fdabed0f74.svg)

Also, since any non-zero multiple of an eigenvector is an eigenvector as well, the eigenvector basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$ can consist of these multiples instead. So the invertible matrix $P$ is unique up to multiples of its columns.
tutorials.title: Uniqueness of the Diagonalization

tutorials.name: Diagonalization as a Change of Coordinates
tutorials.problem:
Let ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14152180/assets/3207697e43e4f88223ad85c16964c3103a50c0c999a4ca14417695158d45526b.svg) be a diagonalizable ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14152180/assets/2521651122403a440e682fef383af333958f5b0d1334abe8b0771865d4daf100.svg) matrix. Then we can write
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14152180/assets/d8f75220bef8327a8dfc49a6ae22e79c6f1649aefdc8fb43065e0616975a8c5c.svg)
where

- ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14152180/assets/1aaddf0d4be4d873ff6c0600b0b239e0565a05ca8daaff7ca92bd5c70bebcf03.svg) is an invertible matrix whose columns are eigenvectors ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14152180/assets/13cfebc7f22b3c6cfe7a66492040f9c7682e27e72b0a9adbc033e6a815c68fd9.svg) and ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14152180/assets/d0c6e1eed1577bd5d71e38657d494bf53798b9c1f52c54e4a270e200df1cc351.svg) of ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14152180/assets/c2c85081d1f89d74b8ebb2761496d211d7052193809b7864e7983437f5d0b80f.svg) and

- ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14152180/assets/5914524b1d3db63c66998b75ca1d00a5dc4e294d2a8f10fe384d2b2ebf2af38e.svg) is a diagonal matrix whose diagonal entries are the corresponding eigenvalues ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14152180/assets/ff5243fdeda78658220d1bcd4ac9b5963157b5e1f8b6a31231c68a6743248b19.svg) and ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14152180/assets/4a2dd44cea07e06ccec03fff120c7fdbcebe19ad7a31d8abde1ab95c8a6b53a1.svg)

To understand this better, we need to distinguish between two coordinate systems.

In ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14152180/assets/fb3130e489fdca80d1a077702861c20532fe613f9942d48fa1ec24055494a383.svg) the **standard basis** is
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14152180/assets/d29d3ee4ae42a8d4ee5304cb0d29c6c811838d7b893a3a831b1b1b8b3af12561.svg)

So, if a vector is written as
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14152180/assets/bbbc0379f1691a30dec4c34ec6171db1f116bec12a24891169957af68164f8d3.svg)
then ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14152180/assets/12adb8ba7ed45d89c9d9a80eb7c06616c41999e9fac57732bc24d2b55e1f8073.svg) The numbers ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14152180/assets/349015631ec44ef653936c85586d2c5ef56ba64392b3f92b4b92cbef3e731bc5.svg) and ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14152180/assets/a77a353782459b753313d80235712695d65dc4a44d8d357aa41add6729f81d8f.svg) are the *standard coordinates* of ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14152180/assets/1f3d1a60926323e963d7563529669e5cf8210771c8cbb0379f7a7d90e7c6aeec.svg)

Now let
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14152180/assets/58cdfb66e4c93d643fb97273610b3bbf67c8831516d4ccfc5b7790d55a169b28.svg)

Since the columns of ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14152180/assets/1aaddf0d4be4d873ff6c0600b0b239e0565a05ca8daaff7ca92bd5c70bebcf03.svg) are ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14152180/assets/13cfebc7f22b3c6cfe7a66492040f9c7682e27e72b0a9adbc033e6a815c68fd9.svg) and ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14152180/assets/d0c6e1eed1577bd5d71e38657d494bf53798b9c1f52c54e4a270e200df1cc351.svg) written in standard coordinates, the matrix ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14152180/assets/1aaddf0d4be4d873ff6c0600b0b239e0565a05ca8daaff7ca92bd5c70bebcf03.svg) converts coordinates from the basis ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14152180/assets/be2d796b77bebb31c0c06cef6af82bc9fb606a584a52cc5385cd32c4e143236c.svg) to the standard basis.

So, for any vector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14152180/assets/b2cb236f7a7f426f303b1391f76900b47f7d2fa1ad9c8110d8584182559017fd.svg)
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14152180/assets/7e5a6a4b9bee9550e68c75a3945ad25d41f1de6dd3b089ce89005428da169f9d.svg)

Here, ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14152180/assets/4fa2300af121b336bb0d7845b8e2b3e34be5a517a1bca45b4ec7b6514b2c544d.svg) denotes the standard-coordinate column of the vector, while ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14152180/assets/3f7132e53e5a27bee4c84bdddbac07971ec44ce12539c0e0c23bf0006057e199.svg) denotes the coordinate column of the same vector in the eigenvector basis ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14152180/assets/8d16f7d70344ddea7a4fe48105e5ea75b984f48fd77f6f6eb89d26ad91b65805.svg)

Also, in the basis ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14152180/assets/dab6f1afbeb705eef0eaf1a338c977e9cf6578010ebf95a6fccd1a4a4610dcd4.svg) the eigenvectors have especially simple coordinate columns:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14152180/assets/9f5fec87a4253a3a1741c3380e2c6f9331928883ab2083dc02bf0e8efda6a98a.svg)

This is because
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14152180/assets/306d2bb3211dac2883b1eb6abaed54259272a8bcc6a4e562ff5da6fc52dee520.svg)

So, in the basis ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14152180/assets/dab6f1afbeb705eef0eaf1a338c977e9cf6578010ebf95a6fccd1a4a4610dcd4.svg) the matrix ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14152180/assets/5914524b1d3db63c66998b75ca1d00a5dc4e294d2a8f10fe384d2b2ebf2af38e.svg) acts by scaling the first coordinate by ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14152180/assets/ff5243fdeda78658220d1bcd4ac9b5963157b5e1f8b6a31231c68a6743248b19.svg) and the second coordinate by ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14152180/assets/4a2dd44cea07e06ccec03fff120c7fdbcebe19ad7a31d8abde1ab95c8a6b53a1.svg)

We can summarize this process for any vector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14152180/assets/4fa2300af121b336bb0d7845b8e2b3e34be5a517a1bca45b4ec7b6514b2c544d.svg) as a sequence of three steps:

- first, rewrite ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14152180/assets/4fa2300af121b336bb0d7845b8e2b3e34be5a517a1bca45b4ec7b6514b2c544d.svg) in the eigenvector basis ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14152180/assets/dab6f1afbeb705eef0eaf1a338c977e9cf6578010ebf95a6fccd1a4a4610dcd4.svg)

- then, apply the diagonal matrix ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14152180/assets/5914524b1d3db63c66998b75ca1d00a5dc4e294d2a8f10fe384d2b2ebf2af38e.svg) in that basis,

- finally, convert the result back to standard coordinates.

The diagram below shows this sequence.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14152180/assets/1459b0643f99c186f9710118617f89f34a601526e7154213471404d2feb2aaeb.svg)

tutorials.title: Diagonalization as a Change of Coordinates

tutorial.name: Introduction
tutorial.problem:
A square matrix $A$ is called **diagonalizable** if there exists a diagonal matrix $D$ and an invertible matrix $P$ such that

$$
A = PDP^{-1}.
$$

So, to **diagonalize** a matrix $A,$ we need to find a diagonal matrix $D$ and an invertible matrix $P$ that satisfy the equation above.

For example, let's diagonalize the matrix $A,$ given by

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14152180/assets/0bd7d27ac44c8c87f48b99ac74ca4072ce68892f910666925bb546698fa2f96a.svg)

To diagonalize a $2\times 2$ matrix, we follow a three-step **diagonalization algorithm.**

**Step 1:** Find the eigenvalues of the matrix.

We solve the characteristic equation $\vert A - \lambda I \vert = 0.$ For the given matrix, the eigenvalues are $\color{red}\lambda_1 =2$ and $\color{blue}\lambda_2 =3.$

**Step 2:** Find a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$ consisting of eigenvectors of the matrix.

Following the usual method for computing eigenvectors, we get 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14152180/assets/7f40af1d2e3703b69174bfa78251a97f650cf5fb8d3f3634740178adc8bbba90.svg)

corresponding to the eigenvalues $\color{red}\lambda_1 =2$ and $\color{blue}\lambda_2 =3,$ respectively.

Note that $\left\{ {\color{red}\mathbf{v_1}}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{v_2}}\right\}$ is a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$ since eigenvectors corresponding to distinct eigenvalues are linearly independent. This becomes important later.

**Step 3: ** Construct the matrices $D$ and $P.$

Now that we have our eigenvalues and corresponding eigenvectors, we can construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and invertible matrix $P.$

The matrix $D$ has the eigenvalues of the matrix as its entries on the diagonal. For now, we can write them in any order. So, we let

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14152180/assets/148a0d45cfd87d48985bf68cd9a87cf0b36af6a100a98ff7b35384ffc4a30cfb.svg)

Then, the columns of $P$ are the corresponding eigenvectors. We need to write each eigenvector in the *same* column as its respective eigenvalue in the matrix $D.$ So, we get

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14152180/assets/0de9e31ecb91ab47fcdd76f768f5174e282551f362e912ebfade25e9e4f38515.svg)

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A=PD{P}^{-1} & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can check our solution by computing the product on the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1} & =[\begin{aligned}6 & -6 \\ -2 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -6 \\ 1 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =A\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

tutorial.content:
A square matrix $A$ is called **diagonalizable** if there exists a diagonal matrix $D$ and an invertible matrix $P$ such that

$$
A = PDP^{-1}.
$$

So, to **diagonalize** a matrix $A,$ we need to find a diagonal matrix $D$ and an invertible matrix $P$ that satisfy the equation above.

For example, let's diagonalize the matrix $A,$ given by

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14152180/assets/0bd7d27ac44c8c87f48b99ac74ca4072ce68892f910666925bb546698fa2f96a.svg)

To diagonalize a $2\times 2$ matrix, we follow a three-step **diagonalization algorithm.**

**Step 1:** Find the eigenvalues of the matrix.

We solve the characteristic equation $\vert A - \lambda I \vert = 0.$ For the given matrix, the eigenvalues are $\color{red}\lambda_1 =2$ and $\color{blue}\lambda_2 =3.$

**Step 2:** Find a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$ consisting of eigenvectors of the matrix.

Following the usual method for computing eigenvectors, we get 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14152180/assets/7f40af1d2e3703b69174bfa78251a97f650cf5fb8d3f3634740178adc8bbba90.svg)

corresponding to the eigenvalues $\color{red}\lambda_1 =2$ and $\color{blue}\lambda_2 =3,$ respectively.

Note that $\left\{ {\color{red}\mathbf{v_1}}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{v_2}}\right\}$ is a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$ since eigenvectors corresponding to distinct eigenvalues are linearly independent. This becomes important later.

**Step 3: ** Construct the matrices $D$ and $P.$

Now that we have our eigenvalues and corresponding eigenvectors, we can construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and invertible matrix $P.$

The matrix $D$ has the eigenvalues of the matrix as its entries on the diagonal. For now, we can write them in any order. So, we let

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14152180/assets/148a0d45cfd87d48985bf68cd9a87cf0b36af6a100a98ff7b35384ffc4a30cfb.svg)

Then, the columns of $P$ are the corresponding eigenvectors. We need to write each eigenvector in the *same* column as its respective eigenvalue in the matrix $D.$ So, we get

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14152180/assets/0de9e31ecb91ab47fcdd76f768f5174e282551f362e912ebfade25e9e4f38515.svg)

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A=PD{P}^{-1} & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can check our solution by computing the product on the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1} & =[\begin{aligned}6 & -6 \\ -2 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -6 \\ 1 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =A\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.name: Question 1
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Diagonalizing a 2x2 Matrix Given Its Eigenvalues
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=-2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=8,$ we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & 8\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, to construct the matrix $P,$ we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns: 

- the $1$st column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=-2,$ and

- the $2$nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=8.$

Therefore, we get

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

question.name: Question 1
question.problem:
Consider the matrix $E=[\begin{aligned}-32 & 40 \\ -30 & 38\end{aligned}].$ You're given that ${\lambda }_{1}=-2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=8$ are the eigenvalues of $E$, and
${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}]$, ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$ are the respective eigenvectors. Find the matrices $P$ and $D$ such that $PD{P}^{-1}=E,$ where $D$ is a diagonal matrix.
question.worked_solution:
Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=-2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=8,$ we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & 8\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, to construct the matrix $P,$ we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns: 

- the $1$st column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=-2,$ and

- the $2$nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=8.$

Therefore, we get

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

question.html:
Question 1
?

Consider the matrix E=[−3240−3038]. You're given that λ1=−2 and λ2=8 are the eigenvalues of E, and v1=[43], v2=[22] are the respective eigenvectors. Find the matrices P and D such that PDP−1=E, where D is a diagonal matrix.

a
D=[−2800] and P=[4−232]
b
D=[800−2] and P=[4232]
c
D=[200−8] and P=[3242]
d
D=[−2008] and P=[4232]
e
D=[800−2] and P=[2432]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are λ1=−2 and λ2=8, we construct the diagonal matrix D by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal:

D=[−2008].

Now, to construct the matrix P, we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns:

  • the 1st column is the eigenvector corresponding to λ1=−2, and

  • the 2nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to λ2=8.

Therefore, we get

P=[4232].

observed_steps.name: Question 2
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Diagonalizing a 2x2 Matrix Given Its Eigenvalues
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=-2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-1,$ we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, to construct the matrix $P,$ we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns: 

- the $1$st column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=-2,$ and

- the $2$nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=-1.$

Therefore, we get

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ -2 & -4\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ -2 & -4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ -2 & -4\end{aligned}]}^{-1}.
$$

 

In conclusion, we get $a=-2,$ $b=3,$ and $c=-2.$

question.name: Question 2
question.problem:
Consider the matrix $A$ for which ${\lambda }_{1}=-2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-1$ are eigenvalues, and

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -4\end{aligned}]
$$

are the respective eigenvectors. What are the values of $a,b,c$ given that

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & b \\ c & -4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}a & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}1 & b \\ c & -4\end{aligned}]}^{-1}?
$$
question.worked_solution:
Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=-2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-1,$ we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, to construct the matrix $P,$ we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns: 

- the $1$st column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=-2,$ and

- the $2$nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=-1.$

Therefore, we get

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ -2 & -4\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ -2 & -4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ -2 & -4\end{aligned}]}^{-1}.
$$

 

In conclusion, we get $a=-2,$ $b=3,$ and $c=-2.$

question.html:
Question 2
?

Consider the matrix A for which λ1=−2 and λ2=−1 are eigenvalues, and v1=[1−2],v2=[3−4] are the respective eigenvectors. What are the values of a,b,c given that A=[1bc−4][a00−1][1bc−4]−1?

a
a=1, b=−2, and c=3
b
a=−2, b=−2, and c=3
c
a=2, b=3, and c=−2
d
a=−2, b=3, and c=−2
e
a=2, b=−2, and c=3
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are λ1=−2 and λ2=−1, we construct the diagonal matrix D by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal:

D=[−200−1].

Now, to construct the matrix P, we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns:

  • the 1st column is the eigenvector corresponding to λ1=−2, and

  • the 2nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to λ2=−1.

Therefore, we get

P=[13−2−4].

Finally, we obtain

A=[13−2−4][−200−1][13−2−4]−1.

In conclusion, we get a=−2, b=3, and c=−2.
question.knowledge_point: Diagonalizing a 2x2 Matrix Given Its Eigenvalues

observed_steps.name: Question 3
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Diagonalizing a 2x2 Matrix Given Its Eigenvalues
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, to construct the matrix $P,$ we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns: 

- the $1$st column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=2,$ and

- the $2$nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=-2.$

Therefore, we get

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

question.name: Question 3
question.problem:
Consider the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}6 & 8 \\ -4 & -6\end{aligned}].$ You're given that ${\lambda }_{1}=2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2$ are the eigenvalues of $A$, and
${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$, ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ are the respective eigenvectors. Find the matrices $P$ and $D$ such that $PD{P}^{-1}=A,$ where $D$ is a diagonal matrix.
question.worked_solution:
Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, to construct the matrix $P,$ we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns: 

- the $1$st column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=2,$ and

- the $2$nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=-2.$

Therefore, we get

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Question 3
?

Consider the matrix A=[68−4−6]. You're given that λ1=2 and λ2=−2 are the eigenvalues of A, and v1=[2−1], v2=[−11] are the respective eigenvectors. Find the matrices P and D such that PDP−1=A, where D is a diagonal matrix.

a
D=[02−20] and P=[2−11−11]
b
D=[200−2] and P=[2−1−11]
c
D=[−2002] and P=[21−11]
d
D=[02−20] and P=[2−1−11]
e
D=[2−200] and P=[21−1−1]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are λ1=2 and λ2=−2, we construct the diagonal matrix D by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal:

D=[200−2].

Now, to construct the matrix P, we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns:

  • the 1st column is the eigenvector corresponding to λ1=2, and

  • the 2nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to λ2=−2.

Therefore, we get

P=[2−1−11].

observed_steps.worked_solution:
Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=-1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=3,$ we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, to construct the matrix $P,$ we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns: 

- the $1$st column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=-1,$ and

- the $2$nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=3.$

Therefore, we get

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}-5 & 3 \\ 10 & -2\end{aligned}].
$$

${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 10\end{aligned}]$, ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -2\end{aligned}]$ are the respective eigenvectors. Find the matrices $P$ and $D$ such that $PD{P}^{-1}=B,$ where $D$ is a diagonal  matrix.
question.worked_solution:
Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=-1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=3,$ we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, to construct the matrix $P,$ we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns: 

- the $1$st column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=-1,$ and

- the $2$nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=3.$

Therefore, we get

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}-5 & 3 \\ 10 & -2\end{aligned}].
$$

question.html:
Question 4
?

Consider the matrix B=[53−4−3]. You're given that λ1=−1 and λ2=3 are the eigenvalues of B, and v1=[−510], v2=[3−2] are the respective eigenvectors. Find the matrices P and D such that PDP−1=B, where D is a diagonal matrix.

a
D=[−1003] and P=[−510−32]
b
D=[300−1] and P=[1810−1220]
c
D=[−1003] and P=[−5310−2]
d
D=[−3001] and P=[352−10]
e
D=[300−1] and P=[−5−6104]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are λ1=−1 and λ2=3, we construct the diagonal matrix D by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal:

D=[−1003].

Now, to construct the matrix P, we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns:

  • the 1st column is the eigenvector corresponding to λ1=−1, and

  • the 2nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to λ2=3.

Therefore, we get

P=[−5310−2].

observed_steps.name: Question 5
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Diagonalizing a 2x2 Matrix Given Its Eigenvalues
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=4$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-6,$ we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & -6\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, to construct the matrix $P,$ we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns: 

- the $1$st column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=4,$ and

- the $2$nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=-6.$

Therefore, we get

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
B=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & -6\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}.
$$

 

In conclusion, we get  $a=-6,$ $b=3,$ and $c=-1.$

question.name: Question 5
question.problem:
Consider the matrix $B$ for which ${\lambda }_{1}=4$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-6$ are eigenvalues, and

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]
$$

are the respective eigenvectors. What are the values of $a,b,c$ given that

$$
B=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ b & c\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & a\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ b & c\end{aligned}]}^{-1}?
$$
question.worked_solution:
Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=4$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-6,$ we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & -6\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, to construct the matrix $P,$ we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns: 

- the $1$st column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=4,$ and

- the $2$nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=-6.$

Therefore, we get

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
B=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & -6\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}.
$$

 

In conclusion, we get  $a=-6,$ $b=3,$ and $c=-1.$
