question.name: Question 19
question.problem: Find matrices $P$ and $D$ such that $PD{P}^{-1}=B,$ where $D$ is a diagonal matrix and $B=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}].$
question.worked_solution:
We apply the diagonalization algorithm.

**Step 1.** We need to find the eigenvalues of the matrix $B$ using its characteristic equation $det(B-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 2 \\ -1 & -2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )(-2-\lambda )-2\cdot (-1) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+\lambda  & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda +1) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the eigenvalues of $B$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=0$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-1.$ 

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $B.$

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}B-0I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}]-0[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 0 \\ -1 & -2 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-2{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=-1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}B-(-1)I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}]-(-1)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & 0 \\ -1 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & ={R}_{2}+(\frac{1}{2}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=-1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ as follows:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}]
$$

Question 19
?

Find matrices P and D such that PDP−1=B, where D is a diagonal matrix and B=[12−1−2].

a
D=[200−1] and P=[21−11]
b
D=[000−1] and P=[21−1−1]
c
D=[100−1] and P=[21−1−1]
d
D=[0001] and P=[−23−1−1]
e
D=[000−1] and P=[20−1−1]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We apply the diagonalization algorithm.

Step 1. We need to find the eigenvalues of the matrix B using its characteristic equation det(B−λI)=0:

|1−λ2−1−2−λ|=0(1−λ)(−2−λ)−2⋅(−1)=0λ2+λ=0λ(λ+1)=0

So, the eigenvalues of B are λ1=0 and λ2=−1.

Step 2. Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of B.

  • For λ1=0, we have B−0I=[12−1−2]−0[1001]=[12−1−2]. So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix M which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows: M=[120−1−20]R2:=R2+R1∼[120000] The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the 1st one). Thus, x2 is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain x1=−2x2. Hence, the general solution is [−2x2x2],x2∈R. Setting x2=−1, we get the eigenvector v1=[2−1].

  • For λ2=−1, we have B−(−1)I=[12−1−2]−(−1)[1001]=[22−1−1]. So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix M which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows: M=[220−1−10]R2=R2+(12)R1∼[220000] The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the 1st one). Thus, x2 is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain x1=−x2. Hence, the general solution is [−x2x2],x2∈R. Setting x2=−1, we get the eigenvector v2=[1−1].

Step 3. We construct the diagonal matrix D and the invertible matrix P as follows: D=[000−1],P=[21−1−1]

last_observation.name: Question 19
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Diagonalizing a 2x2 Matrix
last_observation.worked_solution:
We apply the diagonalization algorithm.

**Step 1.** We need to find the eigenvalues of the matrix $B$ using its characteristic equation $det(B-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 2 \\ -1 & -2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )(-2-\lambda )-2\cdot (-1) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+\lambda  & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda +1) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the eigenvalues of $B$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=0$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-1.$ 

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $B.$

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}B-0I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}]-0[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 0 \\ -1 & -2 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-2{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=-1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}B-(-1)I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}]-(-1)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & 0 \\ -1 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & ={R}_{2}+(\frac{1}{2}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=-1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ as follows:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}]
$$

question.name: Question 19
question.problem: Find matrices $P$ and $D$ such that $PD{P}^{-1}=B,$ where $D$ is a diagonal matrix and $B=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}].$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

Question 19
?

Find matrices P and D such that PDP−1=B, where D is a diagonal matrix and B=[12−1−2].

a
D=[200−1] and P=[21−11]
b
D=[000−1] and P=[21−1−1]
c
D=[100−1] and P=[21−1−1]
d
D=[0001] and P=[−23−1−1]
e
D=[000−1] and P=[20−1−1]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We apply the diagonalization algorithm.

Step 1. We need to find the eigenvalues of the matrix B using its characteristic equation det(B−λI)=0:

|1−λ2−1−2−λ|=0(1−λ)(−2−λ)−2⋅(−1)=0λ2+λ=0λ(λ+1)=0

So, the eigenvalues of B are λ1=0 and λ2=−1.

solution.reasoning: The characteristic polynomial is det(B-\lambda I)=\lambda(\lambda+1), so the eigenvalues are 0 and -1. Corresponding eigenvectors are (2,-1)^T and (1,-1)^T: B(2,-1)^T=(0,0)^T and B(1,-1)^T=(-1,1)^T. Option b places these vectors in matching columns of P. Since det(P)=-1, BP=PD implies PDP^{-1}=B. feedback.name: Question 19
feedback.problem: Find matrices $P$ and $D$ such that $PD{P}^{-1}=B,$ where $D$ is a diagonal matrix and $B=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}].$
feedback.worked_solution:
We apply the diagonalization algorithm.

**Step 1.** We need to find the eigenvalues of the matrix $B$ using its characteristic equation $det(B-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 2 \\ -1 & -2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )(-2-\lambda )-2\cdot (-1) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+\lambda  & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda +1) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the eigenvalues of $B$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=0$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-1.$ 

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $B.$

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}B-0I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}]-0[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 0 \\ -1 & -2 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-2{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=-1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}B-(-1)I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}]-(-1)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & 0 \\ -1 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & ={R}_{2}+(\frac{1}{2}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=-1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ as follows:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}]
$$

So, the eigenvalues of B are λ1=0 and λ2=−1.

  • For λ1=0, we have B−0I=[12−1−2]−0[1001]=[12−1−2]. So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix M which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows: M=[120−1−20]R2:=R2+R1∼[120000] The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the 1st one). question.name: Question 20
question.problem:
Given the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}-3 & -2 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]$, 
find a diagonal matrix $D$ and an invertible matrix $P$ such that $D={P}^{-1}AP.$
question.worked_solution:
We apply the diagonalization algorithm.

**Step 1.**  We need to find the eigenvalues of the matrix. Since matrix $A$ is triangular, its eigenvalues are the entries on the main diagonal: 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=-3\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{2}=-2$

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=-3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-3)I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & -2 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]+3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $2$nd one). Thus, ${x}_{1}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}=0.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-2)I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & -2 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]+2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a homogeneous system of linear equations with the matrix as above. Note, the matrix is already in row echelon form. There is one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-2{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ as follows:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Question 20
?

Given the matrix A=[−3−20−2], find a diagonal matrix D and an invertible matrix P such that D=P−1AP.

a
D=[−200−3] and P=[−1−301]
b
D=[3002] and P=[−1−201]
c
D=[2003] and P=[1201]
d
D=[−300−2] and P=[1−201]
e
D=[200−2] and P=[1−20−1]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We apply the diagonalization algorithm.

Step 1. We need to find the eigenvalues of the matrix. Since matrix A is triangular, its eigenvalues are the entries on the main diagonal:

λ1=−3 and λ2=−2

Step 2. Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of A.

  • For λ1=−3, we have A−(−3)I=[−3−20−2]+3[1001]=[0−201]. So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix M which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows: M=[0−20010]R2:=R2+12R1∼[0−20000] The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the 2nd one). Thus, x1 is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain x2=0. Hence, the general solution is [x10],x1∈R. Setting x1=1, we get the eigenvector v1=[10].

  • For λ2=−2, we have A−(−2)I=[−3−20−2]+2[1001]=[−1−200]. So, we have a homogeneous system of linear equations with the matrix as above. Note, the matrix is already in row echelon form. There is one pivot column (the 1st one). Thus, x2 is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain x1=−2x2. Hence, the general solution is [−2x2x2],x2∈R. Setting x2=1, we get the eigenvector v2=[−21].

Step 3. We construct the diagonal matrix D and the invertible matrix P as follows: D=[−300−2],P=[1−201]

last_observation.name: Question 20
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Diagonalizing a 2x2 Matrix
last_observation.worked_solution:
We apply the diagonalization algorithm.

**Step 1.**  We need to find the eigenvalues of the matrix. Since matrix $A$ is triangular, its eigenvalues are the entries on the main diagonal: 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=-3\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{2}=-2$

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=-3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-3)I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & -2 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]+3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $2$nd one). Thus, ${x}_{1}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}=0.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-2)I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & -2 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]+2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a homogeneous system of linear equations with the matrix as above. Note, the matrix is already in row echelon form. There is one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-2{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ as follows:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

question.html:
Question 20
?

Given the matrix A=[−3−20−2], find a diagonal matrix D and an invertible matrix P such that D=P−1AP.

a
D=[−200−3] and P=[−1−301]
b
D=[3002] and P=[−1−201]
c
D=[2003] and P=[1201]
d
D=[−300−2] and P=[1−201]
e
D=[200−2] and P=[1−20−1]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We apply the diagonalization algorithm.

Step 1. We need to find the eigenvalues of the matrix. Since matrix A is triangular, its eigenvalues are the entries on the main diagonal:

λ1=−3 and λ2=−2

Step 2. Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of A.

  • For λ1=−3, we have A−(−3)I=[−3−20−2]+3[1001]=[0−201]. So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix M which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows: M=[0−20010]R2:=R2+12R1∼[0−20000] The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the 2nd one). Thus, x1 is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain x2=0. Hence, the general solution is [x10],x1∈R. Setting x1=1, we get the eigenvector v1=[10].

  • For λ2=−2, we have A−(−2)I=[−3−20−2]+2[1001]=[−1−200]. So, we have a homogeneous system of linear equations with the matrix as above. Note, the matrix is already in row echelon form. There is one pivot column (the 1st one). Thus, x2 is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain x1=−2x2. Hence, the general solution is [−2x2x2],x2∈R. Setting x2=1, we get the eigenvector v2=[−21].

Step 3. We construct the diagonal matrix D and the invertible matrix P as follows: D=[−300−2],P=[1−201]
question.knowledge_point: Diagonalizing a 2x2 Matrix

solution.reasoning: A is triangular, so its eigenvalues are -3 and -2. Corresponding eigenvectors are (1,0)^T and (-2,1)^T: A(1,0)^T=(-3,0)^T and A(-2,1)^T=(4,-2)^T. Option d places these vectors in columns matching D's diagonal. Since det(P)=1 and AP=PD, D=P^{-1}AP. No Math Academy answer key or grade for this question is captured.

feedback.name: Question 20
feedback.problem:
Given the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}-3 & -2 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]$, 
find a diagonal matrix $D$ and an invertible matrix $P$ such that $D={P}^{-1}AP.$
feedback.worked_solution:
We apply the diagonalization algorithm.

**Step 1.**  We need to find the eigenvalues of the matrix. Since matrix $A$ is triangular, its eigenvalues are the entries on the main diagonal: 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=-3\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{2}=-2$

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=-3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-3)I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & -2 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]+3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $2$nd one). Thus, ${x}_{1}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}=0.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-2)I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & -2 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]+2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a homogeneous system of linear equations with the matrix as above. Note, the matrix is already in row echelon form. There is one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-2{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ as follows:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

feedback.html:
Question 20
?

Given the matrix A=[−3−20−2], find a diagonal matrix D and an invertible matrix P such that D=P−1AP.

a
D=[−200−3] and P=[−1−301]
b
D=[3002] and P=[−1−201]
c
D=[2003] and P=[1201]
d
D=[−300−2] and P=[1−201]
e
D=[200−2] and P=[1−20−1]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We apply the diagonalization algorithm.

Step 1. We need to find the eigenvalues of the matrix. Since matrix A is triangular, its eigenvalues are the entries on the main diagonal:

λ1=−3 and λ2=−2

Step 2. Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of A.

  • For λ1=−3, we have A−(−3)I=[−3−20−2]+3[1001]=[0−201]. So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix M which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows: M=[0−20010]R2:=R2+12R1∼[0−20000] The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the 2nd one). Thus, x1 is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain x2=0. Hence, the general solution is [x10],x1∈R. Setting x1=1, we get the eigenvector v1=[10].

  • For λ2=−2, we have A−(−2)I=[−3−20−2]+2[1001]=[−1−200]. So, we have a homogeneous system of linear equations with the matrix as above. Note, the matrix is already in row echelon form. There is one pivot column (the 1st one). Thus, x2 is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain x1=−2x2. Hence, the general solution is [−2x2x2],x2∈R. Setting x2=1, we get the eigenvector v2=[−21].

Step 3. We construct the diagonal matrix D and the invertible matrix P as follows: D=[−300−2],P=[1−201]

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
| $4$ | $8$ |
| --- | --- |
| $12$ | $?$ |
| $20$ | $40$ |

$$

$$

What number is missing from the ratio table?
questions.worked_solution:
We start with the ratio $4:8$ and write it as a fraction:

$$
\frac{4}{8}
$$

So the numerator represents the left-hand entry ($4$), and the denominator represents the right-hand entry ($8$).

We can make a numerator of $12$ by multiplying the numerator and denominator by $3$:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{4\times 3}{8\times 3} & =\frac{12}{24}\end{aligned}
$$

We add this to our ratio table:

| $4$ | $8$ |
| --- | --- |
| $12$ | $24$ |
| $20$ | $40$ |

$$

$$

So, the missing number is $24.$

$$
\frac{4}{1}
$$

We can generate equivalent ratios by finding equivalent fractions:

- To create a numerator of $16,$ we multiply the numerator and denominator of our fraction by $4:$

$$
\frac{4\times 4}{1\times 4}=\frac{16}{4}
$$

- To create a numerator of $20,$ we multiply the numerator and denominator of our fraction by $5:$

$$
\frac{4\times 5}{1\times 5}=\frac{20}{5}

$$
\frac{4\times 7}{1\times 7}=\frac{28}{7}
$$

Finally, we fill in the ratio table:

| $4$ | $1$ |
| --- | --- |
| $16$ | $4$ |
| $20$ | $5$ |
| $28$ | $7$ |

questions.worked_solution:
We start with the ratio $8:24$ and write it as a fraction:

$$
\frac{8}{24}
$$

So the numerator represents the left-hand entry ($8$), and the denominator represents the right-hand entry ($24$).

Now we divide the numerator and the denominator by $8$ to find an equivalent ratio:

$$
\frac{8÷8}{24÷8}=\frac{1}{3}
$$

We can generate equivalent ratios by finding equivalent fractions:

- To create a numerator of $4,$ we multiply the numerator and denominator of our fraction by $4:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1\times 4}{3\times 4}=\frac{4}{12}\end{aligned}
$$

- To create a denominator of $27,$ we multiply the numerator and denominator of our fraction by $9:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1\times 9}{3\times 9} & =\frac{9}{27}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we fill in the ratio table:

| $4$ | $12$ |
| --- | --- |
| $8$ | $24$ |
| $9$ | $27$ |

$$

$$

questions.name: Question 7
questions.problem:
Liam wants to paint a fence. He knows he needs $2$ liters of paint for $32$ square meters of fence. He creates a ratio table to determine the ratio of the volume of paint to the fenced area for different quantities.

| Fence area (square meters) | Paint (liters) |
| --- | --- |
| $32$ | $2$ |
| $80$ | $?$ |
| $160$ | $10$ |

$$

$$

What volume of paint does Liam need to paint $80$ square meters of the fence?
questions.worked_solution:
We start with the ratio $32:2$ and write it as a fraction:

$$
\frac{32}{2}
$$

Now we divide the numerator and the denominator by $2$ to find an equivalent ratio:

$$
\frac{32÷2}{2÷2}=\frac{16}{1}
$$

So the numerator represents the area of the fence in ${\text{m}}^{2}$ ($16$), and the denominator represents the volume of paint in liters ($1$).

We can make a numerator of $80$ by multiplying the numerator and denominator by $5$:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{16\times 5}{1\times 5} & =\frac{80}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

We add this to our ratio table:

| Fence area (square meters) | Paint (liters) |
| --- | --- |
| $32$ | $2$ |
| $80$ | $5$ |
| $160$ | $10$ |

$$

$$

So, Liam needs $5$ liters of paint for $80$ square meters of the fence.

questions.name: Question 8
questions.problem:
In one hour, a crew of $4$ painters can cover $28$ square meters of a wall's surface in a newly constructed building. A construction manager has created a ratio table to determine how many square meters of the wall's surface can be covered in one hour by crews of $6$ and $9$ painters.

| Painters | Square meters |
| --- | --- |
| $4$ | $28$ |
| $6$ | $?$ |
| $9$ | $?$ |

$$

$$

From top to bottom, what are the missing numbers in the ratio table?
questions.worked_solution:
We start with the ratio $4:28$ and write it as a fraction:

$$
\frac{4}{28}
$$

Now we divide the numerator and the denominator by $4$ to find an equivalent ratio:

$$
\frac{4÷4}{28÷4}=\frac{1}{7}
$$

We can generate ratios that are equivalent to $1:7$ by finding more equivalent fractions: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1\times 6}{7\times 6} & =\frac{6}{42} \\ \frac{1\times 9}{7\times 9} & =\frac{9}{63}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we fill in the ratio table:

| Painters | Square meters |
| --- | --- |
| $4$ | $28$ |
| $6$ | $42$ |
| $9$ | $63$ |

$$

$$

So, from top to bottom, the missing numbers are $42$ and $63.$

| $5$ | $4$ |

What number is missing from the ratio table?
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We start with the ratio ${\color{blue}5}:{\color{red}4}$ and write it as a fraction:

$$
\dfrac{\color{blue}5}{\color{red}4}
$$

So the numerator represents the left-hand entry (${\color{blue}5}$), and the denominator represents the right-hand entry (${\color{red}4}$).

We can make a numerator of $20$ by multiplying the numerator and denominator by $4$:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{5\times 4}{4\times 4} & =\frac{20}{16}\end{aligned}
$$

We add this to our ratio table:

| ${\color{blue}5}$ | ${\color{red}4}$ |
| --- | --- |
| ${\color{blue}20}$ | $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{red}16}$ |
| ${\color{blue}25}$ | ${\color{red}20}$ |

So, the missing number is $\color{red}16.$

canonical_examples.problem:
Complete the ratio table below.

| $3$ | $5$ |
| --- | --- |
| $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}?}$ | $10$ |
| $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}?}$ | $35$ |
| $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}?}$ | $50$ |
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We start with the ratio ${\color{blue}3}:{\color{red}5}$ and write it as a fraction:

$$
\dfrac{\color{blue}3}{\color{red}5}
$$

So the numerator represents the left-hand entry (${\color{blue}3}$), and the denominator represents the right-hand entry (${\color{red}5}$).

We can generate equivalent ratios by finding equivalent fractions:

- To create a denominator of $10,$ we multiply the numerator and denominator of our fraction by $2{:}$

$$
\dfrac{{\color{blue}3}\times 2}{{\color{red}5}\times 2} = \dfrac{\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}6}}{\color{red}10}
$$

- To create a denominator of $35,$ we multiply the numerator and denominator of our fraction by $7{:}$

$$
\dfrac{{\color{blue}3}\times 7}{{\color{red}5}\times 7} = \dfrac{\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}21}}{\color{red}35}
$$

- To create a denominator of $50,$ we multiply the numerator and denominator of our fraction by $10{:}$

$$
\dfrac{{\color{blue}3}\times 10}{{\color{red}5}\times 10} = \dfrac{\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}30}}{\color{red}50}
$$

Finally, we fill in the ratio table:

| ${\color{blue}3}$ | ${\color{red}5}$ |
| --- | --- |
| $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}6}$ | ${\color{red}10}$ |
| $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}21}$ | ${\color{red}35}$ |
| $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}30}$ | ${\color{red}50}$ |

\dfrac{{\color{blue}{6}}\div 6}{{\color{red}{18}}\div 6} = \dfrac{{\color{blue}1}}{{\color{red}3}}
$$

$$
\dfrac{{\color{blue}{1}}\times 8}{{\color{red}{3}}\times 8} = \dfrac{\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}8}}{{\color{red}24}}
$$

- To create a numerator of $20,$ we multiply the numerator and denominator of our fraction by $20{:}$

$$
\dfrac{{\color{blue}{1}}\times 20}{{\color{red}{3}}\times 20} = \dfrac{{\color{blue}20}}{\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{red}60}}
$$

Finally, we fill in the ratio table:

| ${\color{blue}6}$ | ${\color{red}18}$ |
| --- | --- |
| $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}8}$ | ${\color{red}24}$ |
| ${\color{blue}20}$ | $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{red}60}$ |

So, from top to bottom, the missing numbers are $8$ and $60.$

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We start with the ratio ${\color{blue}12}:{\color{red}4}$ and write it as a fraction:

$$
\dfrac{{\color{blue}12}}{{\color{red}4}}
$$

 

Now we divide the numerator and the denominator by $4$ to find an equivalent ratio:

$$
\dfrac{{\color{blue}{12}}\div 4}{{\color{red}{4}}\div 4} = \dfrac{{\color{blue}3}}{{\color{red}1}}
$$

We can generate ratios that are equivalent to $3:1$ by finding more equivalent fractions: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3\times 3}{1\times 3} & =\frac{9}{3} \\ \frac{3\times 5}{1\times 5} & =\frac{15}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we fill in the ratio table:

| Reward (in dollars) | Hours of work |
| --- | --- |
| $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}9}$ | $3$ |
| $12$ | $4$ |
| $15$ | $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{red}5}$ |

So, from top to bottom, the missing numbers are $9$ and $5.$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
We start with the ratio $32:2$ and write it as a fraction:

$$
\frac{32}{2}
$$

Now we divide the numerator and the denominator by $2$ to find an equivalent ratio:

$$
\frac{32÷2}{2÷2}=\frac{16}{1}
$$

So the numerator represents the area of the fence in ${\text{m}}^{2}$ ($16$), and the denominator represents the volume of paint in liters ($1$).

We can make a numerator of $80$ by multiplying the numerator and denominator by $5$:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{16\times 5}{1\times 5} & =\frac{80}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

We add this to our ratio table:

| Fence area (square meters) | Paint (liters) |
| --- | --- |
| $32$ | $2$ |
| $80$ | $5$ |
| $160$ | $10$ |

$$

$$

So, Liam needs $5$ liters of paint for $80$ square meters of the fence.

We start with the ratio $4:28$ and write it as a fraction:

$$
\frac{4}{28}

$$
\frac{4÷4}{28÷4}=\frac{1}{7}

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1\times 6}{7\times 6} & =\frac{6}{42} \\ \frac{1\times 9}{7\times 9} & =\frac{9}{63}\end{aligned}
$$

| Painters | Square meters |
| --- | --- |
| $4$ | $28$ |
| $6$ | $42$ |
| $9$ | $63$ |

$$

$$

So, from top to bottom, the missing numbers are $42$ and $63.$

question.html:
Question 3
?

From top to bottom, what are the missing numbers in the ratio table below?



3 5
12 ?
? 30

a
 20 and 18
b
 25 and 18
c
 20 and 21
d
 15 and 15
e
 10 and 15
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We start with the ratio 3:5 and write it as a fraction:

35

So the numerator represents the left-hand entry (3), and the denominator represents the right-hand entry (5).

We can generate equivalent ratios by finding equivalent fractions:

  • To create a numerator of 12, we multiply the numerator and denominator of our fraction by 4: 3×45×4=1220

  • To create a denominator of 30, we multiply the numerator and denominator of our fraction by 6: 3×65×6=1830

Finally, we fill in the ratio table:



3 5
12 20
18 30

So, from top to bottom, the missing numbers are 20 and 18.

last_observation.worked_solution:
We start with the ratio $3:5$ and write it as a fraction:

$$
\frac{3}{5}
$$

So the numerator represents the left-hand entry ($3$), and the denominator represents the right-hand entry ($5$).

We can generate equivalent ratios by finding equivalent fractions:

- To create a numerator of $12,$ we multiply the numerator and denominator of our fraction by $4:$

$$
\frac{3\times 4}{5\times 4}=\frac{12}{20}
$$

- To create a denominator of $30,$ we multiply the numerator and denominator of our fraction by $6:$

$$
\frac{3\times 6}{5\times 6}=\frac{18}{30}
$$

Finally, we fill in the ratio table:

| $3$ | $5$ |
| --- | --- |
| $12$ | $20$ |
| $18$ | $30$ |

$$

$$

So, from top to bottom, the missing numbers are $20$ and $18.$

Question 3

From top to bottom, what are the missing numbers in the ratio table below?



3 5
12 ?
? 30

a
 20 and 18
b
 25 and 18
c
 20 and 21
d
 15 and 15
e
 10 and 15
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We start with the ratio 3:5 and write it as a fraction:

35

So the numerator represents the left-hand entry (3), and the denominator represents the right-hand entry (5).

We can generate equivalent ratios by finding equivalent fractions:

  • To create a numerator of 12, we multiply the numerator and denominator of our fraction by 4: 3×45×4=1220

  • To create a denominator of 30, we multiply the numerator and denominator of our fraction by 6: 3×65×6=1830

Finally, we fill in the ratio table:



3 5
12 20
18 30

So, from top to bottom, the missing numbers are 20 and 18.

$$

$$

question.html:
Question 4
?

From top to bottom, what are the missing numbers in the ratio table below?



5 6
? 24
30 ?

a
 25 and 30
b
 20 and 36
c
 20 and 30
d
 25 and 36
e
 15 and 18
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We start with the ratio 5:6 and write it as a fraction:

56

So the numerator represents the left-hand entry (5), and the denominator represents the right-hand entry (6).

We can generate equivalent ratios by finding equivalent fractions:

  • To create a denominator of 24, we multiply the numerator and denominator of our fraction by 4: 5×46×4=2024

  • To create a numerator of 30, we multiply the numerator and denominator of our fraction by 6: 5×66×6=3036

Finally, we fill in the ratio table:



5 6
20 24
30 36

So, from top to bottom, the missing numbers are 20 and 36.

solution.reasoning: The ratio is 5:6. Multiplying both entries by 4 gives 20:24; multiplying both by 6 gives 30:36. The missing numbers from top to bottom are 20 and 36, option b. No Math Academy answer or grade is captured for this question; the worked example concerns a different table.

| --- | --- |

question.worked_solution:
We start with the ratio $8:24$ and write it as a fraction:

$$
\frac{8}{24}
$$

So the numerator represents the left-hand entry ($8$), and the denominator represents the right-hand entry ($24$).

Now we divide the numerator and the denominator by $8$ to find an equivalent ratio:

$$
\frac{8÷8}{24÷8}=\frac{1}{3}
$$

We can generate equivalent ratios by finding equivalent fractions:

- To create a numerator of $4,$ we multiply the numerator and denominator of our fraction by $4:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1\times 4}{3\times 4}=\frac{4}{12}\end{aligned}
$$

- To create a denominator of $27,$ we multiply the numerator and denominator of our fraction by $9:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1\times 9}{3\times 9} & =\frac{9}{27}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we fill in the ratio table:

| $4$ | $12$ |
| --- | --- |
| $8$ | $24$ |
| $9$ | $27$ |

$$

question.html:
Question 6
?

From top to bottom, what are the missing numbers in the ratio table below?




2 ?
? 16
6 24

a
 3 and 12
b
 8 and 4
c
 8 and 6
d
 1 and 60
e
 12 and 8
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We start with the ratio 6:24 and write it as a fraction:

624

So the numerator represents the left-hand entry (6), and the denominator represents the right-hand entry (24).

We can generate equivalent ratios by finding equivalent fractions:

  • To create a numerator of 2, we divide the numerator and denominator of our fraction by 3: 6÷324÷3=28

  • To create a denominator of 16, we multiply the numerator and denominator of the previous fraction by 2: 2×28×2=416

Finally, we fill in the ratio table:



2 8
4 16
6 24

So, from top to bottom, the missing numbers are 8 and 4.

last_observation.worked_solution:
We start with the ratio $6:24$ and write it as a fraction:

$$
\frac{6}{24}
$$

So the numerator represents the left-hand entry ($6$), and the denominator represents the right-hand entry ($24$).

We can generate equivalent ratios by finding equivalent fractions:

- To create a numerator of $2,$ we divide the numerator and denominator of our fraction by $3:$

$$
\frac{6÷3}{24÷3}=\frac{2}{8}
$$

- To create a denominator of $16,$ we multiply the numerator and denominator of the previous fraction by $2:$

$$
\frac{2\times 2}{8\times 2}=\frac{4}{16}
$$

Finally, we fill in the ratio table:

| $2$ | $8$ |
| --- | --- |
| $4$ | $16$ |
| $6$ | $24$ |

$$

$$

So, from top to bottom, the missing numbers are $8$ and $4.$

? 16
6 24

a
 3 and 12
b
 8 and 4
c
 8 and 6
d
 1 and 60

Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We start with the ratio 6:24 and write it as a fraction:

624

So the numerator represents the left-hand entry (6), and the denominator represents the right-hand entry (24).

We can generate equivalent ratios by finding equivalent fractions:

  • To create a numerator of 2, we divide the numerator and denominator of our fraction by 3: 6÷324÷3=28

  • To create a denominator of 16, we multiply the numerator and denominator of the previous fraction by 2: 2×28×2=416

Finally, we fill in the ratio table:



2 8
4 16
6 24

So, from top to bottom, the missing numbers are 8 and 4.

question.name: Question 7
question.problem:
Liam wants to paint a fence. He knows he needs $2$ liters of paint for $32$ square meters of fence. He creates a ratio table to determine the ratio of the volume of paint to the fenced area for different quantities.

| Fence area (square meters) | Paint (liters) |
| --- | --- |
| $32$ | $2$ |
| $80$ | $?$ |
| $160$ | $10$ |

$$

$$

What volume of paint does Liam need to paint $80$ square meters of the fence?
question.worked_solution:
We start with the ratio $32:2$ and write it as a fraction:

$$
\frac{32}{2}
$$

Now we divide the numerator and the denominator by $2$ to find an equivalent ratio:

$$
\frac{32÷2}{2÷2}=\frac{16}{1}
$$

So the numerator represents the area of the fence in ${\text{m}}^{2}$ ($16$), and the denominator represents the volume of paint in liters ($1$).

We can make a numerator of $80$ by multiplying the numerator and denominator by $5$:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{16\times 5}{1\times 5} & =\frac{80}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

We add this to our ratio table:

| Fence area (square meters) | Paint (liters) |
| --- | --- |
| $32$ | $2$ |
| $80$ | $5$ |
| $160$ | $10$ |

$$

$$

So, Liam needs $5$ liters of paint for $80$ square meters of the fence.

question.name: Question 8
question.problem:
In one hour, a crew of $4$ painters can cover $28$ square meters of a wall's surface in a newly constructed building. A construction manager has created a ratio table to determine how many square meters of the wall's surface can be covered in one hour by crews of $6$ and $9$ painters.

| Painters | Square meters |
| --- | --- |
| $4$ | $28$ |
| $6$ | $?$ |
| $9$ | $?$ |

$$

$$

From top to bottom, what are the missing numbers in the ratio table?
question.worked_solution:
We start with the ratio $4:28$ and write it as a fraction:

$$
\frac{4}{28}
$$

Now we divide the numerator and the denominator by $4$ to find an equivalent ratio:

$$
\frac{4÷4}{28÷4}=\frac{1}{7}
$$

We can generate ratios that are equivalent to $1:7$ by finding more equivalent fractions: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1\times 6}{7\times 6} & =\frac{6}{42} \\ \frac{1\times 9}{7\times 9} & =\frac{9}{63}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we fill in the ratio table:

| Painters | Square meters |
| --- | --- |
| $4$ | $28$ |
| $6$ | $42$ |
| $9$ | $63$ |

$$

question.html:
Question 8
?

In one hour, a crew of 4 painters can cover 28 square meters of a wall's surface in a newly constructed building. A construction manager has created a ratio table to determine how many square meters of the wall's surface can be covered in one hour by crews of 6 and 9 painters.



Painters Square meters
4 28
6 ?
9 ?

From top to bottom, what are the missing numbers in the ratio table?

a
42 and 63
b
36 and 54
c
48 and 72
d
42 and 56
e
56 and 63
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We start with the ratio 4:28 and write it as a fraction:

428

Now we divide the numerator and the denominator by 4 to find an equivalent ratio:

4÷428÷4=17

We can generate ratios that are equivalent to 1:7 by finding more equivalent fractions:

1×67×6=6421×97×9=963

Finally, we fill in the ratio table:



Painters Square meters
4 28
6 42
9 63

So, from top to bottom, the missing numbers are 42 and 63.

feedback.html:
Question 8
?

In one hour, a crew of 4 painters can cover 28 square meters of a wall's surface in a newly constructed building. A construction manager has created a ratio table to determine how many square meters of the wall's surface can be covered in one hour by crews of 6 and 9 painters.



Painters Square meters
4 28
6 ?
9 ?

From top to bottom, what are the missing numbers in the ratio table?

a
42 and 63
b
36 and 54
c
48 and 72
d
42 and 56
e
56 and 63
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We start with the ratio 4:28 and write it as a fraction:

428

Now we divide the numerator and the denominator by 4 to find an equivalent ratio:

4÷428÷4=17

We can generate ratios that are equivalent to 1:7 by finding more equivalent fractions:

1×67×6=6421×97×9=963

Finally, we fill in the ratio table:



Painters Square meters
4 28
6 42
9 63

So, from top to bottom, the missing numbers are 42 and 63.

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
For the transformation $T,$ defined as

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}{e}^{u+v} \\ {e}^{u-v}\end{aligned}].
$$

compute the value of the Jacobian determinant at the point where $[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -5\end{aligned}].$
questions.worked_solution:
Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have $x(u,v)={e}^{u+v}$ and $y(u,v)={e}^{u-v}.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & ={e}^{u+v} & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & ={e}^{u+v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & ={e}^{u-v} & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =-{e}^{u-v}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}{e}^{u+v} & {e}^{u+v} \\ {e}^{u-v} & -{e}^{u-v}\end{aligned}| \\  & ={e}^{u+v}\cdot (-{e}^{u-v})-{e}^{u+v}\cdot {e}^{u-v} \\  & =-{e}^{2u}-{e}^{2u} \\  & =-2{e}^{2u}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, when $[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -5\end{aligned}],$ the value of our Jacobian determinant is

$$
{\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|}_{(0,-5)}=-2{e}^{2(0)}=-2.
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem:
For the transformation $T,$ defined as

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡u \\ -3\operatorname{sin}⁡v\end{aligned}]
$$

compute the value of the Jacobian determinant at the point where $[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\pi /4 \\ \pi /4\end{aligned}].$
questions.worked_solution:
Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have $x(u,v)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡u$ and $y(u,v)=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡v.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡u & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =0 \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =0 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =-3\operatorname{cos}⁡v\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-2\operatorname{sin}⁡u & 0 \\ 0 & -3\operatorname{cos}⁡v\end{aligned}| \\  & =(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡u)\cdot (-3\operatorname{cos}⁡v)-0\cdot 0 \\  & =6\operatorname{sin}⁡u\operatorname{cos}⁡v.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, when $[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\pi /4 \\ \pi /4\end{aligned}],$ the value of our Jacobian determinant is

$$
{\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|}_{(\frac{\pi }{4},\frac{\pi }{4})}=6\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})=3.
$$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem:
Which of the following shows the region in the $uv$-plane where the transformation $T,$ given by 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}u+v \\ {u}^{2}+{v}^{2}\end{aligned}],
$$

is (locally) orientation-reversing?
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that a transformation is (locally) orientation-reversing at the points where the Jacobian determinant is negative:

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}<0
$$

We have

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}u+v \\ {u}^{2}+{v}^{2}\end{aligned}].
$$

Computing the corresponding Jacobian determinant, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2u & 2v\end{aligned}| \\  & =1\cdot (2v)-(2u)\cdot 1 \\  & =2v-2u.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the required regions, we solve the following inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}2v-2u & <0 \\ 2v & <2u \\ v & <u\end{aligned}
$$

 

Notice that the equation 

$$
v=u
$$

defines a straight line, and the coordinates of, say, $(1,-1)$ satisfy the inequality. 

Therefore, the region where the transformation is (locally) orientation-reversing must be the following:

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem:
Which of the following shows the region in the $uv$-plane where the transformation $T,$ given by 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}{e}^{uv} \\ {u}^{2}+v\end{aligned}],
$$

questions.worked_solution:
Recall that a transformation is (locally) orientation-preserving at the points where the Jacobian determinant is positive:

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}>0.
$$

We have

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}{e}^{uv} \\ {u}^{2}+v\end{aligned}].
$$

Computing the corresponding Jacobian determinant, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}v{e}^{uv} & u{e}^{uv} \\ 2u & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =v{e}^{uv}\cdot (1)-(2u)\cdot u{e}^{uv} \\  & ={e}^{uv}(v-2{u}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

To find the required regions, we solve the following inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{uv}(v-2{u}^{2}) & >0 \\ v-2{u}^{2} & >0 \\ v & >2{u}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Notice that the equation 

$$
v=2{u}^{2}
$$

defines a parabola, and the coordinates of, say, $(0,1)$ satisfy the inequality. 

Therefore, the region where the transformation is (locally) orientation-preserving must be the following:

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem:
Consider a small rectangle $Δ$ whose bottom-left corner is located at the point $(-3,3)$ with sides parallel to the coordinate axes in the $uv$-plane and whose area is $\delta A.$ Which of the following gives the best approximation for the area of the image of this rectangle under the action of the transformation $T,$ given by

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}u+{v}^{2} \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v)\end{aligned}]?
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the absolute value of the Jacobian determinant gives the local area scale factor of the transformation at that point:

$$
\text{Area}(T(Δ))≈|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\cdot {{\text{Area}(Δ)}_{⏟}}_{\delta A}
$$

 

Computing the corresponding Jacobian determinant, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 2v \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v)\end{aligned}| \\  & =1\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v)\cdot 2v \\  & =(1-2v)\operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v) \\ {\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|}_{(-3,3)} & =(1-2v)\operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v)\,{|}_{u=-3\,v=3} \\  & =(1-2(3))\operatorname{cos}⁡(-3+3) \\  & =-5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(T(Δ)) & ≈|-5|\cdot \delta A \\  & =5\,\delta A.\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.name: Question 1
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have $x(u,v)={e}^{u+v}$ and $y(u,v)={e}^{u-v}.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & ={e}^{u+v} & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & ={e}^{u+v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & ={e}^{u-v} & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =-{e}^{u-v}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}{e}^{u+v} & {e}^{u+v} \\ {e}^{u-v} & -{e}^{u-v}\end{aligned}| \\  & ={e}^{u+v}\cdot (-{e}^{u-v})-{e}^{u+v}\cdot {e}^{u-v} \\  & =-{e}^{2u}-{e}^{2u} \\  & =-2{e}^{2u}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, when $[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -5\end{aligned}],$ the value of our Jacobian determinant is

$$
{\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|}_{(0,-5)}=-2{e}^{2(0)}=-2.
$$

T:[uv]⟶[eu+veu−v].

compute the value of the Jacobian determinant at the point where [uv]=[0−5].

EXPLANATION

Given a transformation

T:[uv]→[x(u,v)y(u,v)],

the Jacobian determinant of T, denoted ∂(x,y)∂(u,v), is given by

∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=|∂x∂u∂x∂v∂y∂u∂y∂v|.

Here, we have x(u,v)=eu+v and y(u,v)=eu−v.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

∂x∂u=eu+v∂x∂v=eu+v∂y∂u=eu−v∂y∂v=−eu−v

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=|∂x∂u∂x∂v∂y∂u∂y∂v|=|eu+veu+veu−v−eu−v|=eu+v⋅(−eu−v)−eu+v⋅eu−v=−e2u−e2u=−2e2u.

Finally, when [uv]=[0−5], the value of our Jacobian determinant is

∂(x,y)∂(u,v)|(0,−5)=−2e2(0)=−2.

$$

Here, we have $x(u,v)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡u$ and $y(u,v)=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡v.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡u & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =0 \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =0 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =-3\operatorname{cos}⁡v\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-2\operatorname{sin}⁡u & 0 \\ 0 & -3\operatorname{cos}⁡v\end{aligned}| \\  & =(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡u)\cdot (-3\operatorname{cos}⁡v)-0\cdot 0 \\  & =6\operatorname{sin}⁡u\operatorname{cos}⁡v.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, when $[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\pi /4 \\ \pi /4\end{aligned}],$ the value of our Jacobian determinant is

$$
{\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|}_{(\frac{\pi }{4},\frac{\pi }{4})}=6\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})=3.
$$

Question 2
?

For the transformation T, defined as

T:[uv]⟶[2cos⁡u−3sin⁡v]

compute the value of the Jacobian determinant at the point where [uv]=[π/4π/4].

a
3
b
2
c
6
d
4
e
−6
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Given a transformation

T:[uv]→[x(u,v)y(u,v)],

the Jacobian determinant of T, denoted ∂(x,y)∂(u,v), is given by

∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=|∂x∂u∂x∂v∂y∂u∂y∂v|.

Here, we have x(u,v)=2cos⁡u and y(u,v)=−3sin⁡v.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

∂x∂u=−2sin⁡u∂x∂v=0∂y∂u=0∂y∂v=−3cos⁡v

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=|∂x∂u∂x∂v∂y∂u∂y∂v|=|−2sin⁡u00−3cos⁡v|=(−2sin⁡u)⋅(−3cos⁡v)−0⋅0=6sin⁡ucos⁡v.

Finally, when [uv]=[π/4π/4], the value of our Jacobian determinant is

∂(x,y)∂(u,v)|(π4,π4)=6sin⁡(π4)cos⁡(π4)=3.

observed_steps.name: Question 3
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Recall that a transformation is (locally) orientation-reversing at the points where the Jacobian determinant is negative:

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}<0
$$

We have

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}u+v \\ {u}^{2}+{v}^{2}\end{aligned}].
$$

Computing the corresponding Jacobian determinant, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2u & 2v\end{aligned}| \\  & =1\cdot (2v)-(2u)\cdot 1 \\  & =2v-2u.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the required regions, we solve the following inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}2v-2u & <0 \\ 2v & <2u \\ v & <u\end{aligned}
$$

 

Notice that the equation 

$$
v=u
$$

defines a straight line, and the coordinates of, say, $(1,-1)$ satisfy the inequality. 

Therefore, the region where the transformation is (locally) orientation-reversing must be the following:

observed_steps.name: Question 5
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Recall that the absolute value of the Jacobian determinant gives the local area scale factor of the transformation at that point:

$$
\text{Area}(T(Δ))≈|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\cdot {{\text{Area}(Δ)}_{⏟}}_{\delta A}
$$

 

Computing the corresponding Jacobian determinant, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 2v \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v)\end{aligned}| \\  & =1\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v)\cdot 2v \\  & =(1-2v)\operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v) \\ {\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|}_{(-3,3)} & =(1-2v)\operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v)\,{|}_{u=-3\,v=3} \\  & =(1-2(3))\operatorname{cos}⁡(-3+3) \\  & =-5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(T(Δ)) & ≈|-5|\cdot \delta A \\  & =5\,\delta A.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 5
question.problem:
Consider a small rectangle $Δ$ whose bottom-left corner is located at the point $(-3,3)$ with sides parallel to the coordinate axes in the $uv$-plane and whose area is $\delta A.$ Which of the following gives the best approximation for the area of the image of this rectangle under the action of the transformation $T,$ given by

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}u+{v}^{2} \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v)\end{aligned}]?
$$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that the absolute value of the Jacobian determinant gives the local area scale factor of the transformation at that point:

$$
\text{Area}(T(Δ))≈|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\cdot {{\text{Area}(Δ)}_{⏟}}_{\delta A}
$$

 

Computing the corresponding Jacobian determinant, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 2v \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v)\end{aligned}| \\  & =1\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v)\cdot 2v \\  & =(1-2v)\operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v) \\ {\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|}_{(-3,3)} & =(1-2v)\operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v)\,{|}_{u=-3\,v=3} \\  & =(1-2(3))\operatorname{cos}⁡(-3+3) \\  & =-5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(T(Δ)) & ≈|-5|\cdot \delta A \\  & =5\,\delta A.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 1
question.problem:
For the transformation $T,$ defined as

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}{e}^{u+v} \\ {e}^{u-v}\end{aligned}].
$$

compute the value of the Jacobian determinant at the point where $[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -5\end{aligned}].$
question.worked_solution:
Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have $x(u,v)={e}^{u+v}$ and $y(u,v)={e}^{u-v}.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & ={e}^{u+v} & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & ={e}^{u+v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & ={e}^{u-v} & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =-{e}^{u-v}\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 3
question.problem:
Which of the following shows the region in the $uv$-plane where the transformation $T,$ given by 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}u+v \\ {u}^{2}+{v}^{2}\end{aligned}],
$$

is (locally) orientation-reversing?
question.worked_solution:
Recall that a transformation is (locally) orientation-reversing at the points where the Jacobian determinant is negative:

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}<0
$$

We have

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}u+v \\ {u}^{2}+{v}^{2}\end{aligned}].
$$

Computing the corresponding Jacobian determinant, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2u & 2v\end{aligned}| \\  & =1\cdot (2v)-(2u)\cdot 1 \\  & =2v-2u.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the required regions, we solve the following inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}2v-2u & <0 \\ 2v & <2u \\ v & <u\end{aligned}
$$

 

Notice that the equation 

$$
v=u
$$

question.worked_solution:

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}>0.
$$

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}{e}^{uv} \\ {u}^{2}+v\end{aligned}].

question.name: Question 5
question.problem:
Consider a small rectangle $Δ$ whose bottom-left corner is located at the point $(-3,3)$ with sides parallel to the coordinate axes in the $uv$-plane and whose area is $\delta A.$ Which of the following gives the best approximation for the area of the image of this rectangle under the action of the transformation $T,$ given by

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}u+{v}^{2} \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v)\end{aligned}]?
$$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that the absolute value of the Jacobian determinant gives the local area scale factor of the transformation at that point:

$$
\text{Area}(T(Δ))≈|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\cdot {{\text{Area}(Δ)}_{⏟}}_{\delta A}
$$

 

Computing the corresponding Jacobian determinant, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 2v \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v)\end{aligned}| \\  & =1\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v)\cdot 2v \\  & =(1-2v)\operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v) \\ {\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|}_{(-3,3)} & =(1-2v)\operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v)\,{|}_{u=-3\,v=3} \\  & =(1-2(3))\operatorname{cos}⁡(-3+3) \\  & =-5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(T(Δ)) & ≈|-5|\cdot \delta A \\  & =5\,\delta A.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 5
?

Consider a small rectangle Δ whose bottom-left corner is located at the point (−3,3) with sides parallel to the coordinate axes in the uv-plane and whose area is δA. Which of the following gives the best approximation for the area of the image of this rectangle under the action of the transformation T, given by T:[uv]⟶[u+v2sin⁡(u+v)]?

a
12δA
b
7δA
c
5δA
d
6δA
e
2δA
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall that the absolute value of the Jacobian determinant gives the local area scale factor of the transformation at that point:

Area(T(Δ))≈|∂(x,y)∂(u,v)|⋅Area(Δ)⏟δA

Computing the corresponding Jacobian determinant, we obtain the following:

∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=|∂x∂u∂x∂v∂y∂u∂y∂v|=|12vcos⁡(u+v)cos⁡(u+v)|=1⋅cos⁡(u+v)−cos⁡(u+v)⋅2v=(1−2v)cos⁡(u+v)∂(x,y)∂(u,v)|(−3,3)=(1−2v)cos⁡(u+v)|u=−3v=3=(1−2(3))cos⁡(−3+3)=−5

Therefore, we have

Area(T(Δ))≈|−5|⋅δA=5δA.

last_observation.worked_solution:
Recall that the absolute value of the Jacobian determinant gives the local area scale factor of the transformation at that point:

$$
\text{Area}(T(Δ))≈|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\cdot {{\text{Area}(Δ)}_{⏟}}_{\delta A}
$$

 

Computing the corresponding Jacobian determinant, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 2v \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v)\end{aligned}| \\  & =1\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v)\cdot 2v \\  & =(1-2v)\operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v) \\ {\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|}_{(-3,3)} & =(1-2v)\operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v)\,{|}_{u=-3\,v=3} \\  & =(1-2(3))\operatorname{cos}⁡(-3+3) \\  & =-5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(T(Δ)) & ≈|-5|\cdot \delta A \\  & =5\,\delta A.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5
?

Consider a small rectangle Δ whose bottom-left corner is located at the point (−3,3) with sides parallel to the coordinate axes in the uv-plane and whose area is δA. Which of the following gives the best approximation for the area of the image of this rectangle under the action of the transformation T, given by T:[uv]⟶[u+v2sin⁡(u+v)]?

a
12δA
b
7δA
c
5δA
d
6δA
e
2δA
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall that the absolute value of the Jacobian determinant gives the local area scale factor of the transformation at that point:

Area(T(Δ))≈|∂(x,y)∂(u,v)|⋅Area(Δ)⏟δA

Computing the corresponding Jacobian determinant, we obtain the following:

∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=|∂x∂u∂x∂v∂y∂u∂y∂v|=|12vcos⁡(u+v)cos⁡(u+v)|=1⋅cos⁡(u+v)−cos⁡(u+v)⋅2v=(1−2v)cos⁡(u+v)∂(x,y)∂(u,v)|(−3,3)=(1−2v)cos⁡(u+v)|u=−3v=3=(1−2(3))cos⁡(−3+3)=−5

Therefore, we have

Area(T(Δ))≈|−5|⋅δA=5δA.

questions.name: Question 1
questions.worked_solution:
We can write the given problem as the following product:

$$
\boxed{}\,%\times 2=6
$$

Using the relationship between multiplication and division, we can write our problem as:

$$
\boxed{}\,%=6÷2=\frac{6}{2}
$$

To write this fraction as a percentage, we write an equivalent fraction with $100$ as the denominator:

$$
\frac{6}{2}=\frac{6\times 50}{2\times 50}=\frac{300}{100}
$$

Now we can write this fraction as a percentage:

$$
\frac{300}{100}=300\,%
$$

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
Consider the initial value problem

$$
{y}^{′}-5y=f(x),\,y(3)=-2
$$

where $f(x)$ is a $4$-periodic function. Fill in the missing part in the solution of the IVP, where the infinite sum on the right-hand side below represents a particular solution ${y}_{p}$ of the differential equation.

*Hint: In this specific problem, the forcing function $f(x)$ is chosen such that the particular solution ${y}_{p}$ satisfies ${y}_{p}(3)=0.$*

The solution is 

$y(x)∼$   
{{field-1}} 
$+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}cos\,(\frac{\pi n}{2}x)+{b}_{n}sin\,(\frac{\pi n}{2}x))$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the general solution of a linear differential equation of the form ${y}^{′}+P(x)y=f(x)$ is given by

$$
y={y}_{c}+{y}_{p},
$$

where ${y}_{c}$ is the general solution of the corresponding homogeneous equation, and ${y}_{p}$ is a particular solution.

First, we find the homogeneous solution. The general solution of ${y}^{′}-5y=0$ is 

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{5x},
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

Next, we identify the form of the general solution. Because the operator ${y}^{′}-5y$ involves a first derivative, a periodic forcing function $f(x)$ results in a particular solution containing both sine and cosine terms:

$$
y(x)∼A{e}^{5x}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}cos\,(\frac{\pi n}{2}x)+{b}_{n}sin\,(\frac{\pi n}{2}x))
$$

Now, we apply the initial condition $y(3)=-2.$ Using the hint that the particular solution part evaluates to zero at $x=3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y(3) & =A{e}^{5(3)}+{y}_{p}(3) \\ -2 & =A{e}^{15}+0 \\ A & =-2{e}^{-15}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $A$ back into the homogeneous part:

$$
{y}_{c}=(-2{e}^{-15}){e}^{5x}=-2{e}^{5x-15}
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
y(x)∼-2{e}^{5x-15}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}cos\,(\frac{\pi n}{2}x)+{b}_{n}sin\,(\frac{\pi n}{2}x)).
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the initial value problem

$$
{y}^{′}+4y=f(x),\,y(0)=1
$$

where $f(x)$ is a $3$-periodic function. Fill in the missing part in the solution of the IVP, where the infinite sum on the right-hand side below represents a particular solution ${y}_{p}$ of the differential equation.

*Hint: In this specific problem, the forcing function $f(x)$ is chosen such that the particular solution ${y}_{p}$ satisfies ${y}_{p}(0)=0.$*

The solution is 

$y(x)∼$  
{{field-1}} 
$+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}cos\,(\frac{2\pi n}{3}x)+{b}_{n}sin\,(\frac{2\pi n}{3}x))$
questions.worked_solution:

$$

First, we find the homogeneous solution. The general solution of ${y}^{′}+4y=0$ is 

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{-4x},
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

Next, we identify the form of the general solution. Because the operator ${y}^{′}+4y$ involves a first derivative, a periodic forcing function $f(x)$ results in a particular solution containing both sine and cosine terms:

$$

$$

Finally, we substitute $A$ back into the homogeneous part:

$$
{y}_{c}={e}^{-4x}

$$
y(x)∼{e}^{-4x}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}cos\,(\frac{2\pi n}{3}x)+{b}_{n}sin\,(\frac{2\pi n}{3}x)).

questions.problem:
Consider the initial value problem

$$
{y}^{′}+5y=f(x),\,y(0)=2
$$

where $f(x)$ is a $2$-periodic function. Fill in the missing part in the solution of the IVP, where the infinite sum on the right-hand side below represents a particular solution ${y}_{p}$ of the differential equation.

*Hint: In this specific problem, the forcing function $f(x)$ is chosen such that the particular solution ${y}_{p}$ satisfies ${y}_{p}(0)=0.$*

The solution is 

$y(x)∼$  
{{field-1}} 
$+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x))$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the general solution of a linear differential equation of the form ${y}^{′}+P(x)y=f(x)$ is given by

$$
y={y}_{c}+{y}_{p},
$$

where ${y}_{c}$ is the general solution of the corresponding homogeneous equation, and ${y}_{p}$ is a particular solution.

First, we find the homogeneous solution. The general solution of ${y}^{′}+5y=0$ is 

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{-5x},
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

Next, we identify the form of the general solution. Because the operator ${y}^{′}+5y$ involves a first derivative, a periodic forcing function $f(x)$ results in a particular solution containing both sine and cosine terms:

$$
y(x)∼A{e}^{-5x}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x))
$$

Now, we apply the initial condition $y(0)=2.$ Using the hint that the particular solution part evaluates to zero at $x=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & =A{e}^{-5(0)}+{y}_{p}(0) \\ 2 & =A(1)+0 \\ A & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $A$ back into the homogeneous part:

$$
{y}_{c}=2{e}^{-5x}
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
y(x)∼2{e}^{-5x}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x)).
$$

questions.name: Question 6
questions.problem:
$$
{y}^{″}+3{\pi }^{2}y=f(x),\,y(0)=0,\,{y}^{′}(0)=0
$$

Consider the initial value problem above, where $f(x)$ is an odd, $4$-periodic function. Select the missing part in the solution of the IVP, where the second infinite sum on the right-hand side below represents a particular solution of the differential equation.

$$
y(x)∼{{field-1}}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,\frac{12(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}{\pi }^{3}(12-{n}^{2})}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2})
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the general solution of a linear differential equation of the form ${y}^{″}+{\omega }^{2}y=f(x)$ is given by $y={y}_{c}+{y}_{p},$ where ${y}_{c}$ is the solution to the homogeneous equation and ${y}_{p}$ is a particular solution.

First, we address the particular solution ${y}_{p}.$ Since $f(x)$ is an odd function, its Fourier series consists only of sine terms. For a second-order equation with no ${y}^{′}$ (damping) term, the particular solution inherits this property and is also an odd function. This is represented by the term

$$
{y}_{p}(x)={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{12(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}{\pi }^{3}(12-{n}^{2})}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}).
$$

Next, we find the homogeneous solution. The characteristic equation ${\lambda }^{2}+3{\pi }^{2}=0$ gives roots $\lambda =\pm \sqrt{3}\pi \,\text{i}.$ So, we have

$$
{y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{3}\pi x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{3}\pi x).
$$

To find the unknown constants, we apply the initial conditions. Using $y(0)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & =A\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)+{y}_{p}(0) \\ 0 & =A(1)+0+0 \\ A & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Note that ${y}_{p}(0)=0$ because the particular solution is a sine series.

Next, we use the derivative condition ${y}^{′}(0)=0.$ First, we compute the derivative of the total solution (with $A=0$):

$$
{y}^{′}(x)∼B\sqrt{3}\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{3}\pi x)+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{6(-1)^{n}}{n{\pi }^{2}(12-{n}^{2})}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2})
$$

Applying ${y}^{′}(0)=0$ and noting that $\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =B\sqrt{3}\pi +{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{6(-1)^{n}}{n{\pi }^{2}(12-{n}^{2})} \\ B\sqrt{3}\pi  & =-{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{6(-1)^{n}}{n{\pi }^{2}(12-{n}^{2})} \\ B & =-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}\pi }{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{6(-1)^{n}}{n{\pi }^{2}(12-{n}^{2})} \\  & =-{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{6(-1)^{n}}{\sqrt{3}{\pi }^{3}(12-{n}^{2})} \\  & =-{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{2\sqrt{3}(-1)^{n}}{n{\pi }^{3}(12-{n}^{2})}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $B$ back into ${y}_{c}=B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{3}\pi x)$, we find the missing part:

$$
y(x)∼-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{3}\pi x){\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{2\sqrt{3}(-1)^{n}}{n{\pi }^{3}(12-{n}^{2})}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,\frac{12(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}{\pi }^{3}(12-{n}^{2})}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2})
$$

questions.name: Question 7
questions.problem:
$$
{y}^{″}+3y=f(x),\,y(0)=0,\,{y}^{′}(0)=-5
$$

Consider the initial value problem above, where $f(x)$ is an odd, $4\pi $-periodic function. Select the missing part in the solution of the IVP, where the second infinite sum on the right-hand side below represents a particular solution of the differential equation.

$$
y(x)∼{{field-1}}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}sin\,(\frac{n}{2}x)
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the general solution of a linear differential equation of the form ${y}^{″}+{\omega }^{2}y=f(x)$ is given by $y={y}_{c}+{y}_{p},$ where ${y}_{c}$ is the solution to the homogeneous equation and ${y}_{p}$ is a particular solution.

First, we address the particular solution ${y}_{p}.$ Since $f(x)$ is an odd function, its Fourier series consists only of sine terms. For a second-order equation with no ${y}^{′}$ (damping) term, the particular solution inherits this property and is also an odd function. This is represented by the term

$$
{y}_{p}(x)={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}sin\,(\frac{n}{2}x).
$$

Next, we find the homogeneous solution. The characteristic equation ${\lambda }^{2}+3=0$ gives roots $\lambda =\pm \sqrt{3}\text{i}.$ So, we have

$$
{y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{3}x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{3}x).
$$

To find the unknown constants, we apply the initial conditions. Using $y(0)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & =A\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)+{y}_{p}(0) \\ 0 & =A(1)+0+0 \\ A & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Note that ${y}_{p}(0)=0$ because the particular solution is a sine series.

Next, we use the derivative condition ${y}^{′}(0)=-5.$ First, we compute the derivative of the total solution (with $A=0$):

$$
{y}^{′}(x)∼B\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{3}x)+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{n}{2}{b}_{n}cos\,(\frac{n}{2}x)
$$

Applying ${y}^{′}(0)=-5$ and noting that $\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}-5 & =B\sqrt{3}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{n}{2}{b}_{n} \\ B\sqrt{3} & =-5-{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{n}{2}{b}_{n} \\ B & =-\frac{5}{\sqrt{3}}-{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{n{b}_{n}}{2\sqrt{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $B$ back into ${y}_{c}=B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{3}x),$ we find the missing part:

$$
y(x)∼\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{3}x)(-\frac{5}{\sqrt{3}}-{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{n{b}_{n}}{2\sqrt{3}})+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}sin\,(\frac{n}{2}x)
$$

questions.name: Question 8
questions.problem:
$$
{y}^{″}+3y=f(x),\,y(0)=5,\,{y}^{′}(0)=0
$$

Consider the initial value problem above, where $f(x)$ is an even, $2\pi $-periodic function. Select the missing part in the solution of the IVP, where the second infinite sum on the right-hand side below represents a particular solution of the differential equation.

$$
y(x)∼{{field-1}}+{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the general solution of a linear differential equation of the form ${y}^{″}+{\omega }^{2}y=f(x)$ is given by $y={y}_{c}+{y}_{p},$ where ${y}_{c}$ is the solution to the homogeneous equation and ${y}_{p}$ is a particular solution.

First, we address the particular solution ${y}_{p}.$ Since $f(x)$ is an even function and the differential operator contains no ${y}^{′}$ (damping) term, the particular solution inherits the symmetry and is also an even function consisting only of cosine terms. This is represented by the term

$$
{y}_{p}(x)={\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx).
$$

Next, we find the homogeneous solution. The characteristic equation ${\lambda }^{2}+3=0$ gives roots $\lambda =\pm \sqrt{3}\text{i}.$ So, we have

$$
{y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{3}x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{3}x).
$$

To find the unknown constants, we apply the initial conditions. Differentiating the total solution gives

$$
{y}^{′}(x)∼-A\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{3}x)+B\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{3}x)-{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }n{a}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx).
$$

Using the derivative condition ${y}^{′}(0)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(0) & =-A\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)+B\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)-{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }n{a}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(0) \\ 0 & =0+B\sqrt{3}-0 \\ B & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Note that because the total solution is an even function, its derivative is an odd function, which must vanish at $x=0.$

Next, we use the condition $y(0)=5.$ With $B=0,$ the total solution is

$$
y(x)∼A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{3}x)+{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx).
$$

Applying $y(0)=5$ and noting that $\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}5 & =A+{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n} \\ A & =5-{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $A$ back into ${y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{3}x),$ we find the missing part:

$$
y(x)∼\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{3}x)(5-{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n})+{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)
$$

questions.name: Question 9
questions.problem:
$$
{y}^{″}+5y=f(x),\,y(0)=0,\,{y}^{′}(0)=4
$$

Consider the initial value problem above, where $f(x)$ is an odd, $2\pi $-periodic function. Select the missing part in the solution of the IVP, where the second infinite sum on the right-hand side below represents a particular solution of the differential equation.

$$
y(x)∼{{field-1}}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the general solution of a linear differential equation of the form ${y}^{″}+{\omega }^{2}y=f(x)$ is given by $y={y}_{c}+{y}_{p},$ where ${y}_{c}$ is the solution to the homogeneous equation and ${y}_{p}$ is a particular solution.

First, we address the particular solution ${y}_{p}.$ Since $f(x)$ is an odd function, its Fourier series consists only of sine terms. For a second-order equation with no ${y}^{′}$ (damping) term, the particular solution inherits this property and is also an odd function. This is represented by the term

$$
{y}_{p}(x)={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx).
$$

Next, we find the homogeneous solution. The characteristic equation ${\lambda }^{2}+5=0$ gives roots $\lambda =\pm \sqrt{5}\text{i}.$ So, we have

$$
{y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{5}x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{5}x).
$$

To find the unknown constants, we apply the initial conditions. Using $y(0)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & =A\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)+{y}_{p}(0) \\ 0 & =A(1)+0+0 \\ A & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Note that ${y}_{p}(0)=0$ because the particular solution is a sine series.

Next, we use the derivative condition ${y}^{′}(0)=4.$ First, we compute the derivative of the total solution (with $A=0$):

$$
{y}^{′}(x)∼B\sqrt{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{5}x)+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }n{b}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx).
$$

Applying ${y}^{′}(0)=4$ and noting that $\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)=1,$ we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}4 & =B\sqrt{5}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }n{b}_{n} \\ B\sqrt{5} & =4-{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }n{b}_{n} \\ B & =\frac{4}{\sqrt{5}}-{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{n{b}_{n}}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $B$ back into ${y}_{c}=B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{5}x),$ we find the missing part:

$$
y(x)∼\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{5}x)(\frac{4}{\sqrt{5}}-{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{n{b}_{n}}{\sqrt{5}})+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx).
$$
