question.html:
Question 11
?

Consider the linear transformation T:[xy]⟶[2x+4y−x+2y]. Find Ker(T).

a
{[00]}
b
{[x−2x]:x∈R}
c
{[3yy]:y∈R}
d
{[x12x]:x∈R}
e
{[−2yy]:y∈R}
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Finding the kernel of T is equivalent to finding the null space of the standard matrix of T.

For the given linear transformation, the standard matrix is T=[24−12].

Setting x=[xy], we then need to solve the equation Tx=0. First, we reduce T to row echelon form, as follows:

T=[24−12]R2:=R2+12R1∼[2404]

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is x and y. From the second equation, we obtain y=0. Substituting this into the first equation, we have x=0.

Therefore, the kernel of the linear transformation T is {[00]}.
question.knowledge_point: Finding the Kernel of a Linear Transformation

observed_steps.name: Question 12
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Kernel of a Linear Transformation
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Finding the kernel of $T$ is equivalent to finding the null space of the standard matrix of $T.$

Fror the given linear transformation, the standard matrix is $T=[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & -2 \\ -3 & -6 & 3 \\ 4 & 8 & -4\end{aligned}].$ 

Setting $x=[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}],$ we then need to solve the equation $Tx=0.$ First, we find reduce $T$ to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & -2 \\ -3 & -6 & 3 \\ 4 & 8 & -4\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(\frac{3}{2}){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 4 & 8 & -4\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-2){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is $x$, and we have two free variables, $y,$ and $z.$ That means we need to find $x$ in terms of $y$ and $z.$ 

From the first equation, we get 

$$
x=-2y+z.
$$

  

Therefore, the kernel of the linear transformation $\,T$ is $\{[\begin{aligned}-2y+z \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]\,:\,y,z\in R\}.$

question.name: Question 12
question.problem: Consider the linear transformation $T:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}2x+4y-2z \\ -3x-6y+3z \\ 4x+8y-4z\end{aligned}].$ Find $\,\text{Ker}(T).$

$$

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is $x$, and we have two free variables, $y,$ and $z.$ That means we need to find $x$ in terms of $y$ and $z.$

question.html:
Question 12
?

Consider the linear transformation T:[xyz]⟶[2x+4y−2z−3x−6y+3z4x+8y−4z]. Find Ker(T).

a
{[000]}
b
{[xy4x+2y]:x,y∈R}
c
{[x4x+2zz]:x,y∈R}
d
{[−4zy2z]:z∈R}
e
{[−2y+zyz]:y,z∈R}.
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Finding the kernel of T is equivalent to finding the null space of the standard matrix of T.

Fror the given linear transformation, the standard matrix is T=[24−2−3−6348−4].

Setting x=[xyz], we then need to solve the equation Tx=0. First, we find reduce T to row echelon form, as follows:

T=[24−2−3−6348−4]R2:=R2+(32)R1∼[24−200048−4]R3:=R3+(−2)R1∼[24−2000000]

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is x, and we have two free variables, y, and z. That means we need to find x in terms of y and z.

From the first equation, we get x=−2y+z.

Therefore, the kernel of the linear transformation T is {[−2y+zyz]:y,z∈R}.

observed_steps.name: Question 13
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Kernel of a Linear Transformation
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Finding the kernel of $T$ is equivalent to finding the null space of the standard matrix of $T.$

Fror the given linear transformation, the standard matrix is $T=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ 6 & -3 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].$

Setting $x=[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}],$ we then need to solve the equation $Tx=0.$ First, we find reduce $T$ to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ 6 & -3 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-6{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & 9 & -9 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{9}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is $x$ and $y$, and we have one free variable, $z.$ That means we need to find $x$ and $y$ in terms of $z.$

From the second equation, we get $y=z.$ Substituting these into the first equation, we have 

$$
x=2y-z=2z-z=z.
$$

Therefore, the kernel of the linear transformation $\,T$ is $\{[\begin{aligned}z \\ z \\ z\end{aligned}]\,:\,z\in R\}.$

\begin{aligned}T & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ 6 & -3 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-6{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & 9 & -9 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{9}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is $x$ and $y$, and we have one free variable, $z.$ That means we need to find $x$ and $y$ in terms of $z.$

From the second equation, we get $y=z.$ Substituting these into the first equation, we have 

$$
x=2y-z=2z-z=z.
$$

Therefore, the kernel of the linear transformation $\,T$ is $\{[\begin{aligned}z \\ z \\ z\end{aligned}]\,:\,z\in R\}.$

Question 13
?

Consider the linear transformation T:[xyz]⟶[x−2y+z6x−3y−3z0]. Find Ker(T).

a
{[−110]}
b
{[−yy−y]:y∈R}
c
{[−z2zz]:z∈R}
d
{[y+zyz]:y,z∈R}
e
{[zzz]:z∈R}
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Finding the kernel of T is equivalent to finding the null space of the standard matrix of T.

Fror the given linear transformation, the standard matrix is T=[1−216−3−3000].

Setting x=[xyz], we then need to solve the equation Tx=0. First, we find reduce T to row echelon form, as follows:

T=[1−216−3−3000]R2:=R2−6R1∼[1−2109−9000]R2:=19R2∼[1−2101−1000]

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is x and y, and we have one free variable, z. That means we need to find x and y in terms of z.

From the second equation, we get y=z. Substituting these into the first equation, we have x=2y−z=2z−z=z.

Therefore, the kernel of the linear transformation T is {[zzz]:z∈R}.

observed_steps.worked_solution:
Finding the kernel of $\,T\,$ is equivalent to finding the null space of the standard matrix of $\,T.$

For the given linear transformation, the standard matrix is $T=[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 & -6 \\ 1 & -4 & 1 \\ 8 & 2 & 8\end{aligned}].$

Setting $x=[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}],$ we then need to solve the equation $Tx=0.$ First, we reduce $T$ to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 & -6 \\ 1 & -4 & 1 \\ 8 & 2 & 8\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{6}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 & -6 \\ 0 & -\frac{7}{2} & 0 \\ 8 & 2 & 8\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+\frac{4}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 & -6 \\ 0 & -\frac{7}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 6 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+\frac{12}{7}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 & -6 \\ 0 & -\frac{7}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is $x$ and $y$, and we have one free variable, $z.$ That means we need to find $x$ and $y$ in terms of $z.$

From the second equation, we get $y=0.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we have $x=-z.$ 

Therefore, if $x\in \text{Ker}(T),$ then 

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}-z \\ 0 \\ z\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]z,\,z\in R.
$$

This implies that $B=\{[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\}$ is a basis of $\text{Ker}(T).$

Question 14

Find a basis of Ker(T) given that T:[xyz]⟶[3y−6z−6x−4y+x+z2y+8z+8x].

a
{[210]}
b
{[−12−31]}
c
{[−10−3]}

{[110],[0−21]}

{[−101]}
Submit

EXPLANATION

Finding the kernel of T is equivalent to finding the null space of the standard matrix of T.

For the given linear transformation, the standard matrix is T=[−63−61−41828].

Setting x=[xyz], we then need to solve the equation Tx=0. First, we reduce T to row echelon form, as follows:

T=[−63−61−41828]R2:=R2+16R1∼[−63−60−720828]R3:=R3+43R1∼[−63−60−720060]R3:=R3+127R2∼[−63−60−720000]

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is x and y, and we have one free variable, z. That means we need to find x and y in terms of z.

From the second equation, we get y=0. Substituting this into the first equation, we have x=−z.

Therefore, if x∈Ker(T), then

x=[−z0z]=[−101]z,z∈R.

This implies that B={[−101]} is a basis of Ker(T).

observed_steps.name: Question 15
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Kernel of a Linear Transformation
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Finding the kernel of $T$ is equivalent to finding the null space of the standard matrix of $T.$

Fror the given linear transformation, the standard matrix is $T=[\begin{aligned}-9 & -3 & 3 \\ -12 & -4 & 4 \\ 6 & 8 & 10\end{aligned}].$

Setting $x=[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}],$ we then need to solve the equation $Tx=0.$ First, we find reduce $T$ to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T & =[\begin{aligned}-9 & -3 & 3 \\ -12 & -4 & 4 \\ 6 & 8 & 10\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-\frac{4}{3}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-9 & -3 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 6 & 8 & 10\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+\frac{2}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-9 & -3 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 6 & 12\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & ↔{R}_{3} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-9 & -3 & 3 \\ 0 & 6 & 12 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is $x$ and $y$, and we have one free variable, $z.$ That means we need to find $x$ and $y$ in terms of $z.$

From the second equation, we get $y=-2z.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}-9x-3y+3z & =0 \\ -9x-3(-2z)+3z & =0 \\ -9x+9z & =0 \\ x & =z\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the kernel of the linear transformation $\,T$ is $\{[\begin{aligned}z \\ -2z \\ z\end{aligned}]\,:\,z\in R\}.$

Question 15
?

Consider the linear transformation T:[xyz]⟶[−9x−3y+3z−12x−4y+4z6x+8y+10z]. Find Ker(T).

a
{[xx−2zz]:x,z∈R}
b
{[−13z−3zz]:z∈R}
c
{[z−2zz]:z∈R}
d
{[xy2x−3y]:x,y∈R}
e
{[y+zyz]:y,z∈R}
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Finding the kernel of T is equivalent to finding the null space of the standard matrix of T.

Fror the given linear transformation, the standard matrix is T=[−9−33−12−446810].

Setting x=[xyz], we then need to solve the equation Tx=0. First, we find reduce T to row echelon form, as follows:

T=[−9−33−12−446810]R2:=R2+(−43)R1∼[−9−330006810]R3:=R3+23R1∼[−9−330000612]R2↔R3∼[−9−330612000]

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is x and y, and we have one free variable, z. That means we need to find x and y in terms of z.

From the second equation, we get y=−2z. Substituting this into the first equation, we have −9x−3y+3z=0−9x−3(−2z)+3z=0−9x+9z=0x=z

Therefore, the kernel of the linear transformation T is {[z−2zz]:z∈R}.

tutorial.name: The Nullity of a Linear Transformation
tutorial.problem:
The **nullity** of a linear transformation $\mathbf{T}$ is the dimension of its kernel. This means that

$$
\text{nullity}(\mathbf{T}) = \dim(\textrm{Ker}(\mathbf{T})) = \text{nullity}(T).
$$

To compute the dimension of the kernel of $\mathbf{T},$ we just have to reduce the matrix $T$ to row echelon form and count the number of  non-pivot columns.

observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we write down the standard matrix of $\mathbf{T}\mathbin{:}$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14152450/assets/05f4b52e6db509788a7f98278fa003da71fde06817e700d7bbb9fe4827e9551a.svg)

Recall that $\textrm{nullity}(\mathbf{T}) = \textrm{nullity}(T) = \textrm{dim}(\textrm{Null}(T)).$

In order to find $\textrm{dim}(\textrm{Null}(T)),$ we reduce $T$ to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & 0 \\ 4 & 10 & -1 \\ -6 & -12 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & -1 \\ -6 & -12 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has no non-pivot columns. Therefore, 

$$
\textrm{nullity}(\mathbf{T})=\textrm{dim}(\textrm{Null}(T))=0.
$$

observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Nullity of a Linear Transformation
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we write down the standard matrix of $T:$

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Recall that $\text{nullity}(T)=\text{nullity}(T)=\text{dim}(\text{Null}(T)).$ Notice that $T$ has $2$ non-pivot columns. 

Therefore, $\text{nullity}(T)=\text{dim}(\text{Null}(T))=2.$

Finally, we obtain

$$
2\cdot \text{nullity}(T)-4=2\cdot 2-4=0.
$$

observed_steps.name: Question 17
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Nullity of a Linear Transformation
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we write down the standard matrix of $T:$

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & -1 \\ 1 & -1 & 1 \\ -6 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}]
$$

Recall that $\text{nullity}(T)=\text{nullity}(T)=\text{dim}(\text{Null}(T)).$

In order to find $\text{dim}(\text{Null}(T)),$ we reduce $T$ to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & -1 \\ 1 & -1 & 1 \\ -6 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-\frac{1}{2}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & \frac{3}{2} \\ -6 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & \frac{3}{2} \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has $1$ non-pivot column (the $3$rd one). Therefore, 

$$
\text{nullity}(T)=\text{dim}(\text{Null}(T))=1.
$$

observed_steps.name: Question 18
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Nullity of a Linear Transformation
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we write down the standard matrix of $T:$

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}3 & -8 \\ -6 & 16\end{aligned}]
$$

Recall that $\text{nullity}(T)=\text{nullity}(T)=\text{dim}(\text{Null}(T)).$

In order to find $\text{dim}(\text{Null}(T)),$ we reduce $T$ to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -8 \\ -6 & 16\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}3 & -8 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has $1$ non-pivot column (the $2$nd one). 

Therefore, $\text{nullity}(T)=\text{dim}(\text{Null}(T))=1.$

Finally, we obtain

$$
2\cdot \text{nullity}(T)-3=2\cdot 1-3=-1.
$$

Question 18
?

Given the linear transformation T:[xy]⟶[3x−8y16y−6x], find 2⋅nullity(T)−3.

a
−1
b
0
c
−2
d
1
e
−3
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we write down the standard matrix of T:

T=[3−8−616]

Recall that nullity(T)=nullity(T)=dim(Null(T)).

In order to find dim(Null(T)), we reduce T to row echelon form, as follows:

T=[3−8−616]R2:=R2+2R1∼[3−800]

The reduced matrix above has 1 non-pivot column (the 2nd one).

Therefore, nullity(T)=dim(Null(T))=1.

Finally, we obtain

2⋅nullity(T)−3=2⋅1−3=−1.

observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we write down the standard matrix of $T:$

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 & -4 \\ 2 & -6 & 7 \\ 4 & -12 & 16\end{aligned}]
$$

Recall that $\text{nullity}(T)=\text{nullity}(T)=\text{dim}(\text{Null}(T)).$

In order to find $\text{dim}(\text{Null}(T)),$ we reduce $T$ to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 & -4 \\ 2 & -6 & 7 \\ 4 & -12 & 16\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 & -4 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \\ 4 & -12 & 16\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+4{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 & -4 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has $1$ non-pivot columns (the 2nd one).  Therefore, 

$$
\text{nullity}(T)=\text{dim}(\text{Null}(T))=1.
$$

observed_steps.name: Question 20
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Nullity of a Linear Transformation
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we write down the standard matrix of $T:$

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

Recall that $\text{nullity}(T)=\text{nullity}(T)=\text{dim}(\text{Null}(T)).$

In order to find $\text{dim}(\text{Null}(T)),$ we reduce $T$ to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has no non-pivot column. Therefore, $\text{nullity}(T)=\text{dim}(\text{Null}(T))=0.$

Finally, we obtain

$$
2\cdot \text{nullity}(T)-1=2\cdot 0-1=-1.
$$

question.name: Question 1
question.problem:
Consider the linear transformation 
$T:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}4x+2y \\ 6x+3y\end{aligned}]$ 
and the vectors 
${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 6\end{aligned}],{v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 6\end{aligned}].$
Which of the given vectors belong to the kernel of $T?$
question.worked_solution:
A vector $u$ belongs to the kernel of a linear transformation $T$ if $T(u)=0.$ 

Therefore, we need to compute $T({v}_{i})$ for each vector ${v}_{i}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}T({v}_{1}) & =T([\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}8 \\ 12\end{aligned}] \\ T({v}_{2}) & =T([\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 6\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ T({v}_{3}) & =T([\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 6\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\,T({v}_{2})=0,$ we conclude that the only vector that belongs to the kernel of $\,T$ is ${v}_{2}.$

Question 1
?

Consider the linear transformation T:[xy]⟶[4x+2y6x+3y] and the vectors v1=[12],v2=[−36],v3=[−26]. Which of the given vectors belong to the kernel of T?

a
v2 and v3 only
b
v1 and v3 only
c
v1 and v2 only
d
v2 only
e
v3 only
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

A vector u belongs to the kernel of a linear transformation T if T(u)=0.

Therefore, we need to compute T(vi) for each vector vi: T(v1)=T([12])=[812]T(v2)=T([−36])=[00]T(v3)=T([−26])=[46]

Since T(v2)=0, we conclude that the only vector that belongs to the kernel of T is v2.

Consider the linear transformation T:[xy]⟶[4x+3y−12x−9y] and the vectors v1=[34],v2=[−34],v3=[6−8]. Which of the given vectors belong to the kernel of T?

a
v3 only
b
v2 and v3 only
c
v2 only
d
v1 and v2 only
e
v1 and v3 only
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

A vector u belongs to the kernel of a linear transformation T if T(u)=0.

Therefore, we need to compute T(vi) for each vector vi: T(v1)=T([34])=[24−72]T(v2)=T([−34])=[00]T(v3)=T([6−8])=[00]

Since T(v2)=T(v3)=0, we conclude that the only vectors that belong to the kernel of T are v2 and v3.

question.name: Question 4
question.problem:
Consider the linear transformation
$T:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}x+4y \\ y+z \\ x-4z\end{aligned}]$ and the vectors 
${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ Which of the given vectors belong to $\text{Ker}(T)?$
question.worked_solution:
A vector $u$ belongs to the kernel of a linear transformation $T$ if $T(u)=0.$ 

Therefore, we need to compute $T({v}_{i})$ for each ${v}_{i}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}T({v}_{1}) & =T([\begin{aligned}4 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ T({v}_{2}) & =T([\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ T({v}_{3}) & =T([\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Since $T({v}_{1})=T({v}_{2})=T({v}_{3})=0,$ we conclude that the vectors that belong to the kernel of $T$ are ${v}_{1},$ ${v}_{2},$ and ${v}_{3}.$

last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Determining Whether Given Vectors Belong to the Kernel of a Linear Transformation
last_observation.worked_solution:
A vector $u$ belongs to the kernel of a linear transformation $T$ if $T(u)=0.$ 

Therefore, we need to compute $T({v}_{i})$ for each ${v}_{i}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}T({v}_{1}) & =T([\begin{aligned}4 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ T({v}_{2}) & =T([\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ T({v}_{3}) & =T([\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Since $T({v}_{1})=T({v}_{2})=T({v}_{3})=0,$ we conclude that the vectors that belong to the kernel of $T$ are ${v}_{1},$ ${v}_{2},$ and ${v}_{3}.$

question.problem:
Consider the linear transformation
$T:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}x+4y \\ y+z \\ x-4z\end{aligned}]$ and the vectors 
${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ Which of the given vectors belong to $\text{Ker}(T)?$
question.worked_solution:
A vector $u$ belongs to the kernel of a linear transformation $T$ if $T(u)=0.$ 

Therefore, we need to compute $T({v}_{i})$ for each ${v}_{i}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}T({v}_{1}) & =T([\begin{aligned}4 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ T({v}_{2}) & =T([\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ T({v}_{3}) & =T([\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Since $T({v}_{1})=T({v}_{2})=T({v}_{3})=0,$ we conclude that the vectors that belong to the kernel of $T$ are ${v}_{1},$ ${v}_{2},$ and ${v}_{3}.$

Question 4
?

Consider the linear transformation T:[xyz]⟶[x+4yy+zx−4z] and the vectors v1=[4−11],v2=[−41−1],v3=[000]. Which of the given vectors belong to Ker(T)?

a
v1 and v3 only
b
v1 only
c
v1, v2, and v3
d
v2 and v3 only
e
v1 and v2, only
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

A vector u belongs to the kernel of a linear transformation T if T(u)=0.

Therefore, we need to compute T(vi) for each vi: T(v1)=T([4−11])=[000]T(v2)=T([−41−1])=[000]T(v3)=T([000])=[000]

Since T(v1)=T(v2)=T(v3)=0, we conclude that the vectors that belong to the kernel of T are v1, v2, and v3.

solution.reasoning: T(v₁)=(4-4,-1+1,4-4)=(0,0,0), T(v₂)=(-4+4,1-1,-4+4)=(0,0,0), and T(v₃)=(0,0,0). Therefore all three vectors belong to Ker(T). The captured worked solution concerns a different example; no Math Academy answer or grade for the current question is provided.

Question 4

Consider the linear transformation T:[xyz]⟶[x+4yy+zx−4z] and the vectors v1=[4−11],v2=[−41−1],v3=[000]. Which of the given vectors belong to Ker(T)?

a
v1 and v3 only
b
v1 only
c
v1, v2, and v3
d
v2 and v3 only
e
v1 and v2, only
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

A vector u belongs to the kernel of a linear transformation T if T(u)=0.

Therefore, we need to compute T(vi) for each vi: T(v1)=T([4−11])=[000]T(v2)=T([−41−1])=[000]T(v3)=T([000])=[000]

Since T(v1)=T(v2)=T(v3)=0, we conclude that the vectors that belong to the kernel of T are v1, v2, and v3.

question.name: Question 5
question.problem:
Consider the linear transformation 
$T:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}3x+2y \\ -9x-6y\end{aligned}]$ 
and the vectors 
${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}],{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],{v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -6\end{aligned}].$
Which of the given vectors belong to the kernel of $T?$
question.worked_solution:
A vector $u$ belongs to the kernel of a linear transformation $T$ if $T(u)=0.$ 

Therefore, we need to compute $T({v}_{i})$ for each vector ${v}_{i}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}T({v}_{1}) & =T([\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ T({v}_{2}) & =T([\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\ T({v}_{3}) & =T([\begin{aligned}4 \\ -6\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\,T({v}_{1})=T({v}_{3})=0,$ we conclude that the only vectors that belong to the kernel of $\,T$ are $\,{v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{3}.$

feedback.name: Question 5
feedback.problem:
Consider the linear transformation 
$T:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}3x+2y \\ -9x-6y\end{aligned}]$ 
and the vectors 
${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}],{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],{v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -6\end{aligned}].$
Which of the given vectors belong to the kernel of $T?$
feedback.worked_solution:
A vector $u$ belongs to the kernel of a linear transformation $T$ if $T(u)=0.$ 

Therefore, we need to compute $T({v}_{i})$ for each vector ${v}_{i}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}T({v}_{1}) & =T([\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ T({v}_{2}) & =T([\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\ T({v}_{3}) & =T([\begin{aligned}4 \\ -6\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\,T({v}_{1})=T({v}_{3})=0,$ we conclude that the only vectors that belong to the kernel of $\,T$ are $\,{v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{3}.$

question.name: Question 6
question.problem: Consider the linear transformation $T:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}4x-2y \\ -10x+5y\end{aligned}]$ and the vector $\,u=[\begin{aligned}k \\ 6\end{aligned}].$ Find the value of $\,k\,$ such that $\,u\in \text{Ker}(T).$
question.worked_solution:
A vector $u$ belongs to the kernel of a linear transformation $T$ if $T(u)=0.$ 

So, we need to solve the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(u) & =0 \\ [\begin{aligned}4\cdot k-2\cdot 6 \\ -10\cdot k+5\cdot 6\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}4k-12 \\ -10k+30\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}4k-12=0 \\ -10k+30=0.\end{aligned}
$$

The solution to both of these equations is $k=3.$

question.name: Question 8
question.problem: Consider the linear transformation $T:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}3x+y+3z \\ 2x+y+z \\ x-y+5z\end{aligned}]$ and the vector $\,u=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3 \\ k\end{aligned}].$ Find the value of $\,k\,$ such that $\,u\in \text{Ker}(T).$
question.worked_solution:
A vector $u$ belongs to the kernel of a linear transformation $T$ if $T(u)=0.$ 

So, we need to solve the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(u) & =0 \\ [\begin{aligned}3\cdot (-2)+3+3\cdot k \\ 2\cdot (-2)+3+k \\ -2-3+5\cdot k\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}-3+3k \\ -1+k \\ -5+5k\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-3+3k=0 \\ -1+k=0 \\ -5+5k=0.\end{aligned}
$$

The solution to all three of these equations is $k=1.$

question.name: Question 10
question.problem: Consider the linear transformation $T:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}3x+y \\ 15x+5y \\ -6x-2y\end{aligned}]$ and the vector $\,u=[\begin{aligned}k \\ 6 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ Find the value of $\,k\,$ such that $\,u\in \text{Ker}(T).$
question.worked_solution:
A vector $u$ belongs to the kernel of a linear transformation $T$ if $T(u)=0.$ 

So, we need to solve the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(u) & =0 \\ [\begin{aligned}3\cdot k+6 \\ 15\cdot k+5\cdot 6 \\ -6\cdot k-2\cdot 6\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}3k+6 \\ 15k+30 \\ -6k-12\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}3k+6=0 \\ 15k+30=0 \\ -6k-12=0.\end{aligned}
$$

The solution to all three of these equations is $k=-2.$

\{\begin{aligned}3k+6=0 \\ 15k+30=0 \\ -6k-12=0.\end{aligned}

question.name: Question 11
question.problem: Consider the linear transformation $T:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}2x+4y \\ -x+2y\end{aligned}].$ Find $\,\text{Ker}(T).$
question.worked_solution:
Finding the kernel of $\,T\,$ is equivalent to finding the null space of the standard matrix of $\,T.$

For the given linear transformation, the standard matrix is $T=[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}].$

Setting $x=[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}],$ we then need to solve the equation $Tx=0.$ First, we reduce $T$ to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is $x$ and $y.$ From the second equation, we obtain $y=0.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we have $x=0.$ 

Therefore, the kernel of the linear transformation $T$ is $\{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\}.$

question.html:
Question 11
?

Consider the linear transformation T:[xy]⟶[2x+4y−x+2y]. Find Ker(T).

a
{[00]}
b
{[x−2x]:x∈R}
c
{[3yy]:y∈R}
d
{[x12x]:x∈R}
e
{[−2yy]:y∈R}
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Finding the kernel of T is equivalent to finding the null space of the standard matrix of T.

For the given linear transformation, the standard matrix is T=[24−12].

Setting x=[xy], we then need to solve the equation Tx=0. First, we reduce T to row echelon form, as follows:

T=[24−12]R2:=R2+12R1∼[2404]

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is x and y. From the second equation, we obtain y=0. Substituting this into the first equation, we have x=0.

Therefore, the kernel of the linear transformation T is {[00]}.

last_observation.name: Question 11
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Kernel of a Linear Transformation
last_observation.worked_solution:
Finding the kernel of $\,T\,$ is equivalent to finding the null space of the standard matrix of $\,T.$

For the given linear transformation, the standard matrix is $T=[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}].$

Setting $x=[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}],$ we then need to solve the equation $Tx=0.$ First, we reduce $T$ to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is $x$ and $y.$ From the second equation, we obtain $y=0.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we have $x=0.$ 

Therefore, the kernel of the linear transformation $T$ is $\{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\}.$

question.name: Question 11
question.problem: Consider the linear transformation $T:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}2x+4y \\ -x+2y\end{aligned}].$ Find $\,\text{Ker}(T).$
question.worked_solution:
Finding the kernel of $\,T\,$ is equivalent to finding the null space of the standard matrix of $\,T.$

For the given linear transformation, the standard matrix is $T=[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}].$

Setting $x=[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}],$ we then need to solve the equation $Tx=0.$ First, we reduce $T$ to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 11
?

Consider the linear transformation T:[xy]⟶[2x+4y−x+2y]. Find Ker(T).

a
{[00]}
b
{[x−2x]:x∈R}
c
{[3yy]:y∈R}
d
{[x12x]:x∈R}
e
{[−2yy]:y∈R}
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Finding the kernel of T is equivalent to finding the null space of the standard matrix of T.

For the given linear transformation, the standard matrix is T=[24−12].

Setting x=[xy], we then need to solve the equation Tx=0. First, we reduce T to row echelon form, as follows:

T=[24−12]R2:=R2+12R1∼[2404]

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is x and y. From the second equation, we obtain y=0. Substituting this into the first equation, we have x=0.

Therefore, the kernel of the linear transformation T is {[00]}.
question.knowledge_point: Finding the Kernel of a Linear Transformation

solution.reasoning: The kernel satisfies 2x+4y=0 and -x+2y=0. These give x=-2y and x=2y, hence y=0 and x=0. Thus the kernel contains only the zero vector, option a. The captured worked solution concerns a different transformation; no Math Academy answer or grade for this question is provided.

feedback.name: Question 11
feedback.problem: Consider the linear transformation $T:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}2x+4y \\ -x+2y\end{aligned}].$ Find $\,\text{Ker}(T).$
feedback.worked_solution:
Finding the kernel of $\,T\,$ is equivalent to finding the null space of the standard matrix of $\,T.$

For the given linear transformation, the standard matrix is $T=[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}].$

Setting $x=[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}],$ we then need to solve the equation $Tx=0.$ First, we reduce $T$ to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is $x$ and $y.$ From the second equation, we obtain $y=0.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we have $x=0.$ 

Therefore, the kernel of the linear transformation $T$ is $\{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\}.$

Question 11
?

Consider the linear transformation T:[xy]⟶[2x+4y−x+2y]. Find Ker(T).

a
{[00]}
b
{[x−2x]:x∈R}
c
{[3yy]:y∈R}
d
{[x12x]:x∈R}
e
{[−2yy]:y∈R}
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Finding the kernel of T is equivalent to finding the null space of the standard matrix of T.

For the given linear transformation, the standard matrix is T=[24−12].

Setting x=[xy], we then need to solve the equation Tx=0. First, we reduce T to row echelon form, as follows:

T=[24−12]R2:=R2+12R1∼[2404]

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is x and y. From the second equation, we obtain y=0. Substituting this into the first equation, we have x=0.

Therefore, the kernel of the linear transformation T is {[00]}.

question.name: Question 12
question.problem: Consider the linear transformation $T:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}2x+4y-2z \\ -3x-6y+3z \\ 4x+8y-4z\end{aligned}].$ Find $\,\text{Ker}(T).$
question.worked_solution:
Finding the kernel of $T$ is equivalent to finding the null space of the standard matrix of $T.$

Fror the given linear transformation, the standard matrix is $T=[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & -2 \\ -3 & -6 & 3 \\ 4 & 8 & -4\end{aligned}].$ 

Setting $x=[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}],$ we then need to solve the equation $Tx=0.$ First, we find reduce $T$ to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & -2 \\ -3 & -6 & 3 \\ 4 & 8 & -4\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(\frac{3}{2}){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 4 & 8 & -4\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-2){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is $x$, and we have two free variables, $y,$ and $z.$ That means we need to find $x$ in terms of $y$ and $z.$ 

From the first equation, we get 

$$
x=-2y+z.
$$

  

Therefore, the kernel of the linear transformation $\,T$ is $\{[\begin{aligned}-2y+z \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]\,:\,y,z\in R\}.$

question.html:
Question 12
?

Consider the linear transformation T:[xyz]⟶[2x+4y−2z−3x−6y+3z4x+8y−4z]. Find Ker(T).

a
{[000]}
b
{[xy4x+2y]:x,y∈R}
c
{[x4x+2zz]:x,y∈R}
d
{[−4zy2z]:z∈R}
e
{[−2y+zyz]:y,z∈R}.
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Finding the kernel of T is equivalent to finding the null space of the standard matrix of T.

Fror the given linear transformation, the standard matrix is T=[24−2−3−6348−4].

Setting x=[xyz], we then need to solve the equation Tx=0. First, we find reduce T to row echelon form, as follows:

T=[24−2−3−6348−4]R2:=R2+(32)R1∼[24−200048−4]R3:=R3+(−2)R1∼[24−2000000]

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is x, and we have two free variables, y, and z. That means we need to find x in terms of y and z.

From the first equation, we get x=−2y+z.

Therefore, the kernel of the linear transformation T is {[−2y+zyz]:y,z∈R}.

last_observation.name: Question 12
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Kernel of a Linear Transformation
last_observation.worked_solution:
Finding the kernel of $T$ is equivalent to finding the null space of the standard matrix of $T.$

Fror the given linear transformation, the standard matrix is $T=[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & -2 \\ -3 & -6 & 3 \\ 4 & 8 & -4\end{aligned}].$ 

Setting $x=[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}],$ we then need to solve the equation $Tx=0.$ First, we find reduce $T$ to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & -2 \\ -3 & -6 & 3 \\ 4 & 8 & -4\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(\frac{3}{2}){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 4 & 8 & -4\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-2){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is $x$, and we have two free variables, $y,$ and $z.$ That means we need to find $x$ in terms of $y$ and $z.$ 

From the first equation, we get 

$$
x=-2y+z.
$$

  

Therefore, the kernel of the linear transformation $\,T$ is $\{[\begin{aligned}-2y+z \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]\,:\,y,z\in R\}.$

question.name: Question 12
question.problem: Consider the linear transformation $T:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}2x+4y-2z \\ -3x-6y+3z \\ 4x+8y-4z\end{aligned}].$ Find $\,\text{Ker}(T).$

$$
\begin{aligned}T & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & -2 \\ -3 & -6 & 3 \\ 4 & 8 & -4\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(\frac{3}{2}){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 4 & 8 & -4\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-2){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is $x$, and we have two free variables, $y,$ and $z.$ That means we need to find $x$ in terms of $y$ and $z.$ 

From the first equation, we get 

$$
x=-2y+z.
$$

  

Therefore, the kernel of the linear transformation $\,T$ is $\{[\begin{aligned}-2y+z \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]\,:\,y,z\in R\}.$

Question 12
?

Consider the linear transformation T:[xyz]⟶[2x+4y−2z−3x−6y+3z4x+8y−4z]. Find Ker(T).

a
{[000]}
b
{[xy4x+2y]:x,y∈R}
c
{[x4x+2zz]:x,y∈R}
d
{[−4zy2z]:z∈R}
e
{[−2y+zyz]:y,z∈R}.
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Finding the kernel of T is equivalent to finding the null space of the standard matrix of T.

Fror the given linear transformation, the standard matrix is T=[24−2−3−6348−4].

Setting x=[xyz], we then need to solve the equation Tx=0. First, we find reduce T to row echelon form, as follows:

T=[24−2−3−6348−4]R2:=R2+(32)R1∼[24−200048−4]R3:=R3+(−2)R1∼[24−2000000]

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is x, and we have two free variables, y, and z. That means we need to find x in terms of y and z.

From the first equation, we get x=−2y+z.

Therefore, the kernel of the linear transformation T is {[−2y+zyz]:y,z∈R}.
question.knowledge_point: Finding the Kernel of a Linear Transformation

solution.reasoning: All three components of T are multiples of x+2y-z. Thus T(x,y,z)=0 exactly when x=-2y+z, with y and z arbitrary real numbers, giving option e. No Math Academy answer or grade for this question is captured; the worked solution concerns a different example.

feedback.name: Question 12
feedback.problem: Consider the linear transformation $T:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}2x+4y-2z \\ -3x-6y+3z \\ 4x+8y-4z\end{aligned}].$ Find $\,\text{Ker}(T).$
feedback.worked_solution:
Finding the kernel of $T$ is equivalent to finding the null space of the standard matrix of $T.$

Fror the given linear transformation, the standard matrix is $T=[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & -2 \\ -3 & -6 & 3 \\ 4 & 8 & -4\end{aligned}].$ 

Setting $x=[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}],$ we then need to solve the equation $Tx=0.$ First, we find reduce $T$ to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & -2 \\ -3 & -6 & 3 \\ 4 & 8 & -4\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(\frac{3}{2}){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 4 & 8 & -4\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-2){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is $x$, and we have two free variables, $y,$ and $z.$ That means we need to find $x$ in terms of $y$ and $z.$ 

From the first equation, we get 

$$
x=-2y+z.
$$

  

Therefore, the kernel of the linear transformation $\,T$ is $\{[\begin{aligned}-2y+z \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]\,:\,y,z\in R\}.$

Question 12
?

Consider the linear transformation T:[xyz]⟶[2x+4y−2z−3x−6y+3z4x+8y−4z]. Find Ker(T).

a
{[000]}
b
{[xy4x+2y]:x,y∈R}
c
{[x4x+2zz]:x,y∈R}
d
{[−4zy2z]:z∈R}
e
{[−2y+zyz]:y,z∈R}.
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Finding the kernel of T is equivalent to finding the null space of the standard matrix of T.

Fror the given linear transformation, the standard matrix is T=[24−2−3−6348−4].

Setting x=[xyz], we then need to solve the equation Tx=0. First, we find reduce T to row echelon form, as follows:

T=[24−2−3−6348−4]R2:=R2+(32)R1∼[24−200048−4]R3:=R3+(−2)R1∼[24−2000000]

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is x, and we have two free variables, y, and z. That means we need to find x in terms of y and z.

From the first equation, we get x=−2y+z.

Therefore, the kernel of the linear transformation T is {[−2y+zyz]:y,z∈R}.

question.name: Question 13
question.problem: Consider the linear transformation $T:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}x-2y+z \\ 6x-3y-3z \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ Find $\,\text{Ker}(T).$
question.worked_solution:
Finding the kernel of $T$ is equivalent to finding the null space of the standard matrix of $T.$

Fror the given linear transformation, the standard matrix is $T=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ 6 & -3 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].$

Setting $x=[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}],$ we then need to solve the equation $Tx=0.$ First, we find reduce $T$ to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ 6 & -3 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-6{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & 9 & -9 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{9}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is $x$ and $y$, and we have one free variable, $z.$ That means we need to find $x$ and $y$ in terms of $z.$

From the second equation, we get $y=z.$ Substituting these into the first equation, we have 

$$
x=2y-z=2z-z=z.
$$

Therefore, the kernel of the linear transformation $\,T$ is $\{[\begin{aligned}z \\ z \\ z\end{aligned}]\,:\,z\in R\}.$

Question 13
?

Consider the linear transformation T:[xyz]⟶[x−2y+z6x−3y−3z0]. Find Ker(T).

a
{[−110]}
b
{[−yy−y]:y∈R}
c
{[−z2zz]:z∈R}
d
{[y+zyz]:y,z∈R}
e
{[zzz]:z∈R}
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Finding the kernel of T is equivalent to finding the null space of the standard matrix of T.

Fror the given linear transformation, the standard matrix is T=[1−216−3−3000].

Setting x=[xyz], we then need to solve the equation Tx=0. First, we find reduce T to row echelon form, as follows:

T=[1−216−3−3000]R2:=R2−6R1∼[1−2109−9000]R2:=19R2∼[1−2101−1000]

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is x and y, and we have one free variable, z. That means we need to find x and y in terms of z.

From the second equation, we get y=z. Substituting these into the first equation, we have x=2y−z=2z−z=z.

Therefore, the kernel of the linear transformation T is {[zzz]:z∈R}.

last_observation.name: Question 13
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Kernel of a Linear Transformation
last_observation.worked_solution:
Finding the kernel of $T$ is equivalent to finding the null space of the standard matrix of $T.$

Fror the given linear transformation, the standard matrix is $T=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ 6 & -3 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].$

Setting $x=[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}],$ we then need to solve the equation $Tx=0.$ First, we find reduce $T$ to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ 6 & -3 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-6{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & 9 & -9 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{9}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is $x$ and $y$, and we have one free variable, $z.$ That means we need to find $x$ and $y$ in terms of $z.$

From the second equation, we get $y=z.$ Substituting these into the first equation, we have 

$$
x=2y-z=2z-z=z.
$$

Therefore, the kernel of the linear transformation $\,T$ is $\{[\begin{aligned}z \\ z \\ z\end{aligned}]\,:\,z\in R\}.$

Question 13
?

Consider the linear transformation T:[xyz]⟶[x−2y+z6x−3y−3z0]. Find Ker(T).

a
{[−110]}
b
{[−yy−y]:y∈R}
c
{[−z2zz]:z∈R}
d
{[y+zyz]:y,z∈R}
e
{[zzz]:z∈R}
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Finding the kernel of T is equivalent to finding the null space of the standard matrix of T.

Fror the given linear transformation, the standard matrix is T=[1−216−3−3000].

Setting x=[xyz], we then need to solve the equation Tx=0. First, we find reduce T to row echelon form, as follows:

T=[1−216−3−3000]R2:=R2−6R1∼[1−2109−9000]R2:=19R2∼[1−2101−1000]

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is x and y, and we have one free variable, z. That means we need to find x and y in terms of z.

From the second equation, we get y=z. Substituting these into the first equation, we have x=2y−z=2z−z=z.

Therefore, the kernel of the linear transformation T is {[zzz]:z∈R}.
question.knowledge_point: Finding the Kernel of a Linear Transformation

solution.reasoning: The kernel satisfies x-2y+z=0 and 6x-3y-3z=0. Substituting x=2y-z into the second equation gives 9y-9z=0, hence y=z and x=z. Therefore the kernel is all vectors (z,z,z), option e. feedback.name: Question 13
feedback.problem: Consider the linear transformation $T:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}x-2y+z \\ 6x-3y-3z \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ Find $\,\text{Ker}(T).$
feedback.worked_solution:
Finding the kernel of $T$ is equivalent to finding the null space of the standard matrix of $T.$

Fror the given linear transformation, the standard matrix is $T=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ 6 & -3 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].$

Setting $x=[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}],$ we then need to solve the equation $Tx=0.$ First, we find reduce $T$ to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ 6 & -3 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-6{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & 9 & -9 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{9}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is $x$ and $y$, and we have one free variable, $z.$ That means we need to find $x$ and $y$ in terms of $z.$

From the second equation, we get $y=z.$ Substituting these into the first equation, we have 

$$
x=2y-z=2z-z=z.
$$

Therefore, the kernel of the linear transformation $\,T$ is $\{[\begin{aligned}z \\ z \\ z\end{aligned}]\,:\,z\in R\}.$

feedback.html:
Question 13
?

Consider the linear transformation T:[xyz]⟶[x−2y+z6x−3y−3z0]. Find Ker(T).

a
{[−110]}
b
{[−yy−y]:y∈R}
c
{[−z2zz]:z∈R}
d
{[y+zyz]:y,z∈R}
e
{[zzz]:z∈R}
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Finding the kernel of T is equivalent to finding the null space of the standard matrix of T.

Fror the given linear transformation, the standard matrix is T=[1−216−3−3000].

Setting x=[xyz], we then need to solve the equation Tx=0. First, we find reduce T to row echelon form, as follows:

T=[1−216−3−3000]R2:=R2−6R1∼[1−2109−9000]R2:=19R2∼[1−2101−1000]

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is x and y, and we have one free variable, z. That means we need to find x and y in terms of z.

From the second equation, we get y=z. Substituting these into the first equation, we have x=2y−z=2z−z=z.

Therefore, the kernel of the linear transformation T is {[zzz]:z∈R}.
feedback.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Kernel of a Linear Transformation

question.name: Question 14
question.problem: Find a basis of $\,\text{Ker}(T)$ given that $T:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}3y-6z-6x \\ -4y+x+z \\ 2y+8z+8x\end{aligned}].$
question.worked_solution:
Finding the kernel of $\,T\,$ is equivalent to finding the null space of the standard matrix of $\,T.$

For the given linear transformation, the standard matrix is $T=[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 & -6 \\ 1 & -4 & 1 \\ 8 & 2 & 8\end{aligned}].$

Setting $x=[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}],$ we then need to solve the equation $Tx=0.$ First, we reduce $T$ to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 & -6 \\ 1 & -4 & 1 \\ 8 & 2 & 8\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{6}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 & -6 \\ 0 & -\frac{7}{2} & 0 \\ 8 & 2 & 8\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+\frac{4}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 & -6 \\ 0 & -\frac{7}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 6 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+\frac{12}{7}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 & -6 \\ 0 & -\frac{7}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is $x$ and $y$, and we have one free variable, $z.$ That means we need to find $x$ and $y$ in terms of $z.$

From the second equation, we get $y=0.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we have $x=-z.$ 

Therefore, if $x\in \text{Ker}(T),$ then 

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}-z \\ 0 \\ z\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]z,\,z\in R.
$$

This implies that $B=\{[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\}$ is a basis of $\text{Ker}(T).$

EXPLANATION

Finding the kernel of T is equivalent to finding the null space of the standard matrix of T.

For the given linear transformation, the standard matrix is T=[−63−61−41828].

Setting x=[xyz], we then need to solve the equation Tx=0. First, we reduce T to row echelon form, as follows:

T=[−63−61−41828]R2:=R2+16R1∼[−63−60−720828]R3:=R3+43R1∼[−63−60−720060]R3:=R3+127R2∼[−63−60−720000]

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is x and y, and we have one free variable, z. That means we need to find x and y in terms of z.

From the second equation, we get y=0. Substituting this into the first equation, we have x=−z.

Therefore, if x∈Ker(T), then

x=[−z0z]=[−101]z,z∈R.

This implies that B={[−101]} is a basis of Ker(T).

last_observation.name: Question 14
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Kernel of a Linear Transformation
last_observation.worked_solution:
Finding the kernel of $\,T\,$ is equivalent to finding the null space of the standard matrix of $\,T.$

For the given linear transformation, the standard matrix is $T=[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 & -6 \\ 1 & -4 & 1 \\ 8 & 2 & 8\end{aligned}].$

Setting $x=[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}],$ we then need to solve the equation $Tx=0.$ First, we reduce $T$ to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 & -6 \\ 1 & -4 & 1 \\ 8 & 2 & 8\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{6}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 & -6 \\ 0 & -\frac{7}{2} & 0 \\ 8 & 2 & 8\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+\frac{4}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 & -6 \\ 0 & -\frac{7}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 6 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+\frac{12}{7}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 & -6 \\ 0 & -\frac{7}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is $x$ and $y$, and we have one free variable, $z.$ That means we need to find $x$ and $y$ in terms of $z.$

From the second equation, we get $y=0.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we have $x=-z.$ 

Therefore, if $x\in \text{Ker}(T),$ then 

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}-z \\ 0 \\ z\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]z,\,z\in R.
$$

This implies that $B=\{[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\}$ is a basis of $\text{Ker}(T).$

question.name: Question 14
question.problem: Find a basis of $\,\text{Ker}(T)$ given that $T:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}3y-6z-6x \\ -4y+x+z \\ 2y+8z+8x\end{aligned}].$
question.worked_solution:
Finding the kernel of $\,T\,$ is equivalent to finding the null space of the standard matrix of $\,T.$

For the given linear transformation, the standard matrix is $T=[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 & -6 \\ 1 & -4 & 1 \\ 8 & 2 & 8\end{aligned}].$

Setting $x=[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}],$ we then need to solve the equation $Tx=0.$ First, we reduce $T$ to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 & -6 \\ 1 & -4 & 1 \\ 8 & 2 & 8\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{6}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 & -6 \\ 0 & -\frac{7}{2} & 0 \\ 8 & 2 & 8\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+\frac{4}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 & -6 \\ 0 & -\frac{7}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 6 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+\frac{12}{7}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 & -6 \\ 0 & -\frac{7}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is $x$ and $y$, and we have one free variable, $z.$ That means we need to find $x$ and $y$ in terms of $z.$

From the second equation, we get $y=0.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we have $x=-z.$ 

Therefore, if $x\in \text{Ker}(T),$ then 

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}-z \\ 0 \\ z\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]z,\,z\in R.
$$

This implies that $B=\{[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\}$ is a basis of $\text{Ker}(T).$

feedback.name: Question 14
feedback.problem: Find a basis of $\,\text{Ker}(T)$ given that $T:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}3y-6z-6x \\ -4y+x+z \\ 2y+8z+8x\end{aligned}].$
feedback.worked_solution:
Finding the kernel of $\,T\,$ is equivalent to finding the null space of the standard matrix of $\,T.$

For the given linear transformation, the standard matrix is $T=[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 & -6 \\ 1 & -4 & 1 \\ 8 & 2 & 8\end{aligned}].$

Setting $x=[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}],$ we then need to solve the equation $Tx=0.$ First, we reduce $T$ to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 & -6 \\ 1 & -4 & 1 \\ 8 & 2 & 8\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{6}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 & -6 \\ 0 & -\frac{7}{2} & 0 \\ 8 & 2 & 8\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+\frac{4}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 & -6 \\ 0 & -\frac{7}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 6 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+\frac{12}{7}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 & -6 \\ 0 & -\frac{7}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is $x$ and $y$, and we have one free variable, $z.$ That means we need to find $x$ and $y$ in terms of $z.$

From the second equation, we get $y=0.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we have $x=-z.$ 

Therefore, if $x\in \text{Ker}(T),$ then 

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}-z \\ 0 \\ z\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]z,\,z\in R.
$$

This implies that $B=\{[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\}$ is a basis of $\text{Ker}(T).$

question.name: Question 15
question.problem: Consider the linear transformation $T:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}-9x-3y+3z \\ -12x-4y+4z \\ 6x+8y+10z\end{aligned}].$ Find $\,\text{Ker}(T).$
question.worked_solution:
Finding the kernel of $T$ is equivalent to finding the null space of the standard matrix of $T.$

Fror the given linear transformation, the standard matrix is $T=[\begin{aligned}-9 & -3 & 3 \\ -12 & -4 & 4 \\ 6 & 8 & 10\end{aligned}].$

Setting $x=[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}],$ we then need to solve the equation $Tx=0.$ First, we find reduce $T$ to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T & =[\begin{aligned}-9 & -3 & 3 \\ -12 & -4 & 4 \\ 6 & 8 & 10\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-\frac{4}{3}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-9 & -3 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 6 & 8 & 10\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+\frac{2}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-9 & -3 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 6 & 12\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & ↔{R}_{3} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-9 & -3 & 3 \\ 0 & 6 & 12 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is $x$ and $y$, and we have one free variable, $z.$ That means we need to find $x$ and $y$ in terms of $z.$

From the second equation, we get $y=-2z.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}-9x-3y+3z & =0 \\ -9x-3(-2z)+3z & =0 \\ -9x+9z & =0 \\ x & =z\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the kernel of the linear transformation $\,T$ is $\{[\begin{aligned}z \\ -2z \\ z\end{aligned}]\,:\,z\in R\}.$

Question 15
?

Consider the linear transformation T:[xyz]⟶[−9x−3y+3z−12x−4y+4z6x+8y+10z]. Find Ker(T).

a
{[xx−2zz]:x,z∈R}
b
{[−13z−3zz]:z∈R}
c
{[z−2zz]:z∈R}
d
{[xy2x−3y]:x,y∈R}
e
{[y+zyz]:y,z∈R}
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Finding the kernel of T is equivalent to finding the null space of the standard matrix of T.

Fror the given linear transformation, the standard matrix is T=[−9−33−12−446810].

Setting x=[xyz], we then need to solve the equation Tx=0. First, we find reduce T to row echelon form, as follows:

T=[−9−33−12−446810]R2:=R2+(−43)R1∼[−9−330006810]R3:=R3+23R1∼[−9−330000612]R2↔R3∼[−9−330612000]

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is x and y, and we have one free variable, z. That means we need to find x and y in terms of z.

From the second equation, we get y=−2z. Substituting this into the first equation, we have −9x−3y+3z=0−9x−3(−2z)+3z=0−9x+9z=0x=z

Therefore, the kernel of the linear transformation T is {[z−2zz]:z∈R}.

last_observation.name: Question 15
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Kernel of a Linear Transformation
last_observation.worked_solution:
Finding the kernel of $T$ is equivalent to finding the null space of the standard matrix of $T.$

Fror the given linear transformation, the standard matrix is $T=[\begin{aligned}-9 & -3 & 3 \\ -12 & -4 & 4 \\ 6 & 8 & 10\end{aligned}].$

Setting $x=[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}],$ we then need to solve the equation $Tx=0.$ First, we find reduce $T$ to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T & =[\begin{aligned}-9 & -3 & 3 \\ -12 & -4 & 4 \\ 6 & 8 & 10\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-\frac{4}{3}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-9 & -3 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 6 & 8 & 10\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+\frac{2}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-9 & -3 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 6 & 12\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & ↔{R}_{3} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-9 & -3 & 3 \\ 0 & 6 & 12 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is $x$ and $y$, and we have one free variable, $z.$ That means we need to find $x$ and $y$ in terms of $z.$

From the second equation, we get $y=-2z.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}-9x-3y+3z & =0 \\ -9x-3(-2z)+3z & =0 \\ -9x+9z & =0 \\ x & =z\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the kernel of the linear transformation $\,T$ is $\{[\begin{aligned}z \\ -2z \\ z\end{aligned}]\,:\,z\in R\}.$

feedback.name: Question 15
feedback.problem: Consider the linear transformation $T:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}-9x-3y+3z \\ -12x-4y+4z \\ 6x+8y+10z\end{aligned}].$ Find $\,\text{Ker}(T).$
feedback.worked_solution:
Finding the kernel of $T$ is equivalent to finding the null space of the standard matrix of $T.$

Fror the given linear transformation, the standard matrix is $T=[\begin{aligned}-9 & -3 & 3 \\ -12 & -4 & 4 \\ 6 & 8 & 10\end{aligned}].$

Setting $x=[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}],$ we then need to solve the equation $Tx=0.$ First, we find reduce $T$ to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T & =[\begin{aligned}-9 & -3 & 3 \\ -12 & -4 & 4 \\ 6 & 8 & 10\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-\frac{4}{3}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-9 & -3 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 6 & 8 & 10\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+\frac{2}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-9 & -3 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 6 & 12\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & ↔{R}_{3} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-9 & -3 & 3 \\ 0 & 6 & 12 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is $x$ and $y$, and we have one free variable, $z.$ That means we need to find $x$ and $y$ in terms of $z.$

From the second equation, we get $y=-2z.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}-9x-3y+3z & =0 \\ -9x-3(-2z)+3z & =0 \\ -9x+9z & =0 \\ x & =z\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the kernel of the linear transformation $\,T$ is $\{[\begin{aligned}z \\ -2z \\ z\end{aligned}]\,:\,z\in R\}.$

Question 15
?

Consider the linear transformation T:[xyz]⟶[−9x−3y+3z−12x−4y+4z6x+8y+10z]. Find Ker(T).

a
{[xx−2zz]:x,z∈R}
b
{[−13z−3zz]:z∈R}
c
{[z−2zz]:z∈R}
d
{[xy2x−3y]:x,y∈R}
e
{[y+zyz]:y,z∈R}
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Finding the kernel of T is equivalent to finding the null space of the standard matrix of T.

Fror the given linear transformation, the standard matrix is T=[−9−33−12−446810].

Setting x=[xyz], we then need to solve the equation Tx=0. First, we find reduce T to row echelon form, as follows:

T=[−9−33−12−446810]R2:=R2+(−43)R1∼[−9−330006810]R3:=R3+23R1∼[−9−330000612]R2↔R3∼[−9−330612000]

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is x and y, and we have one free variable, z. That means we need to find x and y in terms of z.

From the second equation, we get y=−2z. Substituting this into the first equation, we have −9x−3y+3z=0−9x−3(−2z)+3z=0−9x+9z=0x=z

Therefore, the kernel of the linear transformation T is {[z−2zz]:z∈R}.

question.name: Question 16
question.problem: Given the linear transformation $T:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}0x+0y \\ 0x+0y\end{aligned}],$ find  $2\cdot \text{nullity}(T)-4.$
question.worked_solution:
First, we write down the standard matrix of $T:$

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Recall that $\text{nullity}(T)=\text{nullity}(T)=\text{dim}(\text{Null}(T)).$ Notice that $T$ has $2$ non-pivot columns. 

Therefore, $\text{nullity}(T)=\text{dim}(\text{Null}(T))=2.$

Finally, we obtain

$$
2\cdot \text{nullity}(T)-4=2\cdot 2-4=0.
$$

question.name: Question 17
question.problem: Given the linear transformation $T:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}2x-z \\ x-y+z \\ 3z-6x\end{aligned}],$ find $\text{nullity}(T).$
question.worked_solution:
First, we write down the standard matrix of $T:$

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & -1 \\ 1 & -1 & 1 \\ -6 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}]
$$

Recall that $\text{nullity}(T)=\text{nullity}(T)=\text{dim}(\text{Null}(T)).$

In order to find $\text{dim}(\text{Null}(T)),$ we reduce $T$ to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & -1 \\ 1 & -1 & 1 \\ -6 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-\frac{1}{2}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & \frac{3}{2} \\ -6 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & \frac{3}{2} \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has $1$ non-pivot column (the $3$rd one). Therefore, 

$$
\text{nullity}(T)=\text{dim}(\text{Null}(T))=1.
$$

question.name: Question 18
question.problem:
Given the linear transformation $T:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}3x-8y \\ 16y-6x\end{aligned}],$
find  $2\cdot \text{nullity}(T)-3.$
question.worked_solution:
First, we write down the standard matrix of $T:$

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}3 & -8 \\ -6 & 16\end{aligned}]
$$

Recall that $\text{nullity}(T)=\text{nullity}(T)=\text{dim}(\text{Null}(T)).$

In order to find $\text{dim}(\text{Null}(T)),$ we reduce $T$ to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -8 \\ -6 & 16\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}3 & -8 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has $1$ non-pivot column (the $2$nd one). 

Therefore, $\text{nullity}(T)=\text{dim}(\text{Null}(T))=1.$

Finally, we obtain

$$
2\cdot \text{nullity}(T)-3=2\cdot 1-3=-1.
$$

question.html:
Question 18
?

Given the linear transformation T:[xy]⟶[3x−8y16y−6x], find 2⋅nullity(T)−3.

a
−1
b
0
c
−2
d
1
e
−3
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we write down the standard matrix of T:

T=[3−8−616]

Recall that nullity(T)=nullity(T)=dim(Null(T)).

In order to find dim(Null(T)), we reduce T to row echelon form, as follows:

T=[3−8−616]R2:=R2+2R1∼[3−800]

The reduced matrix above has 1 non-pivot column (the 2nd one).

Therefore, nullity(T)=dim(Null(T))=1.

Finally, we obtain

2⋅nullity(T)−3=2⋅1−3=−1.

last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Nullity of a Linear Transformation
last_observation.worked_solution:
First, we write down the standard matrix of $T:$

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}3 & -8 \\ -6 & 16\end{aligned}]
$$

Recall that $\text{nullity}(T)=\text{nullity}(T)=\text{dim}(\text{Null}(T)).$

In order to find $\text{dim}(\text{Null}(T)),$ we reduce $T$ to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -8 \\ -6 & 16\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}3 & -8 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has $1$ non-pivot column (the $2$nd one). 

Therefore, $\text{nullity}(T)=\text{dim}(\text{Null}(T))=1.$

Finally, we obtain

$$
2\cdot \text{nullity}(T)-3=2\cdot 1-3=-1.
$$

question.name: Question 19
question.problem:
Given the linear transformation
 $T:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}3y-x-4z \\ 2x+7z-6y \\ 16z+4x-12y\end{aligned}],$ find $\text{nullity}(T).$
question.worked_solution:
First, we write down the standard matrix of $T:$

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 & -4 \\ 2 & -6 & 7 \\ 4 & -12 & 16\end{aligned}]
$$

Recall that $\text{nullity}(T)=\text{nullity}(T)=\text{dim}(\text{Null}(T)).$

In order to find $\text{dim}(\text{Null}(T)),$ we reduce $T$ to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 & -4 \\ 2 & -6 & 7 \\ 4 & -12 & 16\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 & -4 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \\ 4 & -12 & 16\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+4{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 & -4 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has $1$ non-pivot columns (the 2nd one).  Therefore, 

$$
\text{nullity}(T)=\text{dim}(\text{Null}(T))=1.
$$

question.name: Question 20
question.problem: Given the linear transformation $T:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}x+2y \\ 4y+3x\end{aligned}],$ find  $2\cdot \text{nullity}(T)-1.$
question.worked_solution:
First, we write down the standard matrix of $T:$

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

Recall that $\text{nullity}(T)=\text{nullity}(T)=\text{dim}(\text{Null}(T)).$

In order to find $\text{dim}(\text{Null}(T)),$ we reduce $T$ to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has no non-pivot column. Therefore, $\text{nullity}(T)=\text{dim}(\text{Null}(T))=0.$

Finally, we obtain

$$
2\cdot \text{nullity}(T)-1=2\cdot 0-1=-1.
$$

In order to find $\text{dim}(\text{Null}(T)),$ we reduce $T$ to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has no non-pivot column. Therefore, $\text{nullity}(T)=\text{dim}(\text{Null}(T))=0.$

Finally, we obtain

$$
2\cdot \text{nullity}(T)-1=2\cdot 0-1=-1.
$$

Question 20
?

Given the linear transformation T:[xy]⟶[x+2y4y+3x], find 2⋅nullity(T)−1.

a
−1
b
−3
c
0
d
1
e
3
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we write down the standard matrix of T:

T=[1234]

Recall that nullity(T)=nullity(T)=dim(Null(T)).

In order to find dim(Null(T)), we reduce T to row echelon form, as follows:

T=[1234]R2:=R2+(−3)R1∼[120−2]

The reduced matrix above has no non-pivot column. Therefore, nullity(T)=dim(Null(T))=0.

Finally, we obtain

2⋅nullity(T)−1=2⋅0−1=−1.

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: Calculate the circulation $Γ$ of the vector field $F(x,y)=\frac{1}{y}\,i+\frac{1}{x}\,j$ along the circle $C$ with equation ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=9$ oriented counterclockwise.
questions.worked_solution:
The closed curve $C$ is the circle of radius $3$ centered at the origin. It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
r(t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

The circulation $Γ$ measures the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$
It is given by the formula

$$
Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =\frac{1}{y}\,i+\frac{1}{x}\,j \\  & =\frac{1}{3\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\,i+\frac{1}{3\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j \\  & =-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(\frac{1}{3\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\,i+\frac{1}{3\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,j)\cdot (-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =\frac{1}{3\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\cdot (-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+\frac{1}{3\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\cdot 3\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =-1+1 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we conclude that:

$$
\begin{aligned}Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t=0\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14152067/assets/a1883ee3a3a99d43109bae2d2093aef35548dde9753cfb7dc19dfd77a104ec83.png)

Consider the ellipse $E$ and the vector field $F,$ shown above. Let $C$ be any path where $E$ is traversed once in the counterclockwise direction. Which of the following statements are true?

I. ${∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0$

II. ${∮}_{-C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0$

III. ${∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r<0$
questions.worked_solution:
The circulation $Γ$ measures the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$
It is given by the formula

$$
Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

We now recall the following:

- If the force works *with* the motion of the particle (i.e., the force helps to push the particle along the path), then ${∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0.$

- If the force works *against* the motion of the particle (i.e., the force impedes the motion of the particle as it moves along the path), then ${∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r<0.$

With that in mind, let's check each statement.

- Statement I is false, while statement III is true. It's clear from the picture below that $F$ works against the motion of the particle as it moves counterclockwise along $C.$ 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14152067/assets/8595904122fac3431fc959b2fa4aa5a3062bd1bffd1a391a0861fa12f2498054.png)

So, ${∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r<0.$

- Statement II is true. It's clear from the picture below that $F$ assists the motion of the particle as it moves **clockwise** along $C.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14152067/assets/f1f31f2b6eefddedc46b8e845703904c0b4566963e64a644f7a4ab32bb7240c3.png)

So, ${∮}_{-C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

observed_steps.worked_solution:
The closed curve $C$ is the circle of radius $3$ centered at the origin. It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
r(t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

The circulation $Γ$ measures the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$
It is given by the formula

$$
Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =\frac{1}{y}\,i+\frac{1}{x}\,j \\  & =\frac{1}{3\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\,i+\frac{1}{3\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j \\  & =-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(\frac{1}{3\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\,i+\frac{1}{3\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,j)\cdot (-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =\frac{1}{3\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\cdot (-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+\frac{1}{3\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\cdot 3\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =-1+1 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we conclude that:

$$
\begin{aligned}Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t=0\end{aligned}
$$

The closed curve C is the circle of radius 3 centered at the origin. It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as r(t)=3cos⁡ti+3sin⁡tj,0≤t≤2π.

The circulation Γ measures the total work done by a force F in moving a particle along a closed curve C. It is given by the formula Γ=∮CF⋅dr=∫abF(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt.

Along the curve C, we have x=3cos⁡t,y=3sin⁡t.

So,

F(r(t))=1yi+1xj=13sin⁡ti+13cos⁡tj.

Computing r′(t), we get

r′(t)=ddt(3cos⁡t)i+ddt(3sin⁡t)j=−3sin⁡ti+3cos⁡tj.

Γ=∮CF⋅dr=∫02πF(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt=0

question.name: Question 1
question.problem: Calculate the circulation $Γ$ of the vector field $F(x,y)=\frac{1}{y}\,i+\frac{1}{x}\,j$ along the circle $C$ with equation ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=9$ oriented counterclockwise.
question.worked_solution:
The closed curve $C$ is the circle of radius $3$ centered at the origin. It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
r(t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

The circulation $Γ$ measures the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$
It is given by the formula

$$
Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =\frac{1}{y}\,i+\frac{1}{x}\,j \\  & =\frac{1}{3\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\,i+\frac{1}{3\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j \\  & =-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(\frac{1}{3\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\,i+\frac{1}{3\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,j)\cdot (-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =\frac{1}{3\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\cdot (-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+\frac{1}{3\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\cdot 3\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =-1+1 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we conclude that:

$$
\begin{aligned}Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t=0\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

The closed curve C is the circle of radius 3 centered at the origin. It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as r(t)=3cos⁡ti+3sin⁡tj,0≤t≤2π.

The circulation Γ measures the total work done by a force F in moving a particle along a closed curve C. It is given by the formula Γ=∮CF⋅dr=∫abF(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt.

Along the curve C, we have x=3cos⁡t,y=3sin⁡t.

So,

F(r(t))=1yi+1xj=13sin⁡ti+13cos⁡tj.

Computing r′(t), we get

r′(t)=ddt(3cos⁡t)i+ddt(3sin⁡t)j=−3sin⁡ti+3cos⁡tj.

Therefore,

F(r(t))⋅r′(t)=(13sin⁡ti+13cos⁡tj)⋅(−3sin⁡ti+3cos⁡tj)=13sin⁡t⋅(−3sin⁡t)+13cos⁡t⋅3cos⁡t=−1+1=0.

Hence, we conclude that:

Γ=∮CF⋅dr=∫02πF(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt=0
