question.name: Question 13
question.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 & -4 \\ 3 & -3 & -3 \\ -4 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

The vectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ are eigenvectors that correspond to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=4$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-3$ of the matrix $A,$ given above. Find the third eigenvector ${v}_{3}=[a,\,b,\,c]^{T}$ such that the set $\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}\}$ is linearly independent. What is the value of $\frac{a}{b}?$
question.worked_solution:
First, we find all the eigenvalues of $A$ by solving the characteristic equation $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}-4-\lambda  & 0 & -4 \\ 3 & -3-\lambda  & -3 \\ -4 & 0 & 2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-3-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}-4-\lambda  & -4 \\ -4 & 2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-3-\lambda )((-4-\lambda )(2-\lambda )-(-4)(-4)) & =0 \\ (-3-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}+2\lambda -24) & =0 \\ (\lambda +3)(\lambda +6)(\lambda -4) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, ${\lambda }_{1}=4,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-3,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=-6.$ Since we obtained three distinct eigenvalues, the set of eigenvectors $\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}\},$ where each vector corresponds to different eigenvalue, will be linearly independent.

Now, recall that ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ correspond to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=4$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-3.$ Thus, the third eigenvector ${v}_{3}$ must correspond to ${\lambda }_{3}=-6.$ 

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\lambda =-6.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 & -4 \\ 3 & -3 & -3 \\ -4 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]-(-6)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & -4 \\ 3 & 3 & -3 \\ -4 & 0 & 8\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

To find the eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, we have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}-4{x}_{3}=0 \\ 3{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}-3{x}_{3}=0 \\ -4{x}_{1}+8{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$

So, we row-reduce the augmented matrix $M$ to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & -4 & 0 \\ 3 & 3 & -3 & 0 \\ -4 & 0 & 8 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 3 & 0 \\ -4 & 0 & 8 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+4{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns (the $1$st and the $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}=-{x}_{3}.$ From the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}=2{x}_{3}.$
Therefore, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}2{x}_{3} \\ -{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Setting, for instance, ${x}_{3}=1,$ we get the following eigenvector:

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b \\ c\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

a

b
−2
c

det(A−λI)=0|−4−λ0−43−3−λ−3−402−λ|=0(−3−λ)|−4−λ−4−42−λ|=0(−3−λ)((−4−λ)(2−λ)−(−4)(−4))=0(−3−λ)(λ2+2λ−24)=0(λ+3)(λ+6)(λ−4)=0

Hence, λ1=4, λ2=−3, and λ3=−6. Since we obtained three distinct eigenvalues, the set of eigenvectors {v1,v2,v3}, where each vector corresponds to different eigenvalue, will be linearly independent.

Now, recall that v1 and v2 correspond to the eigenvalues λ1=4 and λ2=−3. Thus, the third eigenvector v3 must correspond to λ3=−6.

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation (A−λI)x=0.

In our case, we have λ=−6. So, we obtain

A−λI=[−40−43−3−3−402]−(−6)[100010001]=[20−433−3−408].

To find the eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, we have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations:

{2x1−4x3=03x1+3x2−3x3=0−4x1+8x3=0

So, we row-reduce the augmented matrix M to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

M=[20−4033−30−4080]R1:=12R1R2:=R2+(−3)R1∼[10−200330−4080]R3:=R3+4R1∼[10−2003300000].

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns (the 1st and the 2nd). Thus, x3 is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain x2=−x3. From the first equation, we get x1=2x3. Therefore, the general solution is [2x3−x3x3],x3∈R.

Setting, for instance, x3=1, we get the following eigenvector:

v=[abc]=[2−11]

Finally, ab=2−1=−2.

last_observation.worked_solution:
First, we find all the eigenvalues of $A$ by solving the characteristic equation $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}-4-\lambda  & 0 & -4 \\ 3 & -3-\lambda  & -3 \\ -4 & 0 & 2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-3-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}-4-\lambda  & -4 \\ -4 & 2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-3-\lambda )((-4-\lambda )(2-\lambda )-(-4)(-4)) & =0 \\ (-3-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}+2\lambda -24) & =0 \\ (\lambda +3)(\lambda +6)(\lambda -4) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, ${\lambda }_{1}=4,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-3,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=-6.$ Since we obtained three distinct eigenvalues, the set of eigenvectors $\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}\},$ where each vector corresponds to different eigenvalue, will be linearly independent.

Now, recall that ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ correspond to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=4$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-3.$ Thus, the third eigenvector ${v}_{3}$ must correspond to ${\lambda }_{3}=-6.$ 

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\lambda =-6.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 & -4 \\ 3 & -3 & -3 \\ -4 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]-(-6)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & -4 \\ 3 & 3 & -3 \\ -4 & 0 & 8\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

To find the eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, we have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}-4{x}_{3}=0 \\ 3{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}-3{x}_{3}=0 \\ -4{x}_{1}+8{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$

So, we row-reduce the augmented matrix $M$ to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & -4 & 0 \\ 3 & 3 & -3 & 0 \\ -4 & 0 & 8 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 3 & 0 \\ -4 & 0 & 8 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+4{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns (the $1$st and the $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}=-{x}_{3}.$ From the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}=2{x}_{3}.$
Therefore, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}2{x}_{3} \\ -{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Setting, for instance, ${x}_{3}=1,$ we get the following eigenvector:

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b \\ c\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, $\frac{a}{b}=\frac{2}{-1}=-2.$

$$

Hence, ${\lambda }_{1}=4,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-3,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=-6.$ Since we obtained three distinct eigenvalues, the set of eigenvectors $\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}\},$ where each vector corresponds to different eigenvalue, will be linearly independent.

Now, recall that ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ correspond to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=4$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-3.$ Thus, the third eigenvector ${v}_{3}$ must correspond to ${\lambda }_{3}=-6.$ 

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\lambda =-6.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 & -4 \\ 3 & -3 & -3 \\ -4 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]-(-6)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & -4 \\ 3 & 3 & -3 \\ -4 & 0 & 8\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}

question.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & -3 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]

Find the third eigenvector ${v}_{3}=[a,\,b,\,c]^{T}$ such that the set $\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}\}$ is linearly independent. What is the value of $\frac{a}{b}?$
question.worked_solution:
Since $A$ is an upper triangular matrix, we have that its eigenvalues are the entries in the main diagonal, that is, ${\lambda }_{1}=2,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-3$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=1.$ 

Also, since we obtained three distinct eigenvalues, the set of eigenvectors $\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}\},$ where each vector corresponds to different eigenvalue, will be linearly independent.

Now, recall that ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ correspond to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-3.$ Thus, the third eigenvector ${v}_{3}$ must correspond to ${\lambda }_{3}=1.$ 

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\lambda =1.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & -3 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]-1[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & -4 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

To find the eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, we have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3}=0 \\ -4{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=0 \\ 0=0\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the augmented matrix $M$ is already in its row echelon form:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & -4 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns (the $1$st and the $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}=\frac{1}{4}{x}_{3}.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =-{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3} \\  & =-\frac{1}{4}{x}_{3}+2{x}_{3} \\  & =\frac{7}{4}{x}_{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{7}{4}{x}_{3} \\ \frac{1}{4}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Setting, for instance, ${x}_{3}=4,$ we get the following eigenvector:

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b \\ c\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}7 \\ 1 \\ 4\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, $\frac{a}{b}=\frac{7}{1}=7.$

[\begin{aligned}\frac{7}{4}{x}_{3} \\ \frac{1}{4}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Setting, for instance, ${x}_{3}=4,$ we get the following eigenvector:

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b \\ c\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}7 \\ 1 \\ 4\end{aligned}]
$$

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation (A−λI)x=0.

In our case, we have λ=1. So, we obtain

A−λI=[21−20−31001]−1[100010001]=[11−20−41000].

To find the eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, we have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations:

{x1+x2−2x3=0−4x2+x3=00=0

Notice that the augmented matrix M is already in its row echelon form:

M=[11−200−4100000]

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns (the 1st and the 2nd). Thus, x3 is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain x2=14x3. Substituting this into the first equation, we get

x1=−x2+2x3=−14x3+2x3=74x3.

question.name: Question 15
question.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

The vectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ are eigenvectors that correspond to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2$ of the matrix $A,$ given above. Find the third eigenvector ${v}_{3}=[a,\,b,\,c]^{T}$ such that the set $\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}\}$ is linearly independent. What is the value of $\frac{a}{b}?$
question.worked_solution:
First, we find all the eigenvalues of $A$ by solving the characteristic equation $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}-1-\lambda  & 3 & 2 \\ 2 & 4-\lambda  & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}-1-\lambda  & 3 \\ 2 & 4-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )((-1-\lambda )(4-\lambda )-(3)(2)) & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-3\lambda -10) & =0 \\ -(\lambda -1)(\lambda +2)(\lambda -5) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, ${\lambda }_{1}=1,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=5.$ Since we obtained three distinct eigenvalues, the set of eigenvectors $\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}\},$ where each vector corresponds to different eigenvalue, will be linearly independent.

Now, recall that ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ correspond to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2.$ Thus, the third eigenvector ${v}_{3}$ must correspond to ${\lambda }_{3}=5.$ 

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\lambda =5.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]-5[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 & 2 \\ 2 & -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

To find the eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, we have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-6{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3}=0 \\ 2{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=0 \\ -4{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$

So, we row-reduce the augmented matrix $M$ to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{3}{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \frac{5}{3} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-\frac{12}{5}){R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \frac{5}{3} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns (the $1$st and the $3$rd). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain ${x}_{3}=0.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}=\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2}.$ Therefore, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting, for instance, ${x}_{2}=2,$ we get the following eigenvector:

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b \\ c\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, $\frac{a}{b}=\frac{1}{2}.$

last_observation.name: Question 15
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Eigenvectors of a 3x3 Matrix
last_observation.worked_solution:
First, we find all the eigenvalues of $A$ by solving the characteristic equation $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}-1-\lambda  & 3 & 2 \\ 2 & 4-\lambda  & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}-1-\lambda  & 3 \\ 2 & 4-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )((-1-\lambda )(4-\lambda )-(3)(2)) & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-3\lambda -10) & =0 \\ -(\lambda -1)(\lambda +2)(\lambda -5) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, ${\lambda }_{1}=1,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=5.$ Since we obtained three distinct eigenvalues, the set of eigenvectors $\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}\},$ where each vector corresponds to different eigenvalue, will be linearly independent.

Now, recall that ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ correspond to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2.$ Thus, the third eigenvector ${v}_{3}$ must correspond to ${\lambda }_{3}=5.$ 

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\lambda =5.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]-5[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 & 2 \\ 2 & -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

To find the eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, we have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-6{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3}=0 \\ 2{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=0 \\ -4{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$

So, we row-reduce the augmented matrix $M$ to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{3}{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \frac{5}{3} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-\frac{12}{5}){R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \frac{5}{3} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns (the $1$st and the $3$rd). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain ${x}_{3}=0.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}=\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2}.$ Therefore, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting, for instance, ${x}_{2}=2,$ we get the following eigenvector:

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b \\ c\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, $\frac{a}{b}=\frac{1}{2}.$

question.html:
Question 15
?

A=[−132241001] The vectors v1 and v2 are eigenvectors that correspond to the eigenvalues λ1=1 and λ2=−2 of the matrix A, given above. Find the third eigenvector v3=[a,b,c]T such that the set {v1,v2,v3} is linearly independent. What is the value of ab?

a
12
b
1
c
4
d
0
e
2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we find all the eigenvalues of A by solving the characteristic equation det(A−λI)=0:

det(A−λI)=0|−1−λ3224−λ1001−λ|=0(1−λ)|−1−λ324−λ|=0(1−λ)((−1−λ)(4−λ)−(3)(2))=0(1−λ)(λ2−3λ−10)=0−(λ−1)(λ+2)(λ−5)=0

Hence, λ1=1, λ2=−2, and λ3=5. Since we obtained three distinct eigenvalues, the set of eigenvectors {v1,v2,v3}, where each vector corresponds to different eigenvalue, will be linearly independent.

Now, recall that v1 and v2 correspond to the eigenvalues λ1=1 and λ2=−2. Thus, the third eigenvector v3 must correspond to λ3=5.

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation (A−λI)x=0.

In our case, we have λ=5. So, we obtain

A−λI=[−132241001]−5[100010001]=[−6322−1100−4].

To find the eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, we have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations:

{−6x1+3x2+2x3=02x1−x2+x3=0−4x3=0

So, we row-reduce the augmented matrix M to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

M=[−63202−1100040]R2:=R2+13R1∼[−6320005300040]R3:=R3+(−125)R2∼[−6320005300000]

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns (the 1st and the 3rd). Thus, x2 is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain x3=0. Substituting this into the first equation, we get x1=12x2. Therefore, the general solution is [12x2x20],x2∈R.

Setting, for instance, x2=2, we get the following eigenvector:

v=[abc]=[120]

Finally, ab=12.

solution.reasoning: The trace of A is 4, so the remaining eigenvalue is 4-1-(-2)=5. Since all three eigenvalues are distinct, the third independent eigenvector must correspond to 5. Solving (A-5I)v_3=0 gives c=0 and -6a+3b=0, hence b=2a. A nonzero eigenvector has b≠0, so a/b=1/2, option a. The supplied worked solution concerns a different example; Math Academy's current answer key is not captured.

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: Theresa pours out $\frac{7}{8}$ of the contents of an $8$-cup jug of orange juice for her family's breakfast. How many cups of orange juice did Theresa pour from the jug?
questions.worked_solution:
To find out how many cups of orange juice Theresa poured from the jug, we need to multiply $8$ by $\frac{7}{8}.$ 

To multiply a fraction by a whole number, we multiply the fraction's numerator by the whole number and keep the denominator the same:

$$
\frac{7}{8}\times 8=\frac{7\times 8}{8}=\frac{56}{8}
$$

Finally, we simplify:

$$
\frac{56}{8}=56÷8=7
$$

So, Theresa poured $7$ cups of orange juice from the jug.

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem: Ted made pizzas for his soccer buddies. He put $\frac{1}{4}\,\text{lb}$ of cheese on each pizza. If he made $8$ pizzas, how many pounds of cheese did he use in total?
questions.worked_solution:
To find out how much cheese Ted used, we need to multiply $\frac{1}{4}$ by $8.$

To multiply a fraction by a whole number, we multiply the fraction's numerator by the whole number and keep the denominator the same:

$$
8\times \frac{1}{4}=\frac{8\times 1}{4}=\frac{8}{4}
$$

Finally, we simplify:

$$
\frac{8}{4}=8÷4=2
$$

So, Ted used $2\,\text{lb}$ of cheese to make the pizzas.

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem: A wooden slat is $3\,\text{ft}$ long. Eddie needs to cut a piece that's $\frac{5}{8}$ the length of the slat. How long is the piece he has to cut?
questions.worked_solution:
To find the length of the piece that Eddie has to cut, we have to multiply $3$ by $\frac{5}{8}.$  

To multiply a fraction by a whole number, we multiply the fraction's numerator by the whole number and keep the denominator the same:

$$
\frac{5}{8}\times 3=\frac{5\times 3}{8}=\frac{15}{8}
$$

Finally, we then convert $\frac{15}{8}$ to a mixed number:

$$
15÷8=1\,\text{R}\,7=1\,\frac{7}{8}.
$$

So, Eddie has to cut a piece $1\,\frac{7}{8}\,\text{ft}$ long.

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem: An electrician takes a $4$-meter-long electrical cable from which he has to cut a piece that is $\frac{5}{6}$ of its length. How long will that piece be?
questions.worked_solution:
To find out the length of the piece to be cut, we need to multiply $4$ by $\frac{5}{6}.$  

To multiply a fraction by a whole number, we multiply the fraction's numerator by the whole number and keep the denominator the same:

$$
\frac{5}{6}\times 4=\frac{5\times 4}{6}=\frac{20}{6}
$$

We then reduce this fraction to its lowest terms:

$$
\frac{20}{6}=\frac{20÷2}{6÷2}=\frac{10}{3}.
$$

 

Finally, we then convert $\frac{10}{3}$ to a mixed number:

$$
10÷3=3\,\text{R}\,1=3\,\frac{1}{3}.
$$

So, the piece will be $3\,\frac{1}{3}\,\text{m}$ long.

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem: Sandra is reading a book. She can read $\frac{3}{4}$ of a page in one minute. Compute how many pages she can read in $10$ minutes. Between what two whole numbers does your answer lie?
questions.worked_solution:
To find out how many pages she can read in $10$ minutes, we need to multiply $\frac{3}{4}$ by $10.$

To multiply a fraction by a whole number, we multiply the fraction's numerator by the whole number and keep the denominator the same:

$$
10\times \frac{3}{4}=\frac{10\times 3}{4}=\frac{30}{4}
$$

We then reduce this fraction to its lowest terms:

$$
\frac{30}{4}=\frac{30÷2}{4÷2}=\frac{15}{2}.
$$

Finally, we then convert $\frac{15}{2}$ to a mixed number:

$$
15÷2=7\,\text{R}\,1=7\,\frac{1}{2}.
$$

So, in $10$ minutes, Sandra can read a total of $7\,\frac{1}{2}$ pages of the book, which lies between $7$ and $8$ pages.

questions.name: Question 6
questions.problem: George rides his bike $\frac{9}{10}$ of a mile each day, going from home to school and back. Compute how many miles he rides in $5$ days just by going to school and back. Between what two whole numbers does your answer lie?
questions.worked_solution:
To find out how many kilometers George travels in $5$ days just by going to school and back, we have to multiply $\frac{9}{10}$ by $5.$

To multiply a fraction by a whole number, we multiply the fraction's numerator by the whole number and keep the denominator the same:

$$
5\times \frac{9}{10}=\frac{5\times 9}{10}=\frac{45}{10}
$$

We then reduce this fraction to its lowest terms:

$$
\frac{45}{10}=\frac{45÷5}{10÷5}=\frac{9}{2}.
$$

Finally, we then convert $\frac{9}{2}$ to a mixed number:

$$
9÷2=4\,\text{R}\,1=4\,\frac{1}{2}.
$$

So, in $5$ days, George rides a total of $4\,\frac{1}{2}\,\text{mi},$ which lies between $4$ and $5$ miles.

canonical_examples.problem: Larry filled his water bottle with $12\, \mathrm{oz}$ of drinking water. If he drank $\dfrac34$ of the bottle's contents after exercising, how much water did Larry drink?
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To find out how much water Larry drank, we need to multiply $12$ by $\dfrac{3}{4}.$

To multiply a fraction by a whole number, we multiply the fraction's numerator by the whole number and keep the denominator the same:

$$
\dfrac34 \times 12 = \dfrac{3\times 12}{4} = \dfrac{36}4
$$

Finally, we simplify:

$$
\dfrac{36}{4} = 36 \div 4=9
$$

So, Larry drank $9\,\textrm{oz}$ of water.

To find out the height of the pile of boxes, we have to multiply $\dfrac{3}{4}$ by $5.$

5 \times \dfrac34 = \dfrac{5\times 3}{4} = \dfrac{15}{4}
$$

Finally, we then convert $\dfrac {15}{4}$ to a mixed number:

$$
15 \div 4 = 3\,\textrm{R}\,3 = 3\,\dfrac{3}{4}
$$

So, Greg's stack of boxes was $3\,\dfrac{3}{4}\,\textrm{ft}$ high.

canonical_examples.problem: Mr. Stewart spends $\dfrac56$ hours watching an episode of his favorite TV show. If $5$ episodes are played every week, find the total time he spends watching the show every week. Between what two whole numbers does your answer lie?
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To find out how long Mr. Stewart watches the show each week, we need to multiply $\dfrac{5}{6}$ by $5.$ 

To multiply a fraction by a whole number, we multiply the fraction's numerator by the whole number and keep the denominator the same:

$$
5\times\dfrac56 = \dfrac{5\times 5}{6} = \dfrac{25}6
$$

Finally, we then convert $\dfrac {25}{6}$ to a mixed number:

$$
25 \div 6 = 4\,\textrm{R}\,1 = 4\,\dfrac{1}{6}
$$

So, Mr. Stewart spends a total of  $4\,\dfrac{1}{6}$ hours watching the show, which lies between $4$ and $5$ hours.

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
In this lesson, we'll consider real-life situations where we have to multiply fractions by whole numbers.

Suppose that Justin, a chef, has $8$ large tins of tomatoes. If each tin of tomatoes weighs $\dfrac{5}{4}\,\textrm{lb},$ how many pounds of tomatoes does Justin have in total?

To find out the total weight of tomatoes, we need to multiply $\dfrac{5}{4}\,\textrm{lb}$ by $8.$  

To multiply a fraction by a whole number, we multiply the fraction's numerator by the whole number and keep the denominator the same:

$$
8 \times \dfrac54= \dfrac{8\times 5}{4} = \dfrac{40}4
$$

We can simplify this fraction by interpreting the fraction as a division:

$$
\dfrac{40}{4} =  40 \div 4 = 10
$$

So, in total, Justin has $10\,\textrm{lb}$ of tomatoes.

Question 3
?

A wooden slat is 3ft long. Eddie needs to cut a piece that's 58 the length of the slat. How long is the piece he has to cut?

a
218ft
b
358ft
c
178ft
d
338ft
e
138ft
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To find the length of the piece that Eddie has to cut, we have to multiply 3 by 58.

To multiply a fraction by a whole number, we multiply the fraction's numerator by the whole number and keep the denominator the same:

58×3=5×38=158

Finally, we then convert 158 to a mixed number: 15÷8=1R7=178.

So, Eddie has to cut a piece 178ft long.

question.html:
Question 5
?

Sandra is reading a book. She can read 34 of a page in one minute. Compute how many pages she can read in 10 minutes. Between what two whole numbers does your answer lie?

a
Between 7 and 8 pages
b
Between 6 and 7 pages
c
Between 8 and 9 pages
d
Between 4 and 5 pages
e
Between 3 and 4 pages
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To find out how many pages she can read in 10 minutes, we need to multiply 34 by 10.

To multiply a fraction by a whole number, we multiply the fraction's numerator by the whole number and keep the denominator the same:

10×34=10×34=304

We then reduce this fraction to its lowest terms: 304=30÷24÷2=152.

Finally, we then convert 152 to a mixed number: 15÷2=7R1=712.

So, in 10 minutes, Sandra can read a total of 712 pages of the book, which lies between 7 and 8 pages.

$$
5\times \frac{9}{10}=\frac{5\times 9}{10}=\frac{45}{10}
$$

We then reduce this fraction to its lowest terms:

$$
\frac{45}{10}=\frac{45÷5}{10÷5}=\frac{9}{2}.
$$

Finally, we then convert $\frac{9}{2}$ to a mixed number:

$$
9÷2=4\,\text{R}\,1=4\,\frac{1}{2}.
$$

So, in $5$ days, George rides a total of $4\,\frac{1}{2}\,\text{mi},$ which lies between $4$ and $5$ miles.

question.html:
Question 1
?

Theresa pours out 78 of the contents of an 8-cup jug of orange juice for her family's breakfast. How many cups of orange juice did Theresa pour from the jug?

a
6 cups
b
7 cups
c
87 cups
d
4 cups
e
5 cups
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To find out how many cups of orange juice Theresa poured from the jug, we need to multiply 8 by 78.

To multiply a fraction by a whole number, we multiply the fraction's numerator by the whole number and keep the denominator the same:

78×8=7×88=568

Finally, we simplify:

568=56÷8=7

So, Theresa poured 7 cups of orange juice from the jug.

question.name: Question 2
question.problem: Ted made pizzas for his soccer buddies. He put $\frac{1}{4}\,\text{lb}$ of cheese on each pizza. If he made $8$ pizzas, how many pounds of cheese did he use in total?
question.worked_solution:
To find out how much cheese Ted used, we need to multiply $\frac{1}{4}$ by $8.$

To multiply a fraction by a whole number, we multiply the fraction's numerator by the whole number and keep the denominator the same:

$$
8\times \frac{1}{4}=\frac{8\times 1}{4}=\frac{8}{4}
$$

Finally, we simplify:

$$
\frac{8}{4}=8÷4=2
$$

So, Ted used $2\,\text{lb}$ of cheese to make the pizzas.

question.problem: A wooden slat is $3\,\text{ft}$ long. Eddie needs to cut a piece that's $\frac{5}{8}$ the length of the slat. How long is the piece he has to cut?
question.worked_solution:
To find the length of the piece that Eddie has to cut, we have to multiply $3$ by $\frac{5}{8}.$  

To multiply a fraction by a whole number, we multiply the fraction's numerator by the whole number and keep the denominator the same:

$$
\frac{5}{8}\times 3=\frac{5\times 3}{8}=\frac{15}{8}
$$

Finally, we then convert $\frac{15}{8}$ to a mixed number:

$$
15÷8=1\,\text{R}\,7=1\,\frac{7}{8}.
$$

So, Eddie has to cut a piece $1\,\frac{7}{8}\,\text{ft}$ long.

last_observation.worked_solution:
To find the length of the piece that Eddie has to cut, we have to multiply $3$ by $\frac{5}{8}.$  

To multiply a fraction by a whole number, we multiply the fraction's numerator by the whole number and keep the denominator the same:

$$
\frac{5}{8}\times 3=\frac{5\times 3}{8}=\frac{15}{8}
$$

Finally, we then convert $\frac{15}{8}$ to a mixed number:

$$
15÷8=1\,\text{R}\,7=1\,\frac{7}{8}.
$$

So, Eddie has to cut a piece $1\,\frac{7}{8}\,\text{ft}$ long.

question.html:
Question 3
?

A wooden slat is 3ft long. Eddie needs to cut a piece that's 58 the length of the slat. How long is the piece he has to cut?

a
218ft
b
358ft
c
178ft
d
338ft
e
138ft
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To find the length of the piece that Eddie has to cut, we have to multiply 3 by 58.

To multiply a fraction by a whole number, we multiply the fraction's numerator by the whole number and keep the denominator the same:

58×3=5×38=158

Finally, we then convert 158 to a mixed number: 15÷8=1R7=178.

So, Eddie has to cut a piece 178ft long.

Question 3
?

A wooden slat is 3ft long. Eddie needs to cut a piece that's 58 the length of the slat. How long is the piece he has to cut?

a
218ft
b
358ft
c
178ft
d
338ft
e
138ft
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To find the length of the piece that Eddie has to cut, we have to multiply 3 by 58.

To multiply a fraction by a whole number, we multiply the fraction's numerator by the whole number and keep the denominator the same:

58×3=5×38=158

Finally, we then convert 158 to a mixed number: 15÷8=1R7=178.

So, Eddie has to cut a piece 178ft long.

question.name: Question 4
question.problem: An electrician takes a $4$-meter-long electrical cable from which he has to cut a piece that is $\frac{5}{6}$ of its length. How long will that piece be?
question.worked_solution:
To find out the length of the piece to be cut, we need to multiply $4$ by $\frac{5}{6}.$  

To multiply a fraction by a whole number, we multiply the fraction's numerator by the whole number and keep the denominator the same:

$$
\frac{5}{6}\times 4=\frac{5\times 4}{6}=\frac{20}{6}
$$

We then reduce this fraction to its lowest terms:

$$
\frac{20}{6}=\frac{20÷2}{6÷2}=\frac{10}{3}.
$$

 

Finally, we then convert $\frac{10}{3}$ to a mixed number:

$$
10÷3=3\,\text{R}\,1=3\,\frac{1}{3}.
$$

So, the piece will be $3\,\frac{1}{3}\,\text{m}$ long.

question.html:
Question 4
?

An electrician takes a 4-meter-long electrical cable from which he has to cut a piece that is 56 of its length. How long will that piece be?

a
312m
b
112m
c
113m
d
213m
e
313m
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To find out the length of the piece to be cut, we need to multiply 4 by 56.

To multiply a fraction by a whole number, we multiply the fraction's numerator by the whole number and keep the denominator the same:

56×4=5×46=206

We then reduce this fraction to its lowest terms: 206=20÷26÷2=103.

Finally, we then convert 103 to a mixed number: 10÷3=3R1=313.

So, the piece will be 313m long.

last_observation.name: Question 4
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Multiplying a Fraction by a Whole Number: Result Is a Mixed Number
last_observation.worked_solution:
To find out the length of the piece to be cut, we need to multiply $4$ by $\frac{5}{6}.$  

To multiply a fraction by a whole number, we multiply the fraction's numerator by the whole number and keep the denominator the same:

$$
\frac{5}{6}\times 4=\frac{5\times 4}{6}=\frac{20}{6}
$$

We then reduce this fraction to its lowest terms:

$$
\frac{20}{6}=\frac{20÷2}{6÷2}=\frac{10}{3}.
$$

 

Finally, we then convert $\frac{10}{3}$ to a mixed number:

$$
10÷3=3\,\text{R}\,1=3\,\frac{1}{3}.
$$

So, the piece will be $3\,\frac{1}{3}\,\text{m}$ long.

question.html:
Question 4
?

An electrician takes a 4-meter-long electrical cable from which he has to cut a piece that is 56 of its length. How long will that piece be?

a
312m
b
112m
c
113m
d
213m
e
313m
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To find out the length of the piece to be cut, we need to multiply 4 by 56.

To multiply a fraction by a whole number, we multiply the fraction's numerator by the whole number and keep the denominator the same:

56×4=5×46=206

We then reduce this fraction to its lowest terms: 206=20÷26÷2=103.

Finally, we then convert 103 to a mixed number: 10÷3=3R1=313.

So, the piece will be 313m long.

Question 4
?

An electrician takes a 4-meter-long electrical cable from which he has to cut a piece that is 56 of its length. How long will that piece be?

a
312m
b
112m
c
113m
d
213m
e
313m
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To find out the length of the piece to be cut, we need to multiply 4 by 56.

To multiply a fraction by a whole number, we multiply the fraction's numerator by the whole number and keep the denominator the same:

56×4=5×46=206

We then reduce this fraction to its lowest terms: 206=20÷26÷2=103.

Finally, we then convert 103 to a mixed number: 10÷3=3R1=313.

So, the piece will be 313m long.

question.name: Question 5
question.problem: Sandra is reading a book. She can read $\frac{3}{4}$ of a page in one minute. Compute how many pages she can read in $10$ minutes. Between what two whole numbers does your answer lie?
question.worked_solution:
To find out how many pages she can read in $10$ minutes, we need to multiply $\frac{3}{4}$ by $10.$

To multiply a fraction by a whole number, we multiply the fraction's numerator by the whole number and keep the denominator the same:

$$
10\times \frac{3}{4}=\frac{10\times 3}{4}=\frac{30}{4}
$$

We then reduce this fraction to its lowest terms:

$$
\frac{30}{4}=\frac{30÷2}{4÷2}=\frac{15}{2}.
$$

Finally, we then convert $\frac{15}{2}$ to a mixed number:

$$
15÷2=7\,\text{R}\,1=7\,\frac{1}{2}.
$$

So, in $10$ minutes, Sandra can read a total of $7\,\frac{1}{2}$ pages of the book, which lies between $7$ and $8$ pages.

question.html:
Question 5
?

Sandra is reading a book. She can read 34 of a page in one minute. Compute how many pages she can read in 10 minutes. Between what two whole numbers does your answer lie?

a
Between 7 and 8 pages
b
Between 6 and 7 pages
c
Between 8 and 9 pages
d
Between 4 and 5 pages
e
Between 3 and 4 pages
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To find out how many pages she can read in 10 minutes, we need to multiply 34 by 10.

To multiply a fraction by a whole number, we multiply the fraction's numerator by the whole number and keep the denominator the same:

10×34=10×34=304

We then reduce this fraction to its lowest terms: 304=30÷24÷2=152.

Finally, we then convert 152 to a mixed number: 15÷2=7R1=712.

So, in 10 minutes, Sandra can read a total of 712 pages of the book, which lies between 7 and 8 pages.

question.html:
Question 5
?

Sandra is reading a book. She can read 34 of a page in one minute. Compute how many pages she can read in 10 minutes. Between what two whole numbers does your answer lie?

a
Between 7 and 8 pages
b
Between 6 and 7 pages
c
Between 8 and 9 pages
d
Between 4 and 5 pages
e
Between 3 and 4 pages
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To find out how many pages she can read in 10 minutes, we need to multiply 34 by 10.

To multiply a fraction by a whole number, we multiply the fraction's numerator by the whole number and keep the denominator the same:

10×34=10×34=304

We then reduce this fraction to its lowest terms: 304=30÷24÷2=152.

Finally, we then convert 152 to a mixed number: 15÷2=7R1=712.

So, in 10 minutes, Sandra can read a total of 712 pages of the book, which lies between 7 and 8 pages.

question.name: Question 6
question.problem: George rides his bike $\frac{9}{10}$ of a mile each day, going from home to school and back. Compute how many miles he rides in $5$ days just by going to school and back. Between what two whole numbers does your answer lie?
question.worked_solution:
To find out how many kilometers George travels in $5$ days just by going to school and back, we have to multiply $\frac{9}{10}$ by $5.$

To multiply a fraction by a whole number, we multiply the fraction's numerator by the whole number and keep the denominator the same:

$$
5\times \frac{9}{10}=\frac{5\times 9}{10}=\frac{45}{10}
$$

We then reduce this fraction to its lowest terms:

$$
\frac{45}{10}=\frac{45÷5}{10÷5}=\frac{9}{2}.
$$

Finally, we then convert $\frac{9}{2}$ to a mixed number:

$$
9÷2=4\,\text{R}\,1=4\,\frac{1}{2}.
$$

So, in $5$ days, George rides a total of $4\,\frac{1}{2}\,\text{mi},$ which lies between $4$ and $5$ miles.

Question 6
?

George rides his bike 910 of a mile each day, going from home to school and back. Compute how many miles he rides in 5 days just by going to school and back. Between what two whole numbers does your answer lie?

a
Between 4 and 5 miles
b
Between 2 and 3 miles
c
Between 3 and 4 miles
d
Between 1 and 2 miles
e
Between 5 and 6 miles
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To find out how many kilometers George travels in 5 days just by going to school and back, we have to multiply 910 by 5.

To multiply a fraction by a whole number, we multiply the fraction's numerator by the whole number and keep the denominator the same:

5×910=5×910=4510

We then reduce this fraction to its lowest terms: 4510=45÷510÷5=92.

Finally, we then convert 92 to a mixed number: 9÷2=4R1=412.

So, in 5 days, George rides a total of 412mi, which lies between 4 and 5 miles.

To find out how many kilometers George travels in $5$ days just by going to school and back, we have to multiply $\frac{9}{10}$ by $5.$

To multiply a fraction by a whole number, we multiply the fraction's numerator by the whole number and keep the denominator the same:

$$
5\times \frac{9}{10}=\frac{5\times 9}{10}=\frac{45}{10}
$$

We then reduce this fraction to its lowest terms:

$$
\frac{45}{10}=\frac{45÷5}{10÷5}=\frac{9}{2}.
$$

Finally, we then convert $\frac{9}{2}$ to a mixed number:

$$
9÷2=4\,\text{R}\,1=4\,\frac{1}{2}.
$$

So, in $5$ days, George rides a total of $4\,\frac{1}{2}\,\text{mi},$ which lies between $4$ and $5$ miles.

question.html:
Question 6
?

George rides his bike 910 of a mile each day, going from home to school and back. Compute how many miles he rides in 5 days just by going to school and back. Between what two whole numbers does your answer lie?

a
Between 4 and 5 miles
b
Between 2 and 3 miles
c
Between 3 and 4 miles
d
Between 1 and 2 miles
e
Between 5 and 6 miles
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To find out how many kilometers George travels in 5 days just by going to school and back, we have to multiply 910 by 5.

To multiply a fraction by a whole number, we multiply the fraction's numerator by the whole number and keep the denominator the same:

5×910=5×910=4510

We then reduce this fraction to its lowest terms: 4510=45÷510÷5=92.

Finally, we then convert 92 to a mixed number: 9÷2=4R1=412.

So, in 5 days, George rides a total of 412mi, which lies between 4 and 5 miles.
question.knowledge_point: Determining Whole Number Bounds of a Multiplication Problem

solution.reasoning: The daily round trip is already included in the stated distance. In 5 days George rides 5\times\frac{9}{10}=\frac{45}{10}=4\frac{1}{2} miles, which lies between 4 and 5 miles, matching choice a. No Math Academy answer or grade for this question is captured; the worked example concerns a different problem.

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
Consider the boundary value problem

$$
{y}^{″}+4y=f(x)
$$

on $[-3,3]$, where $f$ is $6$-periodic and odd. Which Fourier-series form is appropriate for a particular solution ${y}_{p}?$

$\,$
${y}_{p}(x)=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
Because $f$ is $6$-periodic on $[-3,3]$, we have $L=3$, so Fourier series on this interval use the basis 

$$
cos\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3})\,\text{and}\,sin\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3}).
$$

Next, since $f$ is odd, its Fourier series contains only sine terms. For a second-order equation with no ${y}^{′}$ (damping) term, the particular solution inherits this property and is also an odd function.

Therefore, the appropriate form for ${y}_{p}$ is a sine series:

$$
{y}_{p}(x)={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3})
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem:
Consider the boundary value problem

$$
{y}^{″}+\frac{1}{2}\,y=f(x)
$$

on $[-2,2]$, where $f$ is $4$-periodic and even. Which Fourier-series form is appropriate for a particular solution ${y}_{p}?$

$\,$
${y}_{p}(x)=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
Because $f$ is $4$-periodic on $[-2,2]$, we have $L=2$, so Fourier series on this interval use the basis

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2})\,\text{and}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}).
$$

Next, since $f$ is even, its Fourier series contains only cosine terms. For a second-order equation with no ${y}^{′}$ (damping) term, the particular solution inherits this property and is also an even function.

Therefore, the appropriate form for ${y}_{p}$ is a cosine series:

$$
{y}_{p}(x)={\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2})
$$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem:
Consider the boundary value problem

$$
{y}^{″}+\frac{1}{2}\,y=f(x)
$$

on $[-5,5]$, where $f$ is $10$-periodic and odd. Which Fourier-series form is appropriate for a particular solution ${y}_{p}?$

$\,$
${y}_{p}(x)=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
Because $f$ is $10$-periodic on $[-5,5]$, we have $L=5$, so Fourier series on this interval use the basis 

$$
cos\,(\frac{n\pi x}{5})\,\text{and}\,sin\,(\frac{n\pi x}{5}).
$$

Next, since $f$ is odd, its Fourier series contains only sine terms. For a second-order equation with no ${y}^{′}$ (damping) term, the particular solution inherits this property and is also an odd function.

Therefore, the appropriate form for ${y}_{p}$ is a sine series:

$$
{y}_{p}(x)={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{5})
$$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem:
Consider the boundary value problem

$$
{y}^{″}+2y=f(x)
$$

on $[-4,4]$, where $f$ is $8$-periodic and even. Which Fourier-series form is appropriate for a particular solution ${y}_{p}?$

$\,$
${y}_{p}(x)=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
Because $f$ is $8$-periodic on $[-4,4]$, we have $L=4$, so Fourier series on this interval use the basis

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{4})\,\text{and}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{4}).
$$

Next, since $f$ is even, its Fourier series contains only cosine terms. For a second-order equation with no ${y}^{′}$ (damping) term, the particular solution inherits this property and is also an even function.

Therefore, the appropriate form for ${y}_{p}$ is a cosine series:

$$
{y}_{p}(x)={\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{4})
$$

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem:
Consider the boundary value problem

$$
{y}^{″}+7y=f(x)
$$

on $[-5,5]$, where $f$ is $10$-periodic and even. Which Fourier-series form is appropriate for a particular solution ${y}_{p}?$

$\,$
${y}_{p}(x)=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
Because $f$ is $10$-periodic on $[-5,5]$, we have $L=5$, so Fourier series on this interval use the basis

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{5})\,\text{and}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{5}).
$$

Next, since $f$ is even, its Fourier series contains only cosine terms. For a second-order equation with no ${y}^{′}$ (damping) term, the particular solution inherits this property and is also an even function.

Therefore, the appropriate form for ${y}_{p}$ is a cosine series:

$$
{y}_{p}(x)={\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{5})
$$

questions.name: Question 6
questions.problem:
Consider the boundary value problem

$$
{y}^{″}+10y=f(x),\,{y}^{′}(0)=0,\,{y}^{′}(1)=6
$$

where $f(x)$ is $4$-periodic and odd. Select the missing part in the solution of the BVP, where the infinite sum on the right-hand side below represents a particular solution ${y}_{p}$ of the differential equation.

*Hint: In this specific problem, the forcing function $f(x)$ is chosen such that the particular solution ${y}_{p}$ satisfies ${y}_{p}^{′}(0)=0$ and ${y}_{p}^{′}(1)=0.$*

$$
y(x)∼{{field-1}}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}sin\,(\frac{n\pi x}{2}).
$$
questions.worked_solution:
We write the solution as $y={y}_{c}+{y}_{p}$, where ${y}_{c}$ solves the homogeneous equation and ${y}_{p}$ is a particular solution.

First, solve the homogeneous equation ${y}^{″}+10y=0.$ Its general solution is

$$
{y}_{c}(x)=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{10}x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{10}x).
$$

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
{y}^{′}(x)=-A\sqrt{10}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{10}x)+B\sqrt{10}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{10}x)+{y}_{p}^{′}(x).
$$

Now, we use the hint. Since ${y}_{p}^{′}(0)=0$ and ${y}_{p}^{′}(1)=0$, we have

$$
{y}^{′}(0)={y}_{c}^{′}(0)\,\text{and}\,{y}^{′}(1)={y}_{c}^{′}(1).
$$

Next, we apply the boundary conditions. 

- Use ${y}^{′}(0)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(0) & =0+B\sqrt{10}(1)+{y}_{p}^{′}(0) \\ 0 & =B\sqrt{10}+0 \\ B & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, ${y}_{c}(x)=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{10}x).$

- Use ${y}^{′}(1)=6$ with $B=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(1) & =-A\sqrt{10}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{10})+{y}_{p}^{′}(1) \\ 6 & =-A\sqrt{10}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{10})+0 \\ A & =-\frac{6}{\sqrt{10}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{10})}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
y(x)∼-\frac{6}{\sqrt{10}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{10})}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{10}x)+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}sin\,(\frac{n\pi x}{2}).
$$

questions.name: Question 7
questions.problem:
Consider the boundary value problem

$$
{y}^{″}+4y=f(x),\,y(0)=0,\,y(1)=3
$$

where $f(x)$ is $1$-periodic and even. Select the missing part in the solution of the BVP, where the infinite sum on the right-hand side below represents a particular solution ${y}_{p}$ of the differential equation.

*Hint: In this specific problem, the forcing function $f(x)$ is chosen such that the particular solution ${y}_{p}$ satisfies ${y}_{p}(0)=0$ and ${y}_{p}(1)=0.$*

$$
y(x)∼{{field-1}}+{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2n\pi x).
$$
questions.worked_solution:
We write the solution as $y={y}_{c}+{y}_{p}$, where ${y}_{c}$ solves the homogeneous equation and ${y}_{p}$ is a particular solution.

First, solve the homogeneous equation ${y}^{″}+4y=0.$ Its general solution is

$$
{y}_{c}(x)=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x).
$$

Now, we use the hint. Since ${y}_{p}(0)=0$ and ${y}_{p}(1)=0$, we have

$$
y(0)={y}_{c}(0)\,\text{and}\,y(1)={y}_{c}(1).
$$

Next, we apply the boundary conditions.

- Use $y(0)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & =A\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)+{y}_{p}(0) \\ 0 & =A(1)+B(0)+0 \\ A & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, ${y}_{c}(x)=B\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x).$

- Use $y(1)=3$ with $A=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(1) & =B\operatorname{sin}⁡(2)+{y}_{p}(1) \\ 3 & =B\operatorname{sin}⁡(2)+0 \\ B & =\frac{3}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2)}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
y(x)∼\frac{3}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2)}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)+{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2n\pi x).
$$

questions.name: Question 8
questions.problem:
Consider the boundary value problem

$$
{y}^{″}+7y=f(x),\,{y}^{′}(0)=0,\,{y}^{′}(1)=4
$$

where $f(x)$ is $2$-periodic and odd. Select the missing part in the solution of the BVP, where the infinite sum on the right-hand side below represents a particular solution ${y}_{p}$ of the differential equation.

*Hint: In this specific problem, the forcing function $f(x)$ is chosen such that the particular solution ${y}_{p}$ satisfies ${y}_{p}^{′}(0)=0$ and ${y}_{p}^{′}(1)=0.$*

$$
y(x)∼{{field-1}}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x).
$$
questions.worked_solution:
We write the solution as $y={y}_{c}+{y}_{p}$, where ${y}_{c}$ solves the homogeneous equation and ${y}_{p}$ is a particular solution.

First, solve the homogeneous equation ${y}^{″}+7y=0.$ Its general solution is

$$
{y}_{c}(x)=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{7}x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{7}x).
$$

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
{y}^{′}(x)=-A\sqrt{7}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{7}x)+B\sqrt{7}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{7}x)+{y}_{p}^{′}(x).
$$

Now, we use the hint. Since ${y}_{p}^{′}(0)=0$ and ${y}_{p}^{′}(1)=0$, we have

$$
{y}^{′}(0)={y}_{c}^{′}(0)\,\text{and}\,{y}^{′}(1)={y}_{c}^{′}(1).
$$

Next, we apply the boundary conditions. 

- Use ${y}^{′}(0)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(0) & =0+B\sqrt{7}(1)+{y}_{p}^{′}(0) \\ 0 & =B\sqrt{7}+0 \\ B & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, ${y}_{c}(x)=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{7}x).$

- Use ${y}^{′}(1)=4$ with $B=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(1) & =-A\sqrt{7}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{7})+{y}_{p}^{′}(1) \\ 4 & =-A\sqrt{7}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{7})+0 \\ A & =-\frac{4}{\sqrt{7}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{7})}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
y(x)∼-\frac{4}{\sqrt{7}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{7})}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{7}x)+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x).
$$

questions.name: Question 9
questions.problem:
Consider the boundary value problem

$$
{y}^{″}+5y=f(x),\,{y}^{′}(0)=0,\,{y}^{′}(1)=4
$$

where $f(x)$ is $2$-periodic and even. Select the missing part in the solution of the BVP, where the infinite sum on the right-hand side below represents a particular solution ${y}_{p}$ of the differential equation.

*Hint: In this specific problem, the forcing function $f(x)$ is chosen such that the particular solution ${y}_{p}$ satisfies ${y}_{p}^{′}(0)=0$ and ${y}_{p}^{′}(1)=0.$*

$$
y(x)∼{{field-1}}+{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x).
$$
questions.worked_solution:
We write the solution as $y={y}_{c}+{y}_{p}$, where ${y}_{c}$ solves the homogeneous equation and ${y}_{p}$ is a particular solution.

First, solve the homogeneous equation ${y}^{″}+5y=0.$ Its general solution is

$$
{y}_{c}(x)=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{5}x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{5}x).
$$

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
{y}^{′}(x)=-A\sqrt{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{5}x)+B\sqrt{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{5}x)+{y}_{p}^{′}(x).
$$

Now, we use the hint. Since ${y}_{p}^{′}(0)=0$ and ${y}_{p}^{′}(1)=0$, we have

$$
{y}^{′}(0)={y}_{c}^{′}(0)\,\text{and}\,{y}^{′}(1)={y}_{c}^{′}(1).
$$

Next, we apply the boundary conditions. 

- Use ${y}^{′}(0)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(0) & =0+B\sqrt{5}(1)+{y}_{p}^{′}(0) \\ 0 & =B\sqrt{5}+0 \\ B & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, ${y}_{c}(x)=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{5}x).$

- Use ${y}^{′}(1)=4$ with $B=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(1) & =-A\sqrt{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{5})+{y}_{p}^{′}(1) \\ 4 & =-A\sqrt{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{5})+0 \\ A & =-\frac{4}{\sqrt{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{5})}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
y(x)∼-\frac{4}{\sqrt{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{5})}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{5}x)+{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x).
$$

questions.name: Question 10
questions.problem:
Consider the boundary value problem

$$
{y}^{″}+5y=f(x),\,{y}^{′}(0)=0,\,{y}^{′}(1)=2
$$

where $f(x)$ is $1$-periodic and odd. Select the missing part in the solution of the BVP, where the infinite sum on the right-hand side below represents a particular solution ${y}_{p}$ of the differential equation.

*Hint: In this specific problem, the forcing function $f(x)$ is chosen such that the particular solution ${y}_{p}$ satisfies ${y}_{p}^{′}(0)=0$ and ${y}_{p}^{′}(1)=0.$*

$$
y(x)∼{{field-1}}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2n\pi x).
$$
questions.worked_solution:
We write the solution as $y={y}_{c}+{y}_{p}$, where ${y}_{c}$ solves the homogeneous equation and ${y}_{p}$ is a particular solution.

First, solve the homogeneous equation ${y}^{″}+5y=0.$ Its general solution is

$$
{y}_{c}(x)=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{5}x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{5}x).
$$

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
{y}^{′}(x)=-A\sqrt{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{5}x)+B\sqrt{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{5}x)+{y}_{p}^{′}(x).
$$

Now, we use the hint. Since ${y}_{p}^{′}(0)=0$ and ${y}_{p}^{′}(1)=0$, we have

$$
{y}^{′}(0)={y}_{c}^{′}(0)\,\text{and}\,{y}^{′}(1)={y}_{c}^{′}(1).
$$

Next, we apply the boundary conditions. 

- Use ${y}^{′}(0)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(0) & =0+B\sqrt{5}(1)+{y}_{p}^{′}(0) \\ 0 & =B\sqrt{5}+0 \\ B & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, ${y}_{c}(x)=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{5}x).$

- Use ${y}^{′}(1)=2$ with $B=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(1) & =-A\sqrt{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{5})+{y}_{p}^{′}(1) \\ 2 & =-A\sqrt{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{5})+0 \\ A & =-\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{5})}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
y(x)∼-\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{5})}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{5}x)+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2n\pi x).
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Identifying the Form of the Fourier Series For the Solution
canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the boundary value problem

$$
y''+8y=f(x)
$$

on $[-3,3]$, where $f$ is $6$-periodic and even. What Fourier-series form is appropriate for a particular solution $y_p?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Because $f$ is $6$-periodic on $[-3,3]$, we have $L=3$, so Fourier series on this interval use the basis

$$
\cos\left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{3}\right)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\sin\left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{3}\right).
$$

Next, since $f$ is even, its Fourier series contains only cosine terms. For a second-order equation with no $y'$ (damping) term, the particular solution inherits this property and is also an even function.

Therefore, the appropriate form for $y_p$ is a cosine series:

$$
y_p(x)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} a_n\cos\left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{3}\right)
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Solving BVPs Using Fourier Series
canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the boundary value problem

$$
y''+2y=f(x), \qquad y'(0)=0,\quad y'(1)=-5
$$

where $f(x)$ is $2$-periodic and even. Fill in the missing part in the solution of the BVP, where the infinite sum on the right-hand side below represents a particular solution $y_p$ of the differential equation.

*Hint: In this specific problem, the forcing function $f(x)$ is chosen such that the particular solution $y_p$ satisfies $y_p'(0) = 0$ and $y_p'(1) = 0.$*
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14152880/assets/50bc50685896c736abcf63fd30cee09ac314c98714ed91251e568d714611c5ec.svg)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We write the solution as $y=y_c+y_p$, where $y_c$ solves the homogeneous equation and $y_p$ is a particular solution.

First, solve the homogeneous equation $y''+2y=0.$ Its general solution is

$$
y_c(x)=A\cos(\sqrt{2}x)+B\sin(\sqrt{2}x).
$$

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
y'(x)=-A\sqrt{2}\sin(\sqrt{2}x)+B\sqrt{2}\cos(\sqrt{2}x)+y_p'(x).
$$

Now, we use the hint. Since $y_p'(0)=0$ and $y_p'(1)=0$, we have

$$
y'(0)=y_c'(0)\qquad\text{and}\qquad y'(1)=y_c'(1).
$$

Next, we apply the boundary conditions.

- Use $y'(0)=0{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(0) & =0+B\sqrt{2}(1)+{y}_{p}^{′}(0) \\ 0 & =B\sqrt{2}+0 \\ B & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, $y_c(x)=A\cos(\sqrt{2}x).$

- Use $y'(1)=-5$ with $B=0{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(1) & =-A\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2})+{y}_{p}^{′}(1) \\ -5 & =-A\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2})+0 \\ A & =\frac{5}{\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2})}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
y(x)\sim \bbox[4pt, border: solid 0.5pt gray]{\dfrac{5}{\sqrt{2}\sin(\sqrt{2})}\cos(\sqrt{2}x)}
+\sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n\cos(n\pi x).
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
In this topic, we will use Fourier series to solve boundary value problems with periodic forcing functions.

As before, we consider a second-order linear differential equation with constant coefficients and forcing function $f(x)$, for which the general solution can be written as

$$
y=y_c+y_p,
$$

where $y_c$ solves the homogeneous equation and $y_p$ is a particular solution.

The main ideas are similar to those of solving IVPs:

- we choose the correct form of the series for the particular solution $y_p$, and then

- use boundary conditions at the endpoints to determine the constants in the homogeneous part $y_c$ of the solution.

When $f(x)$ is periodic, we often look for $y_p$ as a Fourier series on a symmetric interval $[-L,L].$

Recall that for an equation of the form $y''+\omega^2 y=f(x)$ with no (damping) $y'$ term, the particular solution inherits the parity of $f(x)$:

- If $f$ is *even*, then its Fourier series contains only cosine terms.

- If $f$ is *odd*, then its Fourier series contains only sine terms.

For example, consider the boundary value problem

$$
y''+5y=f(x)
$$

on $[-2,2]$, where $f$ is $4$-periodic and odd. We want the appropriate Fourier series form for a particular solution $y_p$.

Because $f$ is $4$-periodic on $[-2,2]$, we have $L=2$, so the Fourier basis on this interval is

$$
\cos\left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{2}\right)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\sin\left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{2}\right).
$$

Next, since $f$ is odd, its Fourier series contains only sine terms. Since the equation has no $y'$ term, the particular solution inherits the same parity and is also odd.

Therefore, the appropriate form for $y_p$ is a sine series:

$$
y_p(x)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} b_n\sin\left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{2}\right).
$$

Let's see more examples.

tutorials.name: Using Boundary Conditions
tutorials.problem:
Recall that we are considering a second-order linear differential equation with constant coefficients and forcing function $f(x)$, for which the general solution can be written as

$$
y=y_c+y_p,
$$

where $y_c$ solves the homogeneous equation and $y_p$ is a particular solution.

There are many types of boundary conditions (including mixed or Robin-type conditions), but in this lesson, we will focus on the two simplest cases:

- *Dirichlet conditions* (values of $y$ are specified):

$$
y(a)=\alpha
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
y(b)=\beta
$$

- *Neumann conditions* (values of $y'$ are specified):

$$
y'(a)=\alpha
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
y'(b)=\beta
$$

A key simplification is possible if we choose our particular solution $y_p$ to satisfy the corresponding *homogeneous* boundary conditions. For any given $f(x),$ it is always possible to find such a $y_p$. 
This drastically simplifies the computations, as the boundary conditions then determine the constants in $y_c$ directly.

- *Dirichlet-type simplification:* If we choose the forcing so that

$$
y_p(a)=0
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
y_p(b)=0,
$$

then

$$
y(a)=y_c(a)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
y(b)=y_c(b),
$$

so we can solve for the constants in $y_c$ using only the homogeneous solution.

- *Neumann-type simplification:* If we choose the forcing so that

$$
y_p'(a)=0
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
y_p'(b)=0,
$$

then

$$
y'(a)=y_c'(a)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
y'(b)=y_c'(b),
$$

so the derivative conditions determine the constants in $y_c$ directly.

Let's see how this works in practice.

question.html:
Question 1
?
Consider the boundary value problem y″+4y=f(x) on [−3,3], where f is 6-periodic and odd. Which Fourier-series form is appropriate for a particular solution yp? yp(x)=
∑n=1∞bnsin⁡(nπx3)
∑n=0∞ancos⁡(nπx3)
∑n=1∞bnsin⁡(nπx3)
∑n=0∞bnsin⁡(nπx6)
∑n=1∞ancos⁡(nπx6)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Because f is 6-periodic on [−3,3], we have L=3, so Fourier series on this interval use the basis cos(nπx3)andsin(nπx3).

Next, since f is odd, its Fourier series contains only sine terms. For a second-order equation with no y′ (damping) term, the particular solution inherits this property and is also an odd function.

Therefore, the appropriate form for yp is a sine series: yp(x)=∑n=1∞bnsin⁡(nπx3)

observed_steps.name: Question 2
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Identifying the Form of the Fourier Series For the Solution
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Because $f$ is $4$-periodic on $[-2,2]$, we have $L=2$, so Fourier series on this interval use the basis

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2})\,\text{and}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}).
$$

Next, since $f$ is even, its Fourier series contains only cosine terms. For a second-order equation with no ${y}^{′}$ (damping) term, the particular solution inherits this property and is also an even function.

Therefore, the appropriate form for ${y}_{p}$ is a cosine series:

$$
{y}_{p}(x)={\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2})
$$

question.html:
Question 2
?
Consider the boundary value problem y″+12y=f(x) on [−2,2], where f is 4-periodic and even. Which Fourier-series form is appropriate for a particular solution yp? yp(x)=
∑n=1∞ancos⁡(nπx4)
∑n=1∞ancos⁡(nπx4)
∑n=0∞bnsin⁡(nπx4)
∑n=0∞ancos⁡(nπx2)
∑n=1∞bnsin⁡(nπx2)
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Because f is 4-periodic on [−2,2], we have L=2, so Fourier series on this interval use the basis cos⁡(nπx2)andsin⁡(nπx2).

Next, since f is even, its Fourier series contains only cosine terms. For a second-order equation with no y′ (damping) term, the particular solution inherits this property and is also an even function.

Therefore, the appropriate form for yp is a cosine series: yp(x)=∑n=0∞ancos⁡(nπx2)

observed_steps.worked_solution:
Because $f$ is $10$-periodic on $[-5,5]$, we have $L=5$, so Fourier series on this interval use the basis 

$$
cos\,(\frac{n\pi x}{5})\,\text{and}\,sin\,(\frac{n\pi x}{5}).
$$

Next, since $f$ is odd, its Fourier series contains only sine terms. For a second-order equation with no ${y}^{′}$ (damping) term, the particular solution inherits this property and is also an odd function.

Therefore, the appropriate form for ${y}_{p}$ is a sine series:

$$
{y}_{p}(x)={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{5})
$$

question.html:
Question 3
?
Consider the boundary value problem y″+12y=f(x) on [−5,5], where f is 10-periodic and odd. Which Fourier-series form is appropriate for a particular solution yp? yp(x)=
∑n=1∞bnsin⁡(nπx5)
∑n=0∞ancos⁡(nπx5)
∑n=1∞bnsin⁡(nπx5)
∑n=0∞bnsin⁡(nπx10)
∑n=1∞ancos⁡(nπx10)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Because f is 10-periodic on [−5,5], we have L=5, so Fourier series on this interval use the basis cos(nπx5)andsin(nπx5).

Next, since f is odd, its Fourier series contains only sine terms. For a second-order equation with no y′ (damping) term, the particular solution inherits this property and is also an odd function.

Therefore, the appropriate form for yp is a sine series: yp(x)=∑n=1∞bnsin⁡(nπx5)

observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Identifying the Form of the Fourier Series For the Solution
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Because $f$ is $8$-periodic on $[-4,4]$, we have $L=4$, so Fourier series on this interval use the basis

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{4})\,\text{and}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{4}).
$$

Next, since $f$ is even, its Fourier series contains only cosine terms. For a second-order equation with no ${y}^{′}$ (damping) term, the particular solution inherits this property and is also an even function.

Therefore, the appropriate form for ${y}_{p}$ is a cosine series:

$$
{y}_{p}(x)={\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{4})
$$

question.html:
Question 4
?
Consider the boundary value problem y″+2y=f(x) on [−4,4], where f is 8-periodic and even. Which Fourier-series form is appropriate for a particular solution yp? yp(x)=
∑n=1∞bnsin⁡(nπx4)
∑n=0∞ancos⁡(nπx4)
∑n=1∞bnsin⁡(nπx4)
∑n=0∞bnsin⁡(nπx8)
∑n=1∞ancos⁡(nπx8)
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Because f is 8-periodic on [−4,4], we have L=4, so Fourier series on this interval use the basis cos⁡(nπx4)andsin⁡(nπx4).

Next, since f is even, its Fourier series contains only cosine terms. For a second-order equation with no y′ (damping) term, the particular solution inherits this property and is also an even function.

Therefore, the appropriate form for yp is a cosine series: yp(x)=∑n=0∞ancos⁡(nπx4)

observed_steps.worked_solution:
Because $f$ is $10$-periodic on $[-5,5]$, we have $L=5$, so Fourier series on this interval use the basis

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{5})\,\text{and}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{5}).
$$

Next, since $f$ is even, its Fourier series contains only cosine terms. For a second-order equation with no ${y}^{′}$ (damping) term, the particular solution inherits this property and is also an even function.

Therefore, the appropriate form for ${y}_{p}$ is a cosine series:

$$
{y}_{p}(x)={\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{5})
$$

question.html:
Question 5
?
Consider the boundary value problem y″+7y=f(x) on [−5,5], where f is 10-periodic and even. Which Fourier-series form is appropriate for a particular solution yp? yp(x)=
∑n=0∞ancos⁡(nπx5)
∑n=0∞bnsin⁡(nπx10)
∑n=0∞ancos⁡(nπx5)
∑n=1∞bnsin⁡(nπx5)
∑n=1∞ancos⁡(nπx10)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Because f is 10-periodic on [−5,5], we have L=5, so Fourier series on this interval use the basis cos⁡(nπx5)andsin⁡(nπx5).

Next, since f is even, its Fourier series contains only cosine terms. For a second-order equation with no y′ (damping) term, the particular solution inherits this property and is also an even function.

Therefore, the appropriate form for yp is a cosine series: yp(x)=∑n=0∞ancos⁡(nπx5)

tutorial.name: Using Boundary Conditions
tutorial.problem:
Recall that we are considering a second-order linear differential equation with constant coefficients and forcing function $f(x)$, for which the general solution can be written as

$$
y=y_c+y_p,
$$

where $y_c$ solves the homogeneous equation and $y_p$ is a particular solution.

There are many types of boundary conditions (including mixed or Robin-type conditions), but in this lesson, we will focus on the two simplest cases:

- *Dirichlet conditions* (values of $y$ are specified):

$$
y(a)=\alpha
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
y(b)=\beta
$$

- *Neumann conditions* (values of $y'$ are specified):

$$
y'(a)=\alpha
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
y'(b)=\beta
$$

A key simplification is possible if we choose our particular solution $y_p$ to satisfy the corresponding *homogeneous* boundary conditions. For any given $f(x),$ it is always possible to find such a $y_p$. 
This drastically simplifies the computations, as the boundary conditions then determine the constants in $y_c$ directly.

- *Dirichlet-type simplification:* If we choose the forcing so that

$$
y_p(a)=0
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
y_p(b)=0,
$$

then

$$
y(a)=y_c(a)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
y(b)=y_c(b),
$$

so we can solve for the constants in $y_c$ using only the homogeneous solution.

- *Neumann-type simplification:* If we choose the forcing so that

$$
y_p'(a)=0
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
y_p'(b)=0,
$$

then

$$
y'(a)=y_c'(a)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
y'(b)=y_c'(b),
$$

so the derivative conditions determine the constants in $y_c$ directly.

Let's see how this works in practice.

observed_steps.worked_solution:
We write the solution as $y=y_c+y_p$, where $y_c$ solves the homogeneous equation and $y_p$ is a particular solution.

First, solve the homogeneous equation $y''+2y=0.$ Its general solution is

$$
y_c(x)=A\cos(\sqrt{2}x)+B\sin(\sqrt{2}x).
$$

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
y'(x)=-A\sqrt{2}\sin(\sqrt{2}x)+B\sqrt{2}\cos(\sqrt{2}x)+y_p'(x).
$$

Now, we use the hint. Since $y_p'(0)=0$ and $y_p'(1)=0$, we have

$$
y'(0)=y_c'(0)\qquad\text{and}\qquad y'(1)=y_c'(1).
$$

Next, we apply the boundary conditions.

- Use $y'(0)=0{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(0) & =0+B\sqrt{2}(1)+{y}_{p}^{′}(0) \\ 0 & =B\sqrt{2}+0 \\ B & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, $y_c(x)=A\cos(\sqrt{2}x).$

- Use $y'(1)=-5$ with $B=0{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(1) & =-A\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2})+{y}_{p}^{′}(1) \\ -5 & =-A\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2})+0 \\ A & =\frac{5}{\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2})}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
y(x)\sim \bbox[4pt, border: solid 0.5pt gray]{\dfrac{5}{\sqrt{2}\sin(\sqrt{2})}\cos(\sqrt{2}x)}
+\sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n\cos(n\pi x).
$$

question.problem:
Consider the boundary value problem

$$
y''+2y=f(x), \qquad y'(0)=0,\quad y'(1)=-5
$$

where $f(x)$ is $2$-periodic and even. Fill in the missing part in the solution of the BVP, where the infinite sum on the right-hand side below represents a particular solution $y_p$ of the differential equation.

*Hint: In this specific problem, the forcing function $f(x)$ is chosen such that the particular solution $y_p$ satisfies $y_p'(0) = 0$ and $y_p'(1) = 0.$*

y(x)∼-\frac{6}{\sqrt{10}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{10})}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{10}x)+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}sin\,(\frac{n\pi x}{2}).

question.html:
Question 6
?
Consider the boundary value problem y″+10y=f(x),y′(0)=0,y′(1)=6 where f(x) is 4-periodic and odd. Select the missing part in the solution of the BVP, where the infinite sum on the right-hand side below represents a particular solution yp of the differential equation.

Hint: In this specific problem, the forcing function f(x) is chosen such that the particular solution yp satisfies yp′(0)=0 and yp′(1)=0.

−610sin⁡(10)cos⁡(10x)
−610sin⁡(10)cos⁡(10x)
610sin⁡(10)cos⁡(10x)
610sin⁡(10)sin⁡(10x)
−610cos⁡(10)cos⁡(10x)
y(x)∼{(−610sin⁡(10)cos⁡(10x))(S0)}+∑n=1∞bnsin(nπx2).
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We write the solution as y=yc+yp, where yc solves the homogeneous equation and yp is a particular solution.

First, solve the homogeneous equation y″+10y=0. Its general solution is yc(x)=Acos⁡(10x)+Bsin⁡(10x).

Computing the derivative, we get y′(x)=−A10sin⁡(10x)+B10cos⁡(10x)+yp′(x).

Now, we use the hint. Since yp′(0)=0 and yp′(1)=0, we have y′(0)=yc′(0)andy′(1)=yc′(1).

Next, we apply the boundary conditions.

  • Use y′(0)=0: y′(0)=0+B10(1)+yp′(0)0=B10+0B=0 So, yc(x)=Acos⁡(10x).

  • Use y′(1)=6 with B=0: y′(1)=−A10sin⁡(10)+yp′(1)6=−A10sin⁡(10)+0A=−610sin⁡(10)

Therefore, the solution is y(x)∼−610sin⁡(10)cos⁡(10x)+∑n=1∞bnsin(nπx2).
question.knowledge_point: Solving BVPs Using Fourier Series

observed_steps.name: Question 7
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Solving BVPs Using Fourier Series
observed_steps.worked_solution:
We write the solution as $y={y}_{c}+{y}_{p}$, where ${y}_{c}$ solves the homogeneous equation and ${y}_{p}$ is a particular solution.

First, solve the homogeneous equation ${y}^{″}+4y=0.$ Its general solution is

$$
{y}_{c}(x)=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x).
$$

Now, we use the hint. Since ${y}_{p}(0)=0$ and ${y}_{p}(1)=0$, we have

$$
y(0)={y}_{c}(0)\,\text{and}\,y(1)={y}_{c}(1).
$$

Next, we apply the boundary conditions.

- Use $y(0)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & =A\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)+{y}_{p}(0) \\ 0 & =A(1)+B(0)+0 \\ A & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, ${y}_{c}(x)=B\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x).$

- Use $y(1)=3$ with $A=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(1) & =B\operatorname{sin}⁡(2)+{y}_{p}(1) \\ 3 & =B\operatorname{sin}⁡(2)+0 \\ B & =\frac{3}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2)}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
y(x)∼\frac{3}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2)}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)+{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2n\pi x).
$$

question.name: Question 7
question.problem:
Consider the boundary value problem

$$
{y}^{″}+4y=f(x),\,y(0)=0,\,y(1)=3
$$

where $f(x)$ is $1$-periodic and even. Select the missing part in the solution of the BVP, where the infinite sum on the right-hand side below represents a particular solution ${y}_{p}$ of the differential equation.

*Hint: In this specific problem, the forcing function $f(x)$ is chosen such that the particular solution ${y}_{p}$ satisfies ${y}_{p}(0)=0$ and ${y}_{p}(1)=0.$*

$$
y(x)∼{{field-1}}+{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2n\pi x).
$$
question.worked_solution:
We write the solution as $y={y}_{c}+{y}_{p}$, where ${y}_{c}$ solves the homogeneous equation and ${y}_{p}$ is a particular solution.

First, solve the homogeneous equation ${y}^{″}+4y=0.$ Its general solution is

$$
{y}_{c}(x)=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x).
$$

Now, we use the hint. Since ${y}_{p}(0)=0$ and ${y}_{p}(1)=0$, we have

$$
y(0)={y}_{c}(0)\,\text{and}\,y(1)={y}_{c}(1).
$$

Next, we apply the boundary conditions.

- Use $y(0)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & =A\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)+{y}_{p}(0) \\ 0 & =A(1)+B(0)+0 \\ A & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, ${y}_{c}(x)=B\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x).$

- Use $y(1)=3$ with $A=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(1) & =B\operatorname{sin}⁡(2)+{y}_{p}(1) \\ 3 & =B\operatorname{sin}⁡(2)+0 \\ B & =\frac{3}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2)}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
y(x)∼\frac{3}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2)}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)+{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2n\pi x).
$$

Question 7
?
Consider the boundary value problem y″+4y=f(x),y(0)=0,y(1)=3 where f(x) is 1-periodic and even. Select the missing part in the solution of the BVP, where the infinite sum on the right-hand side below represents a particular solution yp of the differential equation.

Hint: In this specific problem, the forcing function f(x) is chosen such that the particular solution yp satisfies yp(0)=0 and yp(1)=0.

3sin⁡(2)sin⁡(2πx)
3sin⁡(2)sin⁡(2πx)
3cos⁡(2)cos⁡(2πx)
3sin⁡(2)sin⁡(2x)
3cos⁡(2)cos⁡(2x)
y(x)∼{(3sin⁡(2)sin⁡(2πx))(S0)}+∑n=0∞ancos⁡(2nπx).
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We write the solution as y=yc+yp, where yc solves the homogeneous equation and yp is a particular solution.

First, solve the homogeneous equation y″+4y=0. Its general solution is yc(x)=Acos⁡(2x)+Bsin⁡(2x).

Now, we use the hint. Since yp(0)=0 and yp(1)=0, we have y(0)=yc(0)andy(1)=yc(1).

Next, we apply the boundary conditions.

  • Use y(0)=0: y(0)=Acos⁡(0)+Bsin⁡(0)+yp(0)0=A(1)+B(0)+0A=0 So, yc(x)=Bsin⁡(2x).

  • Use y(1)=3 with A=0: y(1)=Bsin⁡(2)+yp(1)3=Bsin⁡(2)+0B=3sin⁡(2)

Therefore, the solution is y(x)∼3sin⁡(2)sin⁡(2x)+∑n=0∞ancos⁡(2nπx).

observed_steps.worked_solution:
We write the solution as $y={y}_{c}+{y}_{p}$, where ${y}_{c}$ solves the homogeneous equation and ${y}_{p}$ is a particular solution.

First, solve the homogeneous equation ${y}^{″}+7y=0.$ Its general solution is

$$
{y}_{c}(x)=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{7}x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{7}x).
$$

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
{y}^{′}(x)=-A\sqrt{7}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{7}x)+B\sqrt{7}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{7}x)+{y}_{p}^{′}(x).
$$

Now, we use the hint. Since ${y}_{p}^{′}(0)=0$ and ${y}_{p}^{′}(1)=0$, we have

$$
{y}^{′}(0)={y}_{c}^{′}(0)\,\text{and}\,{y}^{′}(1)={y}_{c}^{′}(1).
$$

Next, we apply the boundary conditions. 

- Use ${y}^{′}(0)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(0) & =0+B\sqrt{7}(1)+{y}_{p}^{′}(0) \\ 0 & =B\sqrt{7}+0 \\ B & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, ${y}_{c}(x)=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{7}x).$

- Use ${y}^{′}(1)=4$ with $B=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(1) & =-A\sqrt{7}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{7})+{y}_{p}^{′}(1) \\ 4 & =-A\sqrt{7}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{7})+0 \\ A & =-\frac{4}{\sqrt{7}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{7})}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
y(x)∼-\frac{4}{\sqrt{7}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{7})}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{7}x)+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x).
$$

question.name: Question 8
question.problem:
Consider the boundary value problem

$$
{y}^{″}+7y=f(x),\,{y}^{′}(0)=0,\,{y}^{′}(1)=4
$$

where $f(x)$ is $2$-periodic and odd. Select the missing part in the solution of the BVP, where the infinite sum on the right-hand side below represents a particular solution ${y}_{p}$ of the differential equation.

*Hint: In this specific problem, the forcing function $f(x)$ is chosen such that the particular solution ${y}_{p}$ satisfies ${y}_{p}^{′}(0)=0$ and ${y}_{p}^{′}(1)=0.$*

$$
y(x)∼{{field-1}}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x).
$$
question.worked_solution:
We write the solution as $y={y}_{c}+{y}_{p}$, where ${y}_{c}$ solves the homogeneous equation and ${y}_{p}$ is a particular solution.

First, solve the homogeneous equation ${y}^{″}+7y=0.$ Its general solution is

$$
{y}_{c}(x)=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{7}x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{7}x).
$$

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
{y}^{′}(x)=-A\sqrt{7}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{7}x)+B\sqrt{7}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{7}x)+{y}_{p}^{′}(x).
$$

Now, we use the hint. Since ${y}_{p}^{′}(0)=0$ and ${y}_{p}^{′}(1)=0$, we have

$$
{y}^{′}(0)={y}_{c}^{′}(0)\,\text{and}\,{y}^{′}(1)={y}_{c}^{′}(1).
$$

Next, we apply the boundary conditions. 

- Use ${y}^{′}(0)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(0) & =0+B\sqrt{7}(1)+{y}_{p}^{′}(0) \\ 0 & =B\sqrt{7}+0 \\ B & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, ${y}_{c}(x)=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{7}x).$

- Use ${y}^{′}(1)=4$ with $B=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(1) & =-A\sqrt{7}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{7})+{y}_{p}^{′}(1) \\ 4 & =-A\sqrt{7}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{7})+0 \\ A & =-\frac{4}{\sqrt{7}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{7})}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
y(x)∼-\frac{4}{\sqrt{7}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{7})}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{7}x)+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x).
$$
